context: Ms. Watkins uses a folk saying circulating at Enron to characterize the one-sided economic structure of the Raptor transactions, showing employees understood the fundamental unfairness.

label: Raptor transactions treated as common knowledge but legitimate
original_label: Raptor transactions treated as common knowledge but legitimate
quote: My understanding as an accountant is that a company could never use its own stock to generate a gain or avoid a loss on its income statement. I continued to ask questions and seek answers, primarily from former co-workers in the global finance group, or in the business units that had hedged assets with Raptor. I never heard reassuring explanations. It was my understanding that the Raptor special purpose entities were owned by LJM, the partnership run by Mr. Fastow. For the most part, people seemed to think there was some accounting rule that was allowing this to be acceptable. It was very common knowledge. It wasn't hidden.
context: Ms. Watkins describes how the fundamental accounting violation became accepted across multiple business units and the global finance group through shared belief that some rule permitted it.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Deal approval sheets embedded Skilling's authority over LJM transactions
original_label: Deal approval sheets embedded Skilling's authority over LJM transactions
quote: It was Enron's very strict policy, when completing transactions and deals, to have deal approval sheets, and there was never a name put on the approval block that was not required. And I don't ever remember an instance where signatures were not obtained for every person listed. So that if Mr. Skilling's name consistently appears on the sheets, but it remains unsigned, it was not because he was not obligated to sign it. It was because he just didn't sign it. That is correct. Were those procedures that Mr. Skilling would have understood? Yes.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that the formal deal approval procedure embedded Skilling's required authorization for LJM transactions, and his appearing on sheets without signing was intentional non-compliance with institutional procedure.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: LJM partnership embedded CFO's personal financial interest in deals
original_label: LJM partnership embedded CFO's personal financial interest in deals
quote: Unlike them, our witness this morning was privy to substantially more evidence of the accounting practices used to hide various related party transactions between Enron and what are known as the Raptor entities—special purpose entities owned by LJM2, the limited partnership set up and run by Enron and its former Chief Financial Officer Andrew Fastow. She will testify today that, in her opinion, these transactions were outright manipulations of Enron's income statements, booking fictitious income, and hiding actual losses.
context: Chairman Greenwood describes the structural arrangement where LJM2, run by the CFO, owned the Raptor entities that entered into transactions with Enron, embedding the conflict of interest into the formal corporate structure.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: White Wing sold assets continued to be managed by Enron
original_label: White Wing sold assets continued to be managed by Enron
quote: Now, after Enron sold Promigas to White Wing, who managed and operated that company? The Caribbean business unit. It stayed with the Caribbean business unit. And that was Enron? Yes, that is Enron. But it was not White Wing personnel that managed it. It was Enron personnel who managed it. In fact, the people involved in the day-to-day functioning of Promigas didn't even know they had been—that it had been sold, is that correct? That is correct.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that despite nominally selling Promigas to the SPE, Enron business unit employees continued managing the asset without knowing it had been sold, institutionalizing the fiction of a sale.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Funds flow from operations treatment built into SPE accounting
original_label: Funds flow from operations treatment built into SPE accounting
quote: And I think if it had been a consolidated special purpose entity, it would have been funds flow from borrowings. And those are two very different funds flow items, in terms of how an analyst would evaluate the company. So the SPE structure embedded a particular accounting treatment that made the transaction appear as operating cash flow rather than financing, which was institutionalized in how the structure was documented and approved.
context: Ms. Watkins explains how the off-balance-sheet structure embedded a particular funds-flow accounting treatment that misrepresented the nature of the transaction.

label: New employees onboarded into accepted Raptor hedging practice
original_label: New employees onboarded into accepted Raptor hedging practice
quote: As part of the sale analysis, I reviewed the estimated book values and market values of each asset. A number of assets were hedged with an entity called Raptor. While working for Mr. Fastow in 2001, I was charged with reviewing all assets that Enron considered for sale and determining the likely economic impact of sale. I was highly alarmed by the information I was receiving. In completing my work, certain Enron business units provided me with analyses that showed certain of the hedged losses that had been incurred by Raptor were actually coming back to Enron.
context: Ms. Watkins describes how she was assigned asset review work and business units routinely provided her analyses showing Raptor losses reverting to Enron, treating the practice as normal and established.

label: Skilling pressured McMahon on conflicts, then reassigned him
original_label: Skilling pressured McMahon on conflicts, then reassigned him
quote: Mr. McMahon told me he found the conflicts to be something that—you know, too great for Enron. He did not characterize it as a bonus discussion with me. He characterized it as more of an ultimatum that he was giving Mr. Skilling; Make these changes or I can't stay as Treasurer. And as I recall Mr. McMahon telling me, he felt like that was a strong statement to Mr. Skilling. And, you know, a few days or weeks later he gets a call saying—from Mr. Skilling that Mr. Skilling wanted him to go join a new venture, Enron Networks. And Mr. McMahon told me that he felt like Mr. Skilling was setting him up for a fall.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that when McMahon objected to the LJM conflicts, Skilling responded by reassigning him, effectively punishing his challenge and co-opting him away from oversight.

label: Fastow used strong-arm tactics to pressure banks into LJM investment
original_label: Fastow used strong-arm tactics to pressure banks into LJM investment
quote: I had heard from friends that worked at Chase and Credit Suisse and Bank of America that Mr. Fastow was almost somewhat threatening, that if you didn't invest in LJM, Enron would not use you as a banker or an investment banker again. That he was threatening the institutions, that to get Enron business they should invest in LJM. By the investors that are in LJM2, yes, it appeared to work.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that Fastow coerced outside financial institutions into becoming LJM investors by threatening to withdraw Enron's banking business, co-opting them through economic pressure.

label: Deal approval sheets did not disclose true economic substance
original_label: Deal approval sheets did not disclose true economic substance
quote: I was aware that these Raptor transactions had been presented to the Board, but I said my understanding of the way these things are generally presented, it is high level summaries, and I am not so certain that the true nature was fully disclosed. And he contended that I might be right, and by the end of the discussion, you know, he certainly said he would look into it and order an investigation
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that the Board received high-level summaries of Raptor transactions that obscured their true nature and economics, fragmenting Board knowledge.

label: Vinson & Elkins investigation limited in scope with caveats
original_label: Vinson & Elkins investigation limited in scope with caveats
quote: The caveat on the investigation was that they should not second-guess the accounting treatment. They would not do a detailed transaction analysis, and there would be no discovery-style investigation. Did you know that at this particular time or at some later time? I was not aware that the investigation was being limited. I met with Vinson & Elkins on September 10 for roughly 3 hours and had no indication that it was a limited investigation. I only discovered that it was limited when I read their October 15 response, which was not provided to me. I read it off of this committee's web page. It is fair to say that this, then, was not much of an investigation, was it?
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that Vinson & Elkins imposed narrow caveats on their investigation that prevented detailed analysis of accounting treatment and transaction structure, fragmenting the investigation's ability to surface problems.

label: Risk assessment document circulated only internally to finance and Fastow
original_label: Risk assessment document circulated only internally to finance and Fastow
quote: Well, the bullet point just says the corporation should consider hedging assets in Raptor to minimize, you know, some problems. And if Raptor is supposed to be Mr. Fastow's company, then it is Mr. Fastow's problem. Who would this be distributed to? I am not completely certain of that. I believe it might have gone as high as the Finance Committee of the Board, but from reading the Powers Report, they do not appear to have seen this analysis. It certainly went to Mr. Fastow, and I would imagine that it also went to Mr. Skilling. How about Vinson & Elkins? Would they probably receive this? Probably not. Arthur Andersen? Probably not.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that the risk assessment document identifying the fundamental illegality of Raptor was restricted to internal management and not shared with outside auditors or legal counsel, fragmenting knowledge.

label: Related party footnote wholly inadequate to disclose true nature of transactions
original_label: Related party footnote wholly inadequate to disclose true nature of transactions
quote: Someone reading through Enron's statements, would they have a perspective that those statements fairly represent the status of the company prior to the bankruptcy? I don't think so. I think that related party footnote is wholly inadequate in describing the transactions with Mr. Fastow's partnerships. The Raptor hedges were locking in, supposedly, sales value that Enron had on equity investments that it had made. I think that tended to make readers think that it was a $500 million gain offset by a $500 million loss. Therefore, zero impact on the income statement. However, without the Raptor transactions, Enron would have had a $500 million loss not covered by any gains running through the 2000 income statement.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that public financial statements' disclosure fragmented investors' knowledge by presenting a misleading net effect that obscured the underlying losses that should have been reported.

label: Business units hedging with Raptor but unaware of concentration of risk
original_label: Business units hedging with Raptor but unaware of concentration of risk
quote: The different business units that were hedging their assets with Raptor, as well as the global finance staff under Mr. Fastow. Okay. Mr. Dingell actually read a little bit from this one document which he placed in the record. And it said, Notwithstanding these bad cosmetics, Enron representatives uniformly stated that the Condor and Raptor vehicles were clever, useful vehicles that benefited Enron. So my question—if they are pledged 100 percent with Enron stock, and then they couldn't meet the hedges as the stock started to fall, therefore, they didn't benefit Enron, the employees, or the shareholders of Enron, did they?
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that business units using Raptor hedges did not understand that 100 percent of the risk was backed by Enron's own stock, fragmenting their knowledge of the true risk exposure.

label: Fastow wanted Watkins fired for raising concerns
original_label: Fastow wanted Watkins fired for raising concerns
quote: Well, Ms. Olson told me that she and Ken Lay were both highly alarmed by Mr. Fastow's reaction. He wanted to have me fired. He wanted to seize my computer. He wanted to have you fired? He told people he wanted to have you fired? That is what Ms. Olson told me. Okay. And he wanted your computer? Yes.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that when she raised concerns with Lay, Fastow responded by trying to have her fired and seize her computer, signaling that raising concerns would not be tolerated.

label: Risk officer refused to review concerns about Raptor
original_label: Risk officer refused to review concerns about Raptor
quote: The week leading up to my meeting with Mr. Lay, Mr. Buy was on vacation, and I actually phoned him. I was trying to use him as a sounding board as well. I told him a bit about my concerns and that I had a meeting scheduled with Mr. Lay. I asked him if I could fax him my materials to get his opinion. But did you tell him that, in fact, some of the materials had come from his own shop? No. But I just told him I had some memos that I wanted to fax him and have him look at. I told him I was very concerned about the Raptor transactions, that we had very large accounting issues, and that it was not appropriate to be backstopping these Raptor losses with Enron stock. He said he would rather not see it.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that the Chief Risk Officer explicitly declined to review her concerns about the Raptor transactions despite Raptor being central to his risk management responsibilities, signaling tolerance for non-engagement.

label: Skilling's departure suggested awareness of impending problems
original_label: Skilling's departure suggested awareness of impending problems
quote: In your opinion, why did Mr. Skilling then leave Enron on August 14, 2001? It is my opinion that he could foresee these problems, and he wanted to get as far away from it as possible.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies about Skilling's abrupt resignation, suggesting he possessed knowledge of the problems but chose to exit rather than confront them.

label: Lay parroted Causey's false statement to analysts about Raptor impact
original_label: Lay parroted Causey's false statement to analysts about Raptor impact
quote: An analyst asked the question, Okay. Enron has unwound these Raptor transactions. You have written off the transactions in the third quarter of 2001. If they had never existed at all, what would have been the income statement impact for the year 2000? And Mr. Causey responded that there would have been little or no impact, because we could have done these transactions elsewhere. Was that a true statement? I don't think so, and the Powers Report doesn't think so either. Did Mr. Lay have any comments on that point? Well, Mr. Lay parroted Mr. Causey word for word. And I felt like that was a statement he didn't necessarily know, and it was unwise to parrot the Chief Accounting Officer on that statement.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that Lay repeated a false statement about Raptor's impact on 2000 earnings made by Causey to analysts, endorsing the misrepresentation without scrutiny.

label: Only one executive praised Watkins for raising concerns
original_label: Only one executive praised Watkins for raising concerns
quote: Once you were identified as the author of the anonymous letter you first sent, did any of the executive offices of Enron, of the 50th floor up, ever contact you to discuss with you what you had written? Did anybody praise you for coming forward from the 50th floor? Was there a difference between the reaction of Enron employees below the 50th floor, as opposed to those in charge on the 50th floor and above? Well, the reaction from the employees that have been laid off has been just fantastic. They are very supportive. And then, I would say from 90 percent of the employees that are still there the reaction is also very positive. From the 50th floor, I have only had one person give me an atta girl so to speak, and that was Mr. Ray Bowen.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that senior leadership on the executive floors offered no praise or support for her raising concerns, with only one exception, signaling that such concern-raising was not culturally endorsed.

label: Baxter complained to Skilling but was ineffective
original_label: Baxter complained to Skilling but was ineffective
quote: My understanding is that Mr. Baxter complained that it was inappropriate for a company of our size, of our stature, to do transactions with the CFO's partnership. It is inappropriate. It didn't look good. We shouldn't be doing transactions with the CFO's partnership. From all the records and the presentations that I have reviewed, Mr. Skilling was supposed to be an integral part of the controls and the review process with the LJM transactions. Basically, it appeared that the Raptor transactions had been going on for a number of years. My understanding was that Mr. Skilling was fully aware of them. He is a very hands-on manager. I had also heard rumors that people as close to him as Mr. Baxter had complained to him, and he had done nothing.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that Baxter's complaints to Skilling about the inappropriateness of CFO partnerships were ignored, demonstrating leadership tolerance for the practice despite internal objections.

label: Causey instructed no written buyback agreements in order to maintain sale treatment
original_label: Causey instructed no written buyback agreements in order to maintain sale treatment
quote: As I recall, there were extensive conversations because Promigas was an important asset for the region. We were legally selling it to this White Wing structure. Legally, we were losing control of the asset, and there was a lot of discussion that we wanted it back, we drafted some documents that would be trigger points where the business unit could buy it back. My understanding was that Mr. Causey instructed our business unit that there could be nothing in writing that the business unit could buy it back, or Andersen would not let us have the sale treatment that we were getting in the funds flow statement.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that the Chief Accounting Officer instructed the business unit to destroy evidence of an informal buyback agreement so that Arthur Andersen would approve the sale treatment, demonstrating leadership direction to maintain a false accounting classification.

label: Lay took three months to order investigation after Watkins' initial warning
original_label: Lay took three months to order investigation after Watkins' initial warning
quote: On August 16, I met with Ms. Olson to show her a copy of the letter and discuss it with her. She encouraged me to meet with Mr. Lay personally. Since Mr. Lay was traveling through the rest of the week, she said the meeting would probably take place the week of August 20. I met with Mr. Lay on the afternoon of Wednesday, August 22, 2001. The meeting lasted just over one half hour. At the conclusion of the meeting, Mr. Lay assured me that he would look into my concerns. I met with the Special Committee the week before Christmas, but just to say that we needed to reschedule. They indicated that they were trying to look at evidence first before they conducted interviews.
context: Ms. Watkins' timeline shows that Lay took approximately four months from her initial concerns in August to having the Powers Committee (formed on October 31) begin interviews in December, indicating delayed response tolerance.

label: Vinson & Elkins cleared transactions despite being conflicted counsel
original_label: Vinson & Elkins cleared transactions despite being conflicted counsel
quote: Her initial meeting with Mr. Lay in August prompted an investigation by Vinson & Elkins, assisted by Andersen, the very two parties Ms. Watkins urged Mr. Lay and others not to include in the review because of clear conflicts of interest. Not surprisingly, the report that Vinson & Elkins issued on October 15 was so flawed that Ms. Watkins seriously considered leaving the company. The law firm's written report was issued just 1 day before Enron announced its equity write-down and earnings reductions based on the very Raptor transactions that Ms. Watkins brought to Kenneth Lay's attention.
context: Chairman Greenwood describes how Lay ignored Watkins' warning about conflicts of interest and hired the same firms involved in approving the transactions to investigate them, then their flawed report was issued the day before the restatement.

label: Culture discouraged negative news and rewarded silence
original_label: Culture discouraged negative news and rewarded silence
quote: It is never easy to be a whistleblower, particularly in a company where the mentality did not encourage negative news and negative views. Bearers of bad news are often punished. I was not comfortable confronting either Mr. Skilling or Mr. Fastow with my concerns. To do so I believed would have been a job terminating move. I did not want to do that without the safety net of a job in hand. I felt like it would be an immediate job terminating move. Frankly, I thought it would be fruitless, that nothing would happen.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies about the organizational culture where raising concerns about problems to senior leaders was understood to be career-threatening, discouraging disclosure.

label: Board received high-level summaries obscuring true nature of transactions
original_label: Board received high-level summaries obscuring true nature of transactions
quote: Mr. Lay was aware that these Raptor transactions had been presented to the Board, but I said my understanding of the way these things are generally presented, it is high level summaries, and I am not so certain that the true nature was fully disclosed. And he contended that I might be right, and by the end of the discussion, you know, he certainly said he would look into it and order an investigation, and asked me, you know, what could he do for me, which is when I requested the transfer out of Mr. Fastow's group.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that the Board received only high-level summaries of the Raptor transactions, suggesting leadership tolerated presentation practices that obscured the true nature of the transactions from Board oversight.

label: Enron paid well and stock performed, creating pressure not to rock boat
original_label: Enron paid well and stock performed, creating pressure not to rock boat
quote: Enron paid its people very well. The stock had been performing very well. I think there was a concern by most people that you didn't want to rock the boat. The culture in Enron was voted most innovative. It was voted one of the best places to work. It was the job to have in Houston. The atmosphere was electric. It was fun. You were surrounded by bright people, energized to change the world. You felt somewhat invincible. And, yes, people were arrogant, and it was did have a trader kind of mentality that was sometimes tough to live with. But it was always a fun place to work.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that compensation, stock performance, and the culture of innovation and success created strong incentives for employees to avoid raising concerns, reinforcing leadership tolerance for silence.

label: High retention bonuses paid to insiders while laid-off employees received minimal severance
original_label: High retention bonuses paid to insiders while laid-off employees received minimal severance
quote: Recently it was disclosed, maybe at Salon.com, the retention bonuses that were paid the week before the bankruptcy. Some of the amounts I find shocking for 90 days' retention, and I do not believe that it was in the best interest of creditors to—yes, we should retain certain people, but I don't think they needed to be paid, 3 and 4 times their base salary to stay for 90 days. I think it is an insult to the 4,000 people that were let go with $4,000 checks that there are a handful of people, more than a handful, that were paid $600,000, $1.5 million, $2 million, $450,000. Mean, gargantuan sums of money to agree to stay at Enron for 90 days. I am appalled by that list.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies about the extreme disparity between generous retention bonuses for insiders and minimal severance for laid-off employees, demonstrating leadership prioritization of insider protection.

label: Enron executives could have done Raptor transactions elsewhere
original_label: Enron executives could have done Raptor transactions elsewhere
quote: An analyst asked the question, Okay. Enron has unwound these Raptor transactions. You have written off the transactions in the third quarter of 2001. If they had never existed at all, what would have been the income statement impact for the year 2000? And Mr. Causey responded that there would have been little or no impact, because we could have done these transactions elsewhere.
context: Mr. Causey uses a collective rationalization that the problematic transactions were merely one possible approach among many alternatives, normalizing them as ordinary business practice.

label: Performance ranking system created pressure to meet earnings targets
original_label: Performance ranking system created pressure to meet earnings targets
quote: Everyone was very conscious of what they were contributing in the last 6 months. The performance ranking system judged you on what you contributed to the company in the last 6 months. No old tapes. In that sense, it was very competitive.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that the performance ranking system created intense quarterly pressure on all employees, escalating the pressure to meet targets and making concern-raising risky.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Raptor structure supposedly legitimate though off-balance-sheet with stock collateral
original_label: Raptor structure supposedly legitimate though off-balance-sheet with stock collateral
quote: The White Wing structure was set up such that if the assets that were sold to White Wing were not liquidated and were not sufficient to repay the investors in White Wing, then that structure was backstopped by Enron stock. It appears that some of these vehicles were used for financial statement manipulation. These vehicles have been schematically depicted in The Wall Street Journal and in the Houston Chronicle and a number of press. It supposedly is legitimate. I don't quite understand how these things can be off balance sheet when you have a claw back to the company and to the company's own stock, but somehow or other they appear to be available for use.
context: Ms. Watkins testifies that structures with 100 percent Enron stock collateral and a full claw-back to Enron were treated as legitimate and available for use despite appearing to violate fundamental accounting principles.

label: CEO explains culture shift from engineering to profit focus
original_label: CEO explains culture shift from engineering to profit focus
quote: When people say I changed the culture of Boeing, that was the intent, so it's run like a business rather than a great engineering firm. It is a great engineering firm, but people invest in a company because they want to make money.
context: Harry Stonecipher, former President and Chief Operating Officer of Boeing (as quoted in Chicago Tribune, February 29, 2004), stating publicly the intentional shift in corporate culture away from engineering excellence toward financial returns.

label: MCAS authority increases from initial 0.6 to 2.5 degrees
original_label: MCAS authority increases from initial 0.6 to 2.5 degrees
quote: As originally designed, MCAS was only capable of moving the horizontal stabilizer a maximum of 0.6 degrees. However, in March 2016, one year prior to the FAA's certification of the 737 MAX, when Boeing test pilots found the MAX was not handling well when nearing stalls at lower speeds, Boeing redesigned MCAS to enable it to activate at lower speeds. Moreover, the new version of MCAS was capable of moving the horizontal stabilizer a maximum of 2.5 degrees (as opposed to 0.6 degrees as originally designed). This was a significant technical change with dramatic operational implications.
context: The Committee documents how Boeing incrementally expanded MCAS capability between the initial design and final certification.

label: Plan to downplay MCAS as 'addition to Speed Trim'
original_label: Plan to downplay MCAS as 'addition to Speed Trim'
quote: In May 2013, a group of Boeing employees working on the 737 MAX met to address another concern: If we emphasize MCAS is a new function there may be greater certification and training impact, one Boeing employee wrote in a June 7, 2013, email summarizing the minutes of that meeting. They planned to, Treat [MCAS] as an addition to Speed Trim . . . Externally we would communicate it as an addition to Speed Trim. Internally continue using the acronym MCAS. They agreed to run the strategy by an Authorized Representative (AR) in Boeing's Autoflight group to ensure this strategy is acceptable. An AR, as described previously, is a Boeing employee authorized to conduct certification work on behalf of the FAA, and is supposed to work to uphold the interests of the FAA and the flying public, not the company's private commercial interests. The Boeing AR concurred with Boeing's plan regarding its description of MCAS.
context: Boeing employees documented in meeting minutes their strategy to reframe MCAS terminology to avoid regulatory scrutiny and training costs, which an authorized representative approved.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Cost redefined as rationale for not emphasizing MCAS
original_label: Cost redefined as rationale for not emphasizing MCAS
quote: Problem Statement: Every new buzzword represents a company and airline cost via changed manuals, changed training, changed maintenance manuals. Recommended Action: Investigate deletion of MCAS nomenclature and cover under the umbrella of 'revised speed trim'. This will allow us to maintain the MCAS nomenclature while not driving additional work due to training impacts and maintenance manual expansions.
context: Boeing's ITRACS database entry from May 2013 documenting the rationale for downplaying MCAS, reframing cost avoidance as a legitimate reason to redescribe a safety-critical system.

label: AR 'concurs' with plan to downplay MCAS
original_label: AR 'concurs' with plan to downplay MCAS
quote: The Boeing AR concurred with Boeing's plan regarding its description of MCAS. As stated in the summary of the meeting, This will allow us to maintain the MCAS nomenclature while not driving additional work due to training impacts and maintenance manual expansions.
context: An Authorized Representative—a Boeing employee delegated to represent FAA interests—approved Boeing's strategy to downplay MCAS, drawing him into the normalized practice of treating cost avoidance as a legitimate engineering decision.

label: MCAS redesign not communicated to all FAA offices
original_label: MCAS redesign not communicated to all FAA offices
quote: Most notably, the certification of MCAS illustrates how fragmented communications resulted in information gaps within the FAA concerning this critical system. These information gaps precluded key FAA employees from developing a full understanding of MCAS, its operational performance characteristics, and the safety risks it presented. Furthermore, Boeing failed to communicate fundamental information to all of the FAA offices that should have been aware of key data related to the certification of the 737 MAX. For example: Aircraft Evaluation Group (AEG) – The Seattle AEG was responsible for coordinating and managing proposed pilot training requirements on the 737 MAX. Boeing requested—and the AEG permitted—the removal of reference to MCAS from Boeing's Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM) at the time Boeing was re-designing the system to operate with greater authority. However, the AEG staff remained unaware of the MCAS re-design until after the crash of Lion Air flight 610.
context: The Committee describes how Boeing's redesign of MCAS in March 2016 was not disclosed to FAA offices responsible for pilot training, creating organizational compartmentalization of critical safety information.

label: MCAS authority expands to activate at lower speeds
original_label: MCAS authority expands to activate at lower speeds
quote: Initially, MCAS on the MAX was designed to activate only at higher speeds and in conditions not normally experienced in commercial flight. MCAS was only authorized to activate above a certain G-force and above a certain AOA. However, in March 2016, one year prior to the FAA's certification of the 737 MAX, when Boeing test pilots found the MAX was not handling well when nearing stalls at lower speeds, Boeing redesigned MCAS to enable it to activate at lower speeds.
context: The Committee documents the narrowing of operating envelope restrictions on MCAS between initial design and final certification, each step justified as a technical fix.

label: Countdown clock emphasizes schedule over thoroughness
original_label: Countdown clock emphasizes schedule over thoroughness
quote: To emphasize the significance of the 737 MAX program's schedule to Boeing employees, the Committee learned that senior program officials kept a countdown clock in their conference room. Keith Leverkuhn, the former Vice President and General Manager of the MAX program, described the clock as an excitement generator for Boeing's staff. But he also acknowledged it was to remind staff about the MAX's schedule. One of the mantras that we had was the value of a day, he said, and making sure that we were being prudent with our time, that we were being thorough, but yet, that there was a schedule that needed to be met.
context: Keith Leverkuhn, former 737 MAX Program Manager, explaining how senior leadership used a visible countdown clock to keep the team focused on schedule adherence, signaling that schedule was a primary organizational priority.

label: Chief Project Engineer rewarded after first flight for meeting schedule
original_label: Chief Project Engineer rewarded after first flight for meeting schedule
quote: The Committee has learned that to thank him for keeping to the MAX's production schedule, Boeing gave Michael Teal, the former Chief Project Engineer on the 737 MAX program, restricted stock options after the airplane's first flight in 2016 to show its appreciation for his work.
context: The Committee documents Boeing leadership's financial reward to the Chief Project Engineer specifically for keeping the 737 MAX program on schedule, incentivizing schedule adherence over thorough technical review.

label: Production pressures override safety concerns from plant supervisor
original_label: Production pressures override safety concerns from plant supervisor
quote: In June 2018, Ed Pierson, a senior Boeing plant supervisor at the company's Renton, Washington 737 MAX production factory, emailed Scott Campbell, the 737 General Manager, requesting a meeting about safety concerns. Mr. Pierson described multiple concerns about production and schedule pressures that were impacting quality control and safety issues. As a retired Naval Officer and former Squadron Commanding Officer, wrote Pierson, I know how dangerous even the smallest of defects can be to the safety of an airplane. Frankly right now all my internal warning bells are going off. And for the first time in my life, I'm sorry to say that I'm hesitant about putting my family on a Boeing airplane. In July 2018, five weeks after Mr. Pierson's email, he finally met with Mr. Campbell in Mr. Campbell's office. According to Mr. Pierson's testimony to the Committee, he told Mr. Campbell that in the military they would temporarily halt production if they had the kinds of safety problems that Mr. Pierson was seeing on the MAX factory floor. Mr. Campbell allegedly responded: The military is not a profit-making organization. Rather than heeding Mr. Pierson's dire warnings and thoroughly evaluating his safety concerns, Boeing continued to ramp up production on the 737 MAX.
context: Boeing leadership dismissed a senior supervisor's explicit safety concerns with a reference to profit motive, then continued production acceleration, demonstrating leadership tolerance for dismissing safety warnings in favor of schedule and revenue.

label: Level B training requirement becomes core design objective
original_label: Level B training requirement becomes core design objective
quote: One of the principal goals of the 737 MAX program was that it would require no greater than Level B differences training for pilots to transition from flying the 737 NG to flying the 737 MAX aircraft. On Saturday, May 4, 2013, several weeks before the MCAS strategy meeting referenced above, Michael Teal, the former Chief Project Engineer on the 737 MAX program, sent an email to senior chiefs and functional leaders on the MAX program and listed 14 open significant trade studies/risk issues. One of them specifically addressed the concern that MCAS could increase pilot training requirements: Differences Pilot Training: Ensuring that the level of change on the MAX keeps the Differences training to 16 hours or less of Level B training. Concerns include the impact of the resolution of 25.1322 trade and the Autopilot roll saturation change driven by the addition of MCAS to the flight controls system. In a transcribed interview with Committee staff, Mr. Teal acknowledged that obtaining Level B training on the 737 MAX was a design objective of the MAX program and that he had a role in ensuring that design objective was being met.

Rather, as indicated in the notes from the meeting that are depicted below, the effort needed to address the MCAS issue was described as an easy fix and that the problem itself posed no real requirement violation. Further, in reference to the concern about fail high AOA or fail high Mach resulting in MCAS motion—in other words, that a false reading of a high AOA or a false reading of high airspeed—meeting participants determined that other systems would be reacting to the failure and that there was [n]o need to redesign to address this issue.

original_label: Engineers dismiss faulty AOA concern as pilot training issue

label: Test data on pilot reaction time included in six coordination sheets over 3 years

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards

label: Level B training becomes 'design objective' engineers inherit
original_label: Level B training becomes 'design objective' engineers inherit

Early in the 737 MAX program, for instance, Boeing recognized that the addition of MCAS to the pilot's flight controls system posed a risk to qualifying for Level B (non-simulator) training. label: Boeing CEO argues MCAS did not require pilot knowledge
original_label: Boeing CEO argues MCAS did not require pilot knowledge

label: FAA test pilots knew of MCAS redesign but did not share across offices

ACO staff were aware of the MCAS re-design that occurred in 2016 because it affected tests that they participated in, but they failed to share information about the re-design of MCAS with other FAA offices.
context: The Committee documents how within the FAA, knowledge of MCAS redesign was compartmentalized: test pilots in the ACO knew of it but did not share it with other FAA offices responsible for pilot training and certification oversight, fragmenting organizational knowledge.

label: Delegation of MCAS certification reversed from retained to delegated
original_label: Delegation of MCAS certification reversed from retained to delegated

In November 2016, Boeing submitted the 737 Stabilizer System Description and Safety Analysis (SSA), revision F, to the FAA for acceptance. In December 2016, the FAA's response to Boeing was to accept the submittal and with notation delegated SSA approval to ODA.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards

original_label: Boeing accelerated production despite supervisor safety warnings

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology

label: MCAS described as just software in control law system
original_label: MCAS described as just software in control law system

original_label: Pilots characterized as part of the system redundancy

"So rightly or wrongly, that was the design criteria, and that's how they're being certified with the – the – the system and the pilot working together," he said.

label: Erroneous AOA treated as standard industry assumption
original_label: Erroneous AOA treated as standard industry assumption

Accordingly, we now know that there is a greater risk from unintended activation of MCAS due to erroneous AOA data than we originally thought.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Pilot trim competency assumptions proved optimistic
original_label: Pilot trim competency assumptions proved optimistic
quote: SSAs, such as those performed by Boeing for the MCAS, estimate the likelihood of a flightcrew's improper management of trim system anomalies. Prior to the two accidents, Boeing's estimate of this occurrence may have been reasonable, as judged from witnessing the events in simulation. However, after the two accidents, it appears that the estimate was optimistic.
context: TAB report acknowledging that Boeing's assessment of pilot capability to manage trim anomalies was systematically overestimated before accidents revealed actual pilot performance.

label: System requirements initially incomplete, later modified
original_label: System requirements initially incomplete, later modified
quote: The reviews of the software data package assumed that the system level requirements were complete and final. Upon a more detailed safety analysis, and design scrutiny, the system was modified to address some concerns.
context: TAB describing how software certification review was based on assumptions of completeness that later proved false when safety analysis revealed gaps.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Software development process embedded in formal procedures
original_label: Software development process embedded in formal procedures
quote: The software development process was modified to include Issue Paper (IP) item SW-8a. Effectively, this meant treating the design and verification using a model-based approach. The system requirements allocated to software were initially expressed using a system modelling language and supplied to Collins. Collins would use these models to add appropriate detail so chat code could be developed from them. They were classified as low-level requirements. The requirements processes were separated in two, with the system diagrams now managed by Boeing for both development and verification, and these were then handed to Collins for further refinement to low-level software requirements.
context: TAB report describing how MCAS software development was institutionalized through formal procedures and organizational divisions between Boeing and Collins Aerospace.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Design changes reclassified from remote to catastrophic failure
original_label: Design changes reclassified from remote to catastrophic failure
quote: Simulated CPU and memory failures demonstrated in the eCAB during BASOO certification activity were intended to address two very remote, but possible, postulated hardware failures in the FCC CPU and memory that resulted in nose-down stabilizer movement that was deemed to be unacceptable by the BASOO. Boeing in discussions with the BASOO has since reclassified the hardware failures as catastrophic failure conditions.
context: TAB report showing Boeing reclassifying hardware failure modes to justify design changes, shifting from treating them as remote possibilities to catastrophic conditions.

label: Procedural complexity rationalized through training
original_label: Procedural complexity rationalized through training
quote: The TAB concluded that with the enhanced training package, pilots will be able to successfully complete the separate IAS DISAGREE and AOA DISAGREE NNCs. This was also validated in the JOEB activity and supported by B737NG service history.
context: TAB accepting complex emergency procedures as manageable through training rather than simplifying procedures themselves, rationalizing design complexity.

label: Manual trim forces not evaluated in simulator
original_label: Manual trim forces not evaluated in simulator
quote: The TAB was unable to evaluate the manual control crank/hand wheel forces in the eCAB, since they were not representative of the aircraft. It is anticipated that the B737 MAX FFS will have manual trim crank/hand wheel forces that are satisfactory for training pilots to use manual trim. Consequently, the TAB asked Boeing to provide the manual trim wheel force information that they had gathered, which indicated forces in excess of 50 pounds in the normal and operational envelopes of the aircraft.
context: TAB report identifying critical gap where manual trim wheel forces could not be evaluated in the primary certification simulator, fragmenting safety assessment.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Fault tree probabilities developed inconsistently
original_label: Fault tree probabilities developed inconsistently
quote: Review of Boeing fault trees for the MCAS showed inconsistently developed event probabilities. Upon further discussion with Boeing, the TAB noted that Boeing was still making edits to the fault trees and that the analysis was submitted to the BASOO as a courtesy in draft form. The final version of the analysis will be submitted at a future date.
context: TAB identifying systematic inconsistency in how Boeing developed probabilistic safety analysis, treated as ongoing work rather than fundamental problem.

label: Pilot interactions assumed as correctly managed by training
original_label: Pilot interactions assumed as correctly managed by training
quote: Assumptions were made regarding 14 CFR 25.1302, in that: systems and installed equipment, individually, and in combination with other such systems and equipment, are designed so that qualified flightcrew members trained in their use can safely perform all of the tasks associated with the systems' and equipment's intended functions.
context: TAB report identifying shared regulatory assumption that training would enable pilots to safely manage any system, unchallenged before accidents.

label: Collins software requirements process separated from Boeing systems
original_label: Collins software requirements process separated from Boeing systems
quote: This resulted in new process description documents to describe the capture, review, and verification of these requirements performed by Boeing. It also required an update to the Plan for Software Aspects of Certification (PSAC) and other planning documents at Collins to describe the activities and objectives that Collins was responsible for.
context: TAB report describing organizational fragmentation where Boeing managed system diagrams and Collins managed software requirements, creating separate process documentation.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Exceptional pilot strength requirement reinterpreted
original_label: Exceptional pilot strength requirement reinterpreted
quote: There is currently no FAA regulation or guidance that specifies maximum trim crank/hand wheel forces, other than the qualitative statement in 14 CFR 25.143 (b) that pilot actions for controllability and maneuverability shall not require exceptional piloting skill, alertness, or strength.
context: TAB identifying regulatory gap where high manual trim forces could be rationalized as not requiring exceptional strength due to lack of specific limits.

label: HUD inconsistency with head-down display not detected
original_label: HUD inconsistency with head-down display not detected
quote: The HUD installed in the eCAB did not include the AOA DISAGREE message (amber caution) that was made a non-optional display feature in the Head Down Display (HDD) primary flight display as part of Software Blockpoint 1.5. The guidance in Advisory Circular (AC) 25-11B, Electronic Flight Displays states the following: If the content, arrangement, or format of the HUD is dissimilar to the HDD, it can lead to flightcrew confusion, misinterpretation, and excessive cognitive workload.
context: TAB identifying how critical display inconsistencies between HUD and standard displays were not caught during certification, reflecting fragmentary evaluation.

label: Compliance obligations weakened across successive agreements
original_label: Compliance obligations weakened across successive agreements
quote: Last year the Court denied a proposed plea agreement because it was against the public interest, in part, because Boeing would have had veto power over the Government's choice of an independent monitor. At that time, the Government was insistent that an independent monitor was necessary to remedy Boeing's corporate criminal culture as Boeing was unable to do so on its own, which endangered the flying public. The Court agreed with the Government. Now, however, under the Government's NPA, Boeing is no longer subject to an independent monitor and instead is authorized to pick its own "Independent Compliance Consultant."
context: Court's analysis in dismissal order comparing the rejected 2024 plea agreement to the 2025 NPA, showing erosion of oversight requirements.

label: Escalating pattern of DPA breach after initial fraud charges
original_label: Escalating pattern of DPA breach after initial fraud charges
quote: Subsequently, the Government filed a Criminal Information charging Boeing with conspiracy to defraud and simultaneously entered into a deferred prosecution agreement ("DPA") on January 7, 2021. On May 14, 2024, the Government notified the Court that Boeing breached the DPA for "failing to design, implement, and enforce a compliance and ethics program to prevent and detect violations of U.S. fraud laws throughout its operations." As a result, in July 2024 the parties submitted a plea agreement that required Boeing to plead guilty and serve a term of probation.
context: Court's background section tracing the sequence from initial DPA through breach to attempted plea resolution, showing continuation of non-compliance.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Risk perception shifted from unmanageable to manageable without independent oversight
original_label: Risk perception shifted from unmanageable to manageable without independent oversight
quote: The Government now believes that Boeing can be trusted to select a compliance consultant because Boeing has made "meaningful progress in improving its anti-fraud compliance and ethics programs." In summary, the Government's position in this lawsuit has been that Boeing committed crimes sufficient to justify prosecution, failed to remedy its fraudulent behavior on its own during the DPA which justified a guilty plea and the imposition of an independent monitor, but now Boeing will remedy that dangerous culture by retaining a consultant of its own choosing.
context: Court's analysis showing the Government's reinterpretation of Boeing's trustworthiness and compliance capacity across three successive positions, without objective change in Boeing's demonstrated behavior.

label: Government progressively relaxes oversight standards despite demonstrated non-compliance
original_label: Government progressively relaxes oversight standards despite demonstrated non-compliance
quote: Given Boeing's history related to this case (and the Government's continued failure to gain Boeing's compliance), the Movants are correct that this agreement fails to secure the necessary accountability to ensure the safety of the flying public. The NPA's "weakened provision" is even more concerning than its predecessor. It does not even pretend to address the need for a truly independent compliance monitor given Boeing's troubling history leading up to the Lion Air Flight JT610 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight ET302 crashes and then, while under intense scrutiny by the Government, its breach of the DPA.
context: Court's critical assessment of Government's decision to accept NPA with weaker compliance provisions despite Boeing's documented pattern of non-compliance during prior oversight.

label: Downgrading of fraud risk assessment based on self-reported progress
original_label: Downgrading of fraud risk assessment based on self-reported progress
quote: At that time, the Government was insistent that an independent monitor was necessary to remedy Boeing's corporate criminal culture as Boeing was unable to do so on its own, which endangered the flying public. The Court agreed with the Government. Now, however, under the Government's NPA, Boeing is no longer subject to an independent monitor and instead is authorized to pick its own "Independent Compliance Consultant."
context: Court's comparison showing Government's shift from mandatory independent monitoring to permitting Boeing self-selection of compliance oversight, without demonstrated remediation of the underlying corporate culture.

label: Participating states denied access to critical comments
original_label: Participating states denied access to critical comments
quote: From January 2021, the NTSB and the BEA were consulted on a draft of the final report. The NTSB and the BEA requested in particular that the aspects related to the performance of the crew be better exposed and analysed. These exchanges did not result in satisfying amendments to the final report and led the NTSB and the BEA to request that their comments be appended to the final report. On December 23, 2022, the EAIB published the final report on its website without directly including the BEA's comments in appendix. Instead, the EAIB report contains a link to a BEA document which does not contain the comments that the BEA had finally requested to be appended.
context: BEA press release describing how the Ethiopian investigative authority (EAIB) published the ET-302 accident report while excluding critical technical comments from participating international investigators, fragmenting knowledge of safety analysis.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Crew performance analysis excluded from safety lessons
original_label: Crew performance analysis excluded from safety lessons
quote: The BEA shares the analysis and conclusions of the EAIB report regarding the contribution of the MCAS system of the 737 Max to the accident. BEA's comments are mainly related to the analysis of the crew's performance and its contribution to the accident scenario, in particular during the first part of the flight (between the rupture of the angle of attack vane and the activation of the MCAS system). The BEA considers that this analysis would make it possible to draw safety lessons beyond those related to the MCAS system.
context: BEA noting that the EAIB report narrowed the scope of safety analysis to MCAS alone, excluding crew performance factors that the BEA believed would yield broader safety lessons, thereby redefining what counts as sufficient accident investigation.

label: MCAS authority increased between design iterations
original_label: MCAS authority increased between design iterations
quote: In March 2016, Boeing determined that MCAS should be revised to improve wings-level, flaps up, low Mach stall characteristics and identification. The MCAS was revised such that depending on AOA, it would be capable of commanding incremental stabilizer to a maximum of 2.5 degrees at low Mach decreasing to a Maximum of 0.65 degrees at high Mach.
context: Investigation report documenting how MCAS design authority was expanded from initial design to 2.5 degrees maximum in 2016.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Hazard reclassified from minor to major despite authority increase
original_label: Hazard reclassified from minor to major despite authority increase
quote: TABLE 28: RESULTS OF PRELIMINARY HAZARD ASSESSMENT FOR REVISED MCAS AUTHORITY Hazard: Uncommanded MCAS function operation up to its maximum authority, Hazard classification: Major* *Major Classification: The uncommanded MCAS command to the Maximum nose down authority at low Mach numbers was evaluated in the 737 MAX cab and rated as Minor. The high Mach uncommanded MCAS command and subsequent recovery is the critical flight phase in establishing the hazard rating for erroneous MCAS commands.
context: Investigation report citing Boeing's hazard assessment that classified the expanded MCAS authority as Major risk despite low-Mach testing showing Minor risk.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Uncommanded MCAS treated as readily recognizable
original_label: Uncommanded MCAS treated as readily recognizable
quote: Unintended stabilizer trim inputs are readily recognized by movement of the stab trim wheel, flight path change or increased column forces. Airplane can be returned to steady level flight using available column (elevator) alone or stabilizer trim. Continuous unintended nose down stabilizer trim inputs would be recognized as a Stab Trim or Stab Runaway failure and procedure for Stab Runaway would be followed.
context: Investigation report documenting Boeing's assumptions in hazard classification that treated MCAS failures as readily recognizable and controllable.

label: Hazard assessment simulated generic trim input, not actual failure modes
original_label: Hazard assessment simulated generic trim input, not actual failure modes
quote: To perform these simulator tests, Boeing induced a stabilizer trim input that would simulate the stabilizer moving at a rate and duration consistent with the MCAS function. Using this method to induce the hazard resulted in the following motion of the stabilizer trim wheel, increased column forces, and indication that the Airplane was moving nose down. Boeing indicated to the NTSB that this evaluation was focused on the pilot response to uncommanded MCAS operation, regardless of underlying cause. Thus, the specific failure modes that could lead to uncommanded MCAS activation, such as an erroneous high AOA input to the MCAS, were not simulated as part of these functional hazard assessment validation tests. As a result, additional flight deck effects (such as IAS DISAGREE and ALT DISAGREE alerts and stick shaker activation) resulting from the same underlying failure (for example, erroneous AOA) were not simulated and were not documented in the stabilizer trim and autoflight safety assessment reports reviewed by the NTSB.
context: Investigation documenting how Boeing's hazard assessment tests did not examine the actual failure mode (erroneous AOA) that causes MCAS to activate, resulting in undocumented flight deck effects.

label: AOA DISAGREE alert linked to optional feature, not standard
original_label: AOA DISAGREE alert linked to optional feature, not standard
quote: In 2017, however, within several months after beginning Boeing 737- 8 (MAX) deliveries, Boeing identified that the Boeing 737-8 (MAX) display system software did not correctly implement the AOA DISAGREE alert requirements. As with the Boeing 737 NG, the Boeing display system requirements for the Boeing 737-8 (MAX) called for the activation of the AOA DISAGREE alert as a standard feature on all Airplanes. The software delivered to Boeing, however, linked the AOA DISAGREE alert to the AOA position indicator, which is an optional feature on the Boeing 737 (MAX) series. Accordingly, the software activated the AOA DISAGREE alert only if an airline opted for the AOA indicator. At the time of the accident, Boeing advised that the AOA indicator had been selected by approximately 20% of airlines.
context: Investigation report documenting how Boeing discovered a software discrepancy that prevented AOA DISAGREE alert from appearing unless airlines purchased an optional feature, leaving 80% of aircraft without this safety alert.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Boeing determined AOA DISAGREE absence posed no safety risk
original_label: Boeing determined AOA DISAGREE absence posed no safety risk
quote: When the discrepancy between the AOA display requirements and the software was identified, Boeing determined that the absence of the AOA DISAGREE alert did not adversely impact Airplane safety, certification or operation. Accordingly, Boeing concluded that the existing functionality was acceptable until the originally intended functionality could be implemented in a display system software upgrade scheduled for the third quarter of 2020.
context: Investigation report showing Boeing's determination to accept the absence of a safety alert rather than require retrofit.

label: FAA delegated stabilizer safety analysis to Boeing ODA
original_label: FAA delegated stabilizer safety analysis to Boeing ODA
quote: CP13471 proposed delegation of all Flight Controls Primary & Secondary compliance findings. On April 14, 2015, the FAA approved the delegation of several deliverables; however, they indicated that the deliverable titled '737 Stabilizer System Description and Safety Analysis' (SSA) would be retained by the FAA and will not be proposed for delegation. In November 2016, Boeing submitted the 737 Stabilizer System Description and Safety Analysis (SSA), revision F, to the FAA for acceptance. In December 2016, the FAA's response to Boeing was to 'accept' the submittal and with notation 'delegated SSA approval to ODA.'
context: Investigation documenting FAA's reversal: first retained stabilizer safety analysis for direct review, then delegated approval to Boeing's own Organization Designation Authorization.

label: MAX differences training contained no information about MCAS
original_label: MAX differences training contained no information about MCAS
quote: The MAX difference training was CBT training and it is around 2 hours training, maybe if you sit continuously on your laptop for 6 hrs. There was no simulator training at all. The design of the A/C has some changes like MAX engine is bigger about 84 inches and moved a little bit forward, and Nose gear is extended up about 5.6 inches performance wise the T-OFF weight of MAX is higher than NG.
context: Interview with Ethiopian Airlines captain instructor describing the minimal MAX differences training provided to pilots, which made no mention of MCAS.

label: Training on runaway stabilizer but not on MCAS
original_label: Training on runaway stabilizer but not on MCAS
quote: We have taken training on Runaway Stabilizer; the stabilizer is controlled by Electrical Trim, A/P and manual trim.
context: Interview with first officer who flew accident aircraft, noting that pilots received training on stabilizer runaway but no mention of MCAS.

label: Training department added runaway stabilizer post-Lion Air
original_label: Training department added runaway stabilizer post-Lion Air
quote: The training department introduced Runaway stabilizer on requirement training because it was not there. But once we get this AD it was additionally & necessary in the proficiency training.
context: Interview with Ethiopian Airlines instructor explaining that runaway stabilizer training was added only after receiving the Airworthiness Directive.

label: Boeing bulletin described AOA failure as occurring only in manual flight
original_label: Boeing bulletin described AOA failure as occurring only in manual flight
quote: A thorough study was conducted regarding the airworthiness directive and the FCOM bulletin released after the Lion Air accident. The back ground information from the FCOM bulletin that calls for attention to 'an AOA failure condition that occurs during manual flight only' was assessed during the investigation and was found that it creates confusing to the reader as it appears that the AOA failure condition would only occur during manual flight only. But it was found that the AOA failure condition can occur regardless of the autopilot engagement status and that only activation of MCAS would be dependent on it.
context: Investigation analysis showing how the Boeing FCOM bulletin's language about AOA failure was ambiguous and potentially misleading about when the failure could occur.

label: Pre-accident electrical and flight control problems on accident aircraft
original_label: Pre-accident electrical and flight control problems on accident aircraft
quote: The ET302 airplane experienced flight control system and miscellaneous electrical faults prior to the accident flight. a. Flight control problems started occurring on the ET302 airplane on Dec 3, 2018, eighteen days after delivery. Pilot write ups included temporary fluctuations of vertical speed and altitude as well as a report of the aircraft rolling during autopilot operation and altitude and vertical speed indication on the PFD showed an erratic and exaggerated indication; b. Three days before the accident the Auxiliary Power Unit (APU) Fault Light illuminated, and the APU had a protective shutdown; c. The onboard maintenance function computer message also indicated the Start Converter Unit (SCU) showed the APU's start system was inoperative; d. The Captain's personal computer power outlet had no power; e. None of these pre-accident problems can be explained by a bird strike.
context: Investigation documenting a series of electrical and systems problems on this specific aircraft in the weeks before the accident.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: FCTM guidance recommended maximizing automation in non-normal situations
original_label: FCTM guidance recommended maximizing automation in non-normal situations
quote: Max FCTM 8.19 non normal operation describes that... The non-normal situations guideline stated: 'when a non-normal situation occurs, the Maximum use of auto flight system is recommended to reduce crew workload'
context: Investigation analysis noting that Boeing's Flight Crew Training Manual recommended maximum use of autopilot in non-normal situations, which may have influenced the accident crew's decisions.

label: Auto-throttle failure not communicated to crew
original_label: Auto-throttle failure not communicated to crew
quote: The manufacturer revealed during the investigation that the flight management system responsible for calculating and sending thrust command was affected by the erroneous AOA inputs. There was no flight crew document (FCOM, AFM, QRH...) that states this could happen.
context: Investigation finding that the auto-throttle's dependence on AOA and its failure mode were undocumented in crew procedures.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Hazard assumptions required pilot immediate recognition and action
original_label: Hazard assumptions required pilot immediate recognition and action
quote: The FHA evaluations were conducted by Boeing in their Engineering Cab using FAA guidance regarding pilot response to flight control failures requiring trim input that is contained in FAA Advisory Circular AC25.7C. In particular, Boeing uses the following assumptions in its flight controls FHAs: Uncommanded system inputs are readily recognizable and can be counteracted by overriding the failure by movement of the flight controls in the normal sense by the flight crew and do not require specific procedures. Action to counter the failure shall not require exceptional piloting skill or strength. The pilot will take immediate action to reduce or eliminate increased control forces by re-trimming or changing configuration or flight conditions. Trained flight crew memory procedures shall be followed to address and eliminate or mitigate the failure.
context: Investigation documenting the assumptions underlying Boeing's hazard assessment that MCAS failures would be readily recognized and controllable.

label: Speed Trim System carried over from NG to MAX
original_label: Speed Trim System carried over from NG to MAX
quote: The Speed Trim System, which is part of the Speed Trim System, is implemented as a control law within the flight control computer (FCC), and commands incremental stabilizer trim through the automatic trim control system circuitry. There are two different stabilizer trim rates depending on the position of the flaps. A schedule determines the desired incremental stab deviation from the last trimmed position as a function of airspeed and flap position. The 737-300, 400 and 500 (737 Classic) as well as the -600/700/800/900 (737 NG) family of Airplanes incorporated a Speed Trim System to augment the basic Airplane's speed stability during certain low speed, high thrust flight conditions by moving the horizontal stabilizer during manual flight (autopilot not engaged). The STS was carried over to the 737-7/-8/-9 (737 MAX) family of Airplanes. Additionally, on 737MAX Airplanes, the MCAS function was added to the STS to address the pitch characteristics described above
context: Technical documentation showing how MCAS was added incrementally to an existing system that had been in place on prior 737 models.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Engineering judgment identified failure conditions requiring evaluation
original_label: Engineering judgment identified failure conditions requiring evaluation
quote: To begin an FHA, engineering judgment is used to identify the failure conditions which require evaluation. According to the FHA sections of Boeing's 737 NG/MAX Stabilizer Trim Control System Safety Analysis, performance analyses and piloted simulations were accomplished as needed to help define the hazard categories for the identified conditions.
context: Investigation describing Boeing's process of using engineering judgment to select which failure conditions would be analyzed in hazard assessment, potentially allowing some to be excluded.

label: Collins AOA sensor did not analyze electrical installation failures
original_label: Collins AOA sensor did not analyze electrical installation failures
quote: The analysis part of Collins laboratory simulation test for the AOA vane was presented to the EAIB. Even though bird strikes may be one of the causes, a wide range of power quality problems and error sources that can affect an airplane's electrical and electronic systems resulting in unstable and erroneous AOA Sensor output signals were not analysed. Despite the two fatal accidents and the electrical problems associated with the AOA Sensors, Collins Aerospace did not evaluate the electrical installation and testing procedures being performed by Boeing production. The following partial list could have been considered in the analysis: a. Damaged EWIS resulting in short circuits or open circuits b. Circuit component failures and overloaded circuits resulting in changes to rated voltage, current, resistance c. Reference carrier frequency and amplitude variations d. Improper bonding and/or grounding e. EMI, HIRF, Noise f. Mechanical failures
context: Investigation finding that Collins Aerospace, the AOA sensor manufacturer, did not analyze electrical installation problems that could cause erroneous sensor output.

label: Runaway stabilizer used as frame for understanding MCAS
original_label: Runaway stabilizer used as frame for understanding MCAS
quote: Continuous unintended nose down stabilizer trim inputs would be recognized as a Stab Trim or Stab Runaway failure and procedure for Stab Runaway would be followed.
context: Investigation documenting Boeing's assumption that pilots would interpret MCAS as a known 'runaway stabilizer' problem.

label: Boeing MAX differences training treated as minimal
original_label: Boeing MAX differences training treated as minimal
quote: What is the difference between MAX & NG? The design of the A/C has some changes like MAX engine is bigger about 84 inches and moved a little bit forward, and Nose gear is extended up about 5.6 inches performance wise the T-OFF weight of MAX is higher than NG.
context: Interview with Ethiopian Airlines captain instructor describing the very limited scope of MAX differences training approved by Boeing and the airline.

label: Accident pilots received AD and bulletin on Logipad system
original_label: Accident pilots received AD and bulletin on Logipad system
quote: From the Department data both accident pilots took briefing about the AD and Boeing's BULLETIN. Do you know the accident pilots? Yes I know them both. PF took the briefing by Flash. It was a 2 hours course. He did it on his Laptop and so did FO, same as the captain.
context: Interview with senior ground instructor documenting that both accident pilots completed the AD and bulletin training via online system.

label: Logipad system tracked synchronization but not comprehension
original_label: Logipad system tracked synchronization but not comprehension
quote: We give digital updated data of charts and performance data of B737 A/C for pilots on the Logipad. How do you Know pilots have received data? Will be checked with Logipad synchronization. Pilots will synchronize their Logipad application after return from flight or by policy they have to synchronize every 7 days. The pilots will find new data on what's new section of the Logipad. How do you know if someone has synchronized his Logipad in 7 days? The Logipad system will produce reporting data.
context: Interview with Ethiopian Airlines training manager describing the Logipad system which tracks whether pilots synchronized data but not whether they understood or retained the content.

label: Pilots expected MCAS failure would not affect autopilot
original_label: Pilots expected MCAS failure would not affect autopilot
quote: There might be a chance that the pilot perceived the bulletin in the above discussed manner and believed the problem would disappear given he engages the autopilot, and the reason for his repetitive attempt to engage the autopilot.
context: Investigation analysis suggesting pilots may have misunderstood the AD to mean AOA failure only affected manual flight.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: MCAS hazard rating unchanged despite design expansion
original_label: MCAS hazard rating unchanged despite design expansion
quote: Boeing's requirements document indicated that the preliminary functional hazard assessments of MCAS were re-evaluated by pilot assessments in the motion simulator and by engineering analysis and determined to have not changed in hazard classification as a result of the increase in MCAS authority to 2.5 degrees at low speed.
context: Investigation documenting Boeing's determination that the hazard classification did not change despite tripling the MCAS authority at low speeds.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Column cutout function modified to allow MCAS nose-down motion
original_label: Column cutout function modified to allow MCAS nose-down motion
quote: To accommodate MCAS, the column cutout function in the first officer's switching module was modified to inhibit the aft column cutout switch while MCAS is active, allowing Airplane nose-down stabilizer motion with Airplane nose-up column input.
context: Technical documentation showing how the basic safety feature (column cutout) was modified in hardware design to permit MCAS to override pilot input.

label: MCAS expanded to address low-speed stall characteristics
original_label: MCAS expanded to address low-speed stall characteristics
quote: As the development of the 737 MAX- 8 progressed, the MCAS function was expanded to low Mach numbers to comply with the stall characterstics requirements specified in FAR 25.201 and FAR 25.203.
context: Investigation documenting how MCAS scope expanded from initial pitch control function to encompass low-speed stall characteristics.

label: Pilot simulator sessions did not replicate actual MCAS failure mode
original_label: Pilot simulator sessions did not replicate actual MCAS failure mode
quote: Reproducing the control actions recorded on the FDR resulted in loss of control of the Airplane. Finally, simulator participants were to mimic ET302 actions; however, after moving the STAB TRIM CUTOUT switches to CUTOUT, the crew was to work together to manually trim the Airplane using the trim wheel. The scenario involved both crew members each using one hand on the control column and one hand on the trim wheel. The limitations in replicating forces required moving the trim wheel in Level D simulators, noted in section B, also applied to the E-CAB; it was not able to reproduce the force that would have been required from the ET302 crew.
context: Investigation finding that simulator testing could not replicate the actual forces required by the accident crew to manually trim the aircraft.

label: Approach to stall training conducted with autopilot engaged
original_label: Approach to stall training conducted with autopilot engaged
quote: Most approaches to stall training were given in accordance with the Boeing flight crew training manual FCTM guidelines. Per the manual all approaches to stall training were given with the autopilot engaged and the auto throttle disconnected to simulate an approach to stall condition and the pilot initiates recovery by disengaging the autopilot and following the steps in the approach to stall recovery procedure of the QRH. Additionally the investigation also observed that the FCTM doesn't have a guideline on how to conduct an approach to stall training with the autopilot not engaged nor for a stall condition during departure.
context: Investigation finding that pilots were not trained for stall conditions during manual flight immediately after takeoff, which is when the accident occurred.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: MCAS failures assumed controllable with elevator alone
original_label: MCAS failures assumed controllable with elevator alone
quote: When assessing unintended MCAS activation in the simulator for the FHAs, the function was allowed to perform to its authority and beyond before pilot action was taken to recover. Failures were able to be countered by using elevator alone. Stabilizer trim was available to offload column forces, and stabilizer cutouts were available but not required to counter failures.
context: Investigation documenting that Boeing's hazard assessment assumed MCAS failures could be controlled with column input alone, without requiring stabilizer cutout.

label: Multiple MCAS inputs scenario not formally part of hazard assessment
original_label: Multiple MCAS inputs scenario not formally part of hazard assessment
