quote: Boeing indicated that as part of the development process of MCAS, although not formally part of the FHA, engineering personnel and test pilots considered the scenario of multiple MCAS inputs due to pilot trim action following an erroneous AOA input. Their assessment was that each MCAS input could be controlled with column alone and subsequently re-trimmed to zero column force while maintaining the flight path. Five seconds after cessation of the pilot trim command, the subsequent MCAS command could be controlled in the same manner as the previous instance.
context: Investigation finding that Boeing considered multiple MCAS inputs in informal discussion but not in the formal hazard assessment.

label: MCAS authority expanded to low Mach numbers
original_label: MCAS authority expanded to low Mach numbers
quote: As the development of the 737 MAX 8 progressed, the MCAS function was expanded to low Mach numbers. MCAS is designed to function only during manual flight (autopilot not engaged), with the Airplane's flaps up, at an elevated AOA.
context: Report finding states that MCAS design scope grew beyond initial parameters during development process, expanding its operational envelope incrementally.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Uncommanded MCAS classified as Major not Catastrophic
original_label: Uncommanded MCAS classified as Major not Catastrophic
quote: Uncommanded MCAS function was considered "Major" instead of being categorized as "Catastrophic" during the fault hazard assessment (FHA) by Boeing. Boeing reasoned that such a failure could be countered by using the elevator alone. In addition, stabilizer trim is available to offload column forces, and stabilizer cutout is also available but not required to counter failure. But the associated failures and flight deck effects were not considered in reaching this assessment.
context: Report finding shows Boeing reinterpreted the hazard classification downward, assuming pilot mitigations would work without testing realistic failure scenarios.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: FHA assumed pilot would recognize and address MCAS
original_label: FHA assumed pilot would recognize and address MCAS
quote: During the design process, Boeing failed to consider the potential for uncommanded activation of MCAS, but assumed that pilots would recognize and address it through normaluse of the control column, manual electric trim, and the existing Runaway Stabilizer NNC.
context: Contributory factors section describes Boeing's unvalidated assumption about pilot capability to mitigate a newly designed system failure mode.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: MCAS not mentioned in flight manuals by design choice
original_label: MCAS not mentioned in flight manuals by design choice
quote: During discussions and communications with the FAA in 2016, Boeing proposed removing MCAS from the FCOM and the FAA agreed with that recommendation. FAR 25.1585(b) states that "Information or procedures not directly related to airworthiness or not under the control of the crew must not be included, nor must any procedure that is accepted as basic airmanship." As relevant to this standard, Boeing's rationale for recommending MCAS's removal from the FCOM included that: (1) the MCAS function is automatic and operates in the background, without any control input from the flight crew and (2) Crews were not expected to encounter MCAS in normal operation.
context: Report section on MCAS design and certification describes how Boeing reinterpreted regulatory standards to justify omitting safety-critical system information from crew training.

label: Pilots unaware of MCAS existence and function
original_label: Pilots unaware of MCAS existence and function
quote: The existence of MCAS and its function was not disclosed in any of the manuals provided by the manufacturer. Without MCAS description, function and its effect, it would be more difficult for the flight crew to understand the complexity. Instead of focusing on the runaway stabilizer in the AD, the crew would have been served better if training was provided about the effect of MCAS activation.
context: Report finding on flight crew training describes how pilots were kept in structural ignorance of a critical safety system through omission from manuals and training.

label: AOA sensor design error not communicated to regulators
original_label: AOA sensor design error not communicated to regulators
quote: According to the report, after the ET302 accident, Boeing informed the NTSB they had made an engineering design error in their initial AOA Sensor Hazard Analysis; Neither Boeing, the NTSB, nor the FAA informed Ethiopian authorities about this critical error that was communicated to the NTSB by Boeing four months earlier.
context: Report finding states that Boeing discovered a critical design flaw in the AOA sensor but failed to share this information with the investigating authority or other stakeholders.

label: Multiple failures from single cause not simulated
original_label: Multiple failures from single cause not simulated
quote: The specific failure modes that could lead to uncommanded MCAS activation, such as an erroneous high single AOA input to the MCAS, were not simulated as part of the functional hazard assessment validation tests. As a result, additional flight deck effects such as IAS DISAGREE and ALT DISAGREE were not assessed.
context: Report finding on functional hazard assessment shows that Boeing analyzed MCAS in isolation without examining the full cascade of alerts that would result from the root failure.

label: FHA assessed MCAS effects on flight controls only
original_label: FHA assessed MCAS effects on flight controls only
quote: FHA of MCAS was considered the effect of undue activation of MCAS on flight controls, but it did not consider possible effect of underlying root causes on other systems, displays and warnings. Introduction of MCAS function did not lead to revise the SSA for failures of AOA sensors.
context: Safety recommendation section describes how Boeing's analysis of MCAS was compartmentalized, failing to integrate effects across systems.

label: CBT training omitted MCAS description
original_label: CBT training omitted MCAS description
quote: The B737 MAX Crew difference CBT training prepared by Boeing and delivered to Pilots did not cover the MCAS system. There was CBT training for a few hours long which was supposed to cover the difference between MAX and NG but there was no information related to MCAS description in the system. Instead, It was advised that the Airplane has wide and moved a bit forward body, Size of the Engine which is 84" and the height of the nose gear about 5.6" high.
context: Report finding states that Boeing's training for pilots transitioning to the MAX aircraft systematically excluded information about the safety-critical MCAS system.

label: Boeing declined to clarify safety-critical questions from airline
original_label: Boeing declined to clarify safety-critical questions from airline
quote: Post Lion Air accident and prior to ET-302 accident, Ethiopian Airlines training department communicated to Boeing requesting clarification on the MCAS design and the operational procedures of the FCOM bulletin regarding checklist prioritization and whether run-away stabilizer checklist was enough to handle the situation and the need to include airspeed unreliable checklist. In its reply, Boeing did not answer all asked questions made by Ethiopian airlines training department, indicating that it was related to an ongoing Lion Air accident investigation.
context: Report finding shows that Boeing leadership chose not to respond to critical safety questions from an airline operator, citing an ongoing investigation.

label: Boeing assessment dismissed safety concerns
original_label: Boeing assessment dismissed safety concerns
quote: The investigation found the questions raised by the airline to be safety critical and if Boeing had answered the questions raised by the training department either directly or indirectly through a revision of the FCOM bulletin or a suggested training, it would have significantly altered the outcome.
context: Report conclusion assesses that Boeing management had opportunity to respond to safety-critical questions but failed to do so.

label: MCAS framed as hidden background system not requiring disclosure
original_label: MCAS framed as hidden background system not requiring disclosure
quote: Boeing's rationale for recommending MCAS's removal from the FCOM included that: (1) the MCAS function is automatic and operates in the background, without any control input from the flight crew and (2) Crews were not expected to encounter MCAS in normal operation.
context: Report section on MCAS design rationale describes Boeing's internal reasoning for excluding the system from pilot awareness and training.

label: Flap position requirement for MCAS omitted from AD
original_label: Flap position requirement for MCAS omitted from AD
quote: The critical statement that was omitted from the AD was the flap position. MCAS operates only when the flap is fully up. Following the issuance of this AD, the ETH asked clarification from Boeing via email whether they should do airspeed unreliable procedures first. The response they got was that Boeing could not make further comments as the case was under investigation.
context: Safety recommendation section shows that Boeing withheld critical technical information about MCAS activation conditions from the airworthiness directive.

label: Erroneous AOA scenarios rationalized as not representative
original_label: Erroneous AOA scenarios rationalized as not representative
quote: A miscalibrated sensor scenario for JT610 and a bird strike scenario for ET302 cannot explain the flight control system alerting, maintenance messages and electrical/electronic system faults that were occurring on these airplanes in the weeks and days before their accidents. These accidents were triggered by production quality defects that presented as intermittent system malfunctions.
context: Report findings section describes Boeing's use of alternative failure scenario narratives to dismiss evidence of production quality defects.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: MCAS embedded in flight control law as normal function
original_label: MCAS embedded in flight control law as normal function
quote: The MCAS is a function within the Speed Trim System and, when activated, moves the stabilizer during non-normal flaps up, manual flight, high angle of attack maneuvers to provide a desirable increase in stick for gradient and a reduced pitch up tendency. Similar to the Speed Trim function, the MCAS function is also a flight control law contained within each of the two FCCs.
context: Report system description documents how MCAS was institutionalized as a standard component of the flight control law within the aircraft's computer architecture.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: FHA did not perform fault tree analysis for Major classification
original_label: FHA did not perform fault tree analysis for Major classification
quote: Because uncommanded MCAS function was considered "Major," Boeing did not perform a specific fault tree analysis for an uncommanded MCAS hazard and failed to classify MCAS as a safety-critical system, which would have attracted greater FAA analysis during the certification process.
context: Report finding on MCAS design process describes how Boeing's downgrade of hazard classification created a lower analytical standard.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Cumulative mistrim assumed manageable by elevator alone
original_label: Cumulative mistrim assumed manageable by elevator alone
quote: The control column force to maintain level flight could eventually increase to a level where control forces alone may not be adequate to control the Airplane. The cumulative mistrim could not be countered by using the elevator alone which was contrary to the Boeing assumption during FHA. The events that led to the accident flight showed that in the event of repetitive MCAS activation without sufficient trim commands to return to trimmed flight, the cumulative mistrim could not be countered by using elevator alone.
context: Report finding documents that Boeing's assumptions about pilot capability to manage repetitive MCAS activations proved false in the accident scenario.

label: Airline concerns about checklist prioritization not addressed
original_label: Airline concerns about checklist prioritization not addressed
quote: First; According to the briefing there was no problem with the MCAS system at the time of the accident except being triggered at the wrong moment during the flight due to a single erroneous AOA data. Then why is the system designed in such a way that it operates depending on a single data source, especially when it is of a serious consequences, instead of interrogating data from other AOA sensors? Second; any average skilled pilot experiencing multiple failures, as it were, would react to the abnormalities depending on their sequence of urgency starting with a stick shaker. All simulator trainings, so far provided, require at the first activation of a stick shaker to react in such a way to curb the impending actual stall. It is, though, obvious that all stall warnings are not true as was the case with the Lion Air 737 MAX involved in the accident, but once a pilot identified a stick shaker to be a nuisance, the next thing he would do is the AIRSPEED UNRELIABLE memory item not runaway stabilizer checklist.
context: Email from Ethiopian Airlines training department to Boeing after Lion Air accident raises concerns about design dependencies on single AOA sensor and checklist prioritization conflicts.

label: MCAS described as automatic background function not needing disclosure
original_label: MCAS described as automatic background function not needing disclosure
quote: Without MCAS description, function and its effect, it would be more difficult for the flight crew to understand the complexity. Instead of focusing on the runaway stabilizer in the AD, the crew would have been aware of MCAS which would have provided them with better understanding of the system and raise their chances of mitigating consequences of repetitive MCAS activations in the accident flight.
context: Safety recommendation acknowledges that Boeing's strategy of concealing MCAS information prevented crews from understanding the system's role in the accident scenario.

label: Boeing did not acknowledge electrical malfunctions on MAX aircraft
original_label: Boeing did not acknowledge electrical malfunctions on MAX aircraft
quote: Boeing has never acknowledged the electrical malfunctions that occurred on both MAX airplanes in the months, weeks, and days leading up to their accidents before MCAS was activated on their fatal flights.
context: Report finding states that Boeing failed to recognize or disclose a pattern of electrical system problems on the accident aircraft.

label: Single AOA sensor design made MCAS vulnerable
original_label: Single AOA sensor design made MCAS vulnerable
quote: The MCAS design relied on a single AOA sensor, making it vulnerable to erroneous input from the sensor.
context: Contributory factor identifies that MCAS architecture depended on single sensor input without redundancy, a foundational design choice.

label: MCAS FHA did not evaluate accompanying alerts and indications
original_label: MCAS FHA did not evaluate accompanying alerts and indications
quote: While Boeing considered the possibility of uncommanded MCAS activation as part of its FHA, it did not evaluate all the potential alerts and indications that could accompany a failure leading to an uncommanded MCAS.
context: Contributory factor section describes how Boeing compartmentalized its analysis of the MCAS system failure, isolating it from other flight deck effects.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Combined alerts and indications not evaluated in hazard assessment
original_label: Combined alerts and indications not evaluated in hazard assessment
quote: The combined effect of alerts and indications that impacted pilot's recognition and procedure prioritization were not evaluated by the Manufacturer.
context: Contributory factor identifies that Boeing failed to evaluate how multiple simultaneous alerts would affect pilot decision-making.

label: AOA DISAGREE alert dependent on optional equipment
original_label: AOA DISAGREE alert dependent on optional equipment
quote: In 2017, however, within several months after beginning Boeing 737 MAX 8 deliveries, Boeing identified that the 737 MAX 8 display system software did not correctly implement the AOA DISAGREE alert requirements. As with the Boeing 737 NG, the Boeing display system requirements for the 737 MAX 8 called for the activation of the AOA DISAGREE alert as a standard feature on all Airplanes. The software delivered to Boeing, however, linked the AOA DISAGREE alert to the AOA position indicator, which is an optional feature on the Boeing 737 MAX series. Accordingly, the software activated the AOA DISAGREE alert only if an airline opted for the AOA indicator. At the time of the accident, Boeing advised that the AOA indicator has been selected by approximately 20% of airlines.
context: System description documents a software error that made a critical failure alert dependent on an optional feature, reducing visibility of AOA sensor failures.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Stress and startle effects not considered in crew response assumptions
original_label: Stress and startle effects not considered in crew response assumptions
quote: Stress and startle effects were not considered by the manufacturer when trying to understand how crew might respond to the effects of an AOA sensor fault and the erroneous activation of MCAS.
context: Report finding identifies that Boeing's assumptions about pilot response capabilities failed to account for psychological factors under emergency conditions.

label: Runaway stabilizer procedure inadequate for MCAS
original_label: Runaway stabilizer procedure inadequate for MCAS
quote: The emergency AD pilot procedures were inadequate and unverified. AD 2018-23-51 does not mention the possibility of an auto throttle malfunction due to an erroneous AOA input.
context: Report finding shows that the airworthiness directive provided incomplete procedures that failed to address multiple failure modes resulting from the root AOA sensor fault.

label: MCAS designed as extension of existing Speed Trim System
original_label: MCAS designed as extension of existing Speed Trim System
quote: Boeing implemented aerodynamic changes as well as a stability augmentation function called the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), as an extension of the existing Speed Trim System (STS), to improve Airplane handling characteristics and improve static longitudinal stability at elevated angles of attack.
context: Report section on MCAS design describes Boeing's framing of the new system as an extension of existing technology rather than a novel safety-critical system.

label: Difference training approved as inadequate by regulators
original_label: Difference training approved as inadequate by regulators
quote: The difference training from B737NG to B737MAX provided by the manufacturer was found to be inadequate.
context: Report finding concludes that regulatory approval of Boeing's training program was insufficient to prepare pilots for MAX operations.

label: Intermittent electrical faults not investigated or reported
original_label: Intermittent electrical faults not investigated or reported
quote: Post-accident analysis reveals new Airplane experienced unexplained electrical and electronic faults within weeks of entering service, and in the weeks and days prior to their accidents.
context: Report finding documents that electrical anomalies on the accident aircraft were not investigated or linked to MCAS activation risk.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: MCAS column cutout function modified to allow simultaneous activation
original_label: MCAS column cutout function modified to allow simultaneous activation
quote: The MCAS function requires the stabilizer to move nose down in opposition to the column commands when approaching high angles of attack. To accommodate MCAS, the column cutout function in the first officer's switching module was modified to inhibit the aft column cutout switch while MCAS is active, allowing Airplane nose-down (AND) stabilizer motion with Airplane nose-up (ANU) column input.
context: System description shows how MCAS was embedded in the aircraft's control logic by modifying existing cutout protection mechanisms.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Production defects defined as not triggering MCAS investigations
original_label: Production defects defined as not triggering MCAS investigations
quote: MCAS and the lack of pilot training did not trigger the accident; however it was the failure of the sensors due to the production quality defects. If the intermittent defects did not cause the AOA Sensors to fail on the accident flight, MCAS would not have activated, and the accident would not have occurred.
context: Report finding reframes the root cause as production quality rather than MCAS design, a characterization that may have limited scrutiny of system design.

label: FAA delegated compliance determinations to Boeing via ODA
original_label: FAA delegated compliance determinations to Boeing via ODA
quote: Designees perform a substantial amount of critical work on FAA's behalf—for example, at one Airplane manufacturer, they made about 90 percent of the regulatory compliance determinations for a new Airplane design.
context: Report section on FAA oversight describes organizational fragmentation where Boeing through ODA program made most compliance determinations rather than FAA.

label: MCAS certification not delegated to ODA
original_label: MCAS certification not delegated to ODA
quote: Retention and delegation are accomplished with respect to compliance deliverables not to specific functions i.e., MCAS itself would not be delegated to the ODA.
context: Report section on FAA certification processes notes that despite broad ODA delegation, MCAS was theoretically retained by FAA rather than delegated.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Erroneous AOA classified as Major not Catastrophic hazard
original_label: Erroneous AOA classified as Major not Catastrophic hazard
quote: Uncommanded MCAS function was considered "Major" instead of being categorized as "Catastrophic" during the fault hazard assessment (FHA) by Boeing.
context: Report finding on functional hazard assessment shows Boeing's classification decision downgraded the severity of uncommanded MCAS activation.

label: AOA sensor design error minimized as engineering revision
original_label: AOA sensor design error minimized as engineering revision
quote: In a June 28, 2019, revision to the System Safety Analysis, Boeing informed the NTSB that Erroneous data from the Captain's AOA Sensor is revised to show three separate conditions combined with an OR gate, meaning any one by itself could result in erroneous AOA data: Erroneous AOA-L Sensor, Incorrect AOA output from ADIRU-L output, OR Loss of Power to AOA-L Heater.
context: Report finding shows Boeing's post-accident correction to its hazard analysis, indicating the original analysis had been incomplete.

label: Airline questions not answered due to ongoing investigation
original_label: Airline questions not answered due to ongoing investigation
quote: The manufacturer responded on 3 December 2018: declaring "I am happy to hear that you were able to take part in the Fleet Team meeting and will attempt to answer other questions from your pilots. However, because of our Annex 13 technical support to the [on-going Lion Air] accident investigation, we are unable to answer questions directly related to this event."
context: Email response from Boeing to Ethiopian Airlines describing refusal to clarify MCAS safety concerns, citing accident investigation as reason.

label: AOA failure scenarios not simulated in FHA validation tests
original_label: AOA failure scenarios not simulated in FHA validation tests
quote: During the process of developing and validating the Functional Hazard Analysis (FHA), Boeing considered four failure scenarios including uncommanded MCAS function to the Maximum authority limit of 2.5° of stabilizer movement. The uncommanded MCAS function to Maximum authority was flight simulated to high speed Maximum limit of 0.6°, and also the low speed Maximum limit of 2.5° of stabilizer movement and Boeing did not test repetitive erroneous MCAS activations in a flight simulation, but did consider the possibility of an erroneous AOA sensor potentially leading to repeated MCAS activations.
context: Report finding documents that Boeing acknowledged the possibility of repetitive MCAS activations but did not validate this scenario through simulation testing.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: AD procedures based only on runaway stabilizer checklist
original_label: AD procedures based only on runaway stabilizer checklist
quote: The emergency AD pilot procedures were inadequate and unverified. AD 2018-23-51 does not mention the possibility of an auto throttle malfunction due to an erroneous AOA input; The FAA's AD and Boeing Bulletin released after Lion Air accident focused only on RUNAWAY STABILIZER.
context: Report findings describe how the emergency directive narrowly framed the problem around runaway stabilizer rather than addressing the underlying AOA sensor failure.

label: Sales targets ratcheted upward after reformulation decline
original_label: Sales targets ratcheted upward after reformulation decline
quote: On January 25, 2010, Richard Sackler emailed other members of Purdue's Board: 'By way of background, the most important driver of our sales growth or decline is the performance of all the oxycodone extended release forms in the market (called OER); this is comprised of OxyContin® tablets plus all the generics in the space.' By virtue of OxyContin's importance, certain of the Sacklers placed pressure on executives to meet OxyContin sales goals set by the Board and participated in decision-making regarding Purdue's sales strategies for OxyContin, at times overruling the targets set by Purdue's executives. For example, in January 2010, Purdue executives and certain of the Sacklers engaged in an exchange regarding the executives' proposed 2010 budget. The executives proposed that OxyContin growth should be pegged at 3%. Richard Sackler thought this target was too low and would 'lead to an OxyContin[] tablets forecast that is almost the same as our sales in 2009.'
context: Sackler family board members pressuring management to reject conservative sales targets and pursue higher growth rates for OxyContin, establishing pattern of escalating demands.

label: Post-reformulation strategies to recapture lost high-volume prescriber sales
original_label: Post-reformulation strategies to recapture lost high-volume prescriber sales
quote: Shortly after the introduction of Reformulated OxyContin, Purdue's profits declined, in large part, because some individuals who abused OxyContin moved to more easily manipulated opioids. Purdue executives closely analyzed Purdue's internal data, including data purchased from vendors, in order to target high-volume prescribers and monitor their prescriptions. Purdue ranked the prescribers based on their aggregate opioid prescriptions in deciles from numbers 1 through 10, with 10 being the highest. From 2010 to 2013, Purdue instructed its sales force to primarily focus on the top three deciles of prescribers. The purpose of focusing the sales force on these highest deciles of prescribers was to cause an even higher volume of prescriptions to be written by them.
context: Purdue management's document describing the escalating focus on extreme high-volume prescribers as a strategic response to sales decline.

label: Evolve to Excellence intensifies detailing of highest prescribers
original_label: Evolve to Excellence intensifies detailing of highest prescribers
quote: At the center of these strategies was Purdue's aggressive marketing program that focused on detailing over 100,000 doctors and nurse practitioners nationwide each year, including thousands of prescribers that Purdue knew or should have known were prescribing opioids for uses many of which were not for a medically accepted indication, were unsafe, ineffective, and medically unnecessary, and/or were diverted for uses that lacked a legitimate medical purpose. By 2013, Purdue intensified its detailing of the very highest-volume prescribers, i.e., those writing '25 times as many OxyContin scripts' as their similarly situated peers, because it knew that its detailing was highly effective in causing these prescribers to write more prescriptions for Purdue's opioids. This strategy was referred to as the 'Evolve to Excellence' or 'E2E' program.
context: Settlement agreement reciting how Purdue progressively narrowed and intensified its marketing focus on extreme high-volume prescribers through the E2E program.

label: Pharmacy detailing strategy escalated after reformulation rejection
original_label: Pharmacy detailing strategy escalated after reformulation rejection
quote: Increasingly concerned that pharmacies would not fill OxyContin prescriptions as pharmacies and regulators increased safeguards against the filling of medically unnecessary prescriptions, Purdue developed and implemented a strategy to detail the pharmacies of its highest volume prescribers, including those that Purdue knew were writing medically unnecessary prescriptions, to ensure that Purdue opioids would be dispensed. Further, after Purdue determined that a large number of its prescriptions were still being rejected, Purdue considered an 'alternative distribution strategy' and later developed a program focused on Hysingla through which it paid kickbacks to three specialty pharmacies to dispense prescriptions for Purdue's opioids that traditional pharmacies refused to fill.
context: Settlement document describing how Purdue progressively escalated distribution strategies as legitimate pharmacies increasingly refused to fill suspicious prescriptions.

label: Practice Fusion kickback program grew from exploratory discussions
original_label: Practice Fusion kickback program grew from exploratory discussions
quote: Beginning in or around spring 2014, Purdue discussed paying Practice Fusion to create a CDS alert ('Pain CDS') to prompt providers using Practice Fusion's EHR to take certain clinical actions that Purdue believed would increase prescriptions for Purdue's extended release opioid products ('EROs'), which included OxyContin, Butrans, and Hysingla. From the beginning, the primary purpose of the program was to increase Purdue's ERO prescriptions. On May 4, 2014, a Purdue executive wrote regarding a potential deal with Practice Fusion that '[t]he key is understanding how it grows or protects [prescriptions].' ... From April 2016 through December 2016, Purdue paid kickbacks to Practice Fusion, an electronic health records company ('EHR'), to induce it to recommend and arrange for prescriptions of opioids by creating alerts that would appear within Practice Fusion's software while providers were seeing patients.
context: Settlement describing how Purdue progressed from exploratory discussions about a CDS alert to implementation of a paid kickback scheme with Practice Fusion.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Reformulated OxyContin marketed as abuse-resistant despite FDA cautions
original_label: Reformulated OxyContin marketed as abuse-resistant despite FDA cautions
quote: In April 2010, Purdue received FDA approval to market a reformulated version of OxyContin. Reformulated OxyContin was more difficult to crush or dissolve, but FDA cautioned that Reformulated OxyContin 'is not completely tamper-resistant and those intent on abusing this new formulation will likely find a means to do so. In addition, the product can still be misused or abused and result in overdose by simply administering or ingesting larger than recommended oral doses.'
context: Settlement reciting how Purdue proceeded with marketing Reformulated OxyContin despite explicit FDA warnings that it remained susceptible to abuse.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Abuse and diversion reframed as market shift unrelated to prescribing
original_label: Abuse and diversion reframed as market shift unrelated to prescribing
quote: Purdue attributed approximately 40% of the decline in OxyContin prescriptions in 2010 to 2011 to 'Region Zero' prescribers. Region Zero prescribers were prescribers that Purdue instructed sales representatives not to call on because, based on information maintained by its Abuse and Diversion Detection ('ADD') Program, Purdue determined that 'there is a concern about potential abuse or diversion related activities' by them. Purdue had detailed information (down to the number of prescriptions written, product, and dosage) of Purdue products prescribed by all prescribers, including Region Zero doctors from which it could determine that Purdue had been making substantial profits from these prescriptions.
context: Settlement showing how Purdue classified problematic prescriptions as mere market dynamics rather than evidence of wrongdoing justifying broader safeguards.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: No ceiling dose framing for high-dose oxycodone safety concerns
original_label: No ceiling dose framing for high-dose oxycodone safety concerns
quote: In July 2010, a Purdue sales representative reported: Another physician 'said he had a patient . . . from [the doctor] who was on 80 mg 5 times per day. He thought this was over the top and asked me today what the maximum dose was. He felt this patient was definitely exceeding it. I told him since it was a single entity opioid, there is no ceiling dose. It is only limited by side effects.'
context: Sales representative's call note showing how Purdue personnel used 'no ceiling dose' language to deflect physician concerns about dangerously high opioid dosing.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Titration messaging reframes discontinuation as undertreated pain
original_label: Titration messaging reframes discontinuation as undertreated pain
quote: At the same time, Purdue also refined its marketing message through the S.T.A.R.T. (Supplement, Titrate, Adjust, Reassess, Tailor) initiative by focusing sales conversations with prescribers on titrating patients to dosages. The goal of the program was to discourage patient discontinuation of OxyContin due to perceived lack of pain relief by encouraging providers to increase the OxyContin dosage, or 'titrate up.' For example, a 2011 script stated: 'We discussed the discontinuation rate of extended-release opioids by day 35. One of the potential reasons for discontinuation is the lack of efficacy perhaps as a result of lack of titration.' E2E created a refreshed 2014 version of the script that stated: 'According to an analysis … 57% of patients initiated on some commonly prescribed extended-release opioids are no longer on those products by day 35,'
context: Settlement describing Purdue's marketing scripts that systematically reframed patient discontinuation of OxyContin as a clinical problem requiring higher doses rather than as possible evidence of inappropriate prescribing.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Decile ranking system embeds extreme high-volume prescriber targeting
original_label: Decile ranking system embeds extreme high-volume prescriber targeting
quote: Purdue ranked the prescribers based on their aggregate opioid prescriptions in deciles from numbers 1 through 10, with 10 being the highest. From 2010 to 2013, Purdue instructed its sales force to primarily focus on the top three deciles of prescribers. The purpose of focusing the sales force on these highest deciles of prescribers was to cause an even higher volume of prescriptions to be written by them. Purdue knew, at that time, that the three highest deciles of prescribers combined accounted for only 1.5% of all opioid prescribers nationwide, but wrote 80% of all OxyContin prescriptions nationwide.
context: Settlement describing how Purdue institutionalized targeting of outlier prescribers through formal decile ranking and assignment systems.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: E2E call plans enforce mandatory minimum detailing frequency
original_label: E2E call plans enforce mandatory minimum detailing frequency
quote: Based on a study showing that providers in deciles 7-10 were most responsive to sales calls and were the most prolific writers, the E2E call plans instructed sales representatives to call on the very highest deciles of high-volume prescribers with the most frequency. Specifically, Purdue instructed its sales representatives to call on the highest volume OxyContin prescribers (i.e., those in so-called 'deciles' 7 through 10) at least 24 times a year and 'heavily favor' promoting OxyContin over other Purdue opioids in their messaging.
context: Settlement detailing how E2E formalized call frequency requirements and promotional messaging into binding sales force directives.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Abuse and Diversion Detection program codified in Standard Operating Procedure
original_label: Abuse and Diversion Detection program codified in Standard Operating Procedure
quote: At all relevant times, Purdue maintained an ADD program, through which Purdue had the means and ability to identify prescribers suspected of engaging in abuse and diversion. The ADD program began in or around 2002 and ended in or around February 2018. It was governed during most of that time period by Standard Operating Procedure ('SOP') 1.7.1. SOP 1.7.1 instructed Purdue employees to refer prescribers who displayed indicia of abuse and diversion to ADD. Employees referred these prescribers to ADD by issuing a Report of Concern ('ROC').
context: Settlement describing the formalized ADD system with written SOPs that created institutional infrastructure for identifying problematic prescribers.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Region Zero list embedded in sales planning and compensation systems
original_label: Region Zero list embedded in sales planning and compensation systems
quote: After prescribers were referred to ADD, Purdue reviewed information concerning the prescribers to determine whether Purdue should continue to market its opioids to them. If Purdue determined a sales representative should not continue to call on a prescriber, the prescriber was placed on the Region Zero list. In turn, sales representatives were rewarded with incentive compensation tied to the volume of OxyContin prescriptions generated from the health care providers they had detailed and faced corrective action plans, such as performance improvement plans, when they did not meet their sales goals.
context: Settlement showing how Purdue embedded the ADD/Region Zero system into formal sales incentive structures that tied compensation to prescriber-level volume targets.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Practice Fusion Pain CDS alert embedded in EHR software workflow
original_label: Practice Fusion Pain CDS alert embedded in EHR software workflow
quote: Practice Fusion's EHR system included the capability to prompt prescribers during a patient visit to take certain clinical actions based on particular personal health information and circumstances relayed by the patient. These prompts were known as clinical decision support ('CDS') alerts and were meant to aid the prescriber in making treatment decisions by providing unbiased information consistent with medical practice guidelines. ... The Pain CDS was presented to providers as a neutral medical standard. However, Purdue's primary objective in designing of the CDS alert was to increase its ERO sales, and the Pain CDS deviated from medically accepted standards, CDC guidelines, and FDA-approved labels for Purdue's EROs. ... Although the written contract between Purdue and Practice Fusion expired in mid-2017, the Pain CDS alert was live on Practice Fusion's EHR platform from on or about July 6, 2016 to the spring of 2019. The Pain CDS alerted more than approximately 230 million times during this period.
context: Settlement describing how Purdue embedded its marketing objective into the core workflow technology of thousands of medical practices through the Pain CDS alert.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Sales representative scripts and training materials formalize messaging
original_label: Sales representative scripts and training materials formalize messaging
quote: Purdue's sales and marketing departments prepared scripts, visual aids, brochures, and messaging for representatives to use with the providers they called on. A large part of this marketing was intended to cause the highest volume prescribers in the nation to 'commit' to writing more OxyContin prescriptions. ... In addition, representatives were trained to '[o]vercome . . . objection[s]' raised by providers and get physicians to 'commit' to prescribe more Purdue products. Specifically, representatives were trained to pivot from legitimate physician concerns about addiction to statements about 'dependence' and opioid 'tolerance.' When asked about the safety of high dosages, representatives were instructed to respond that OxyContin 'does not have a ceiling dose.'
context: Settlement describing how Purdue institutionalized persuasion tactics and messaging into standardized sales training materials and scripts.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Order Monitoring System embedded in distribution chain oversight
original_label: Order Monitoring System embedded in distribution chain oversight
quote: At the same time, Purdue had the means and ability to detect suspicious pharmacies through its Order Monitoring System (OMS). Like Purdue's ADD team (and comprised of many of the same personnel), the OMS Committee was empowered to flag suspicious pharmacies, instruct distributors to pause or cancel orders to those pharmacies, and instruct sales representatives not to call on the pharmacies.
context: Settlement describing how Purdue created formal infrastructure (OMS Committee) with explicit power to identify and stop distribution to suspicious outlets.

label: Detailing efficacy framed as market-responsive business practice
original_label: Detailing efficacy framed as market-responsive business practice
quote: Purdue knew that calling on or detailing healthcare providers and pharmacies caused them to prescribe and dispense, respectively, more of Purdue's opioid drugs. In September 2010, at a presentation to Purdue's sales supervisors, a Purdue executive explained: 'As I have stated several times, we know increases in the prescriber call average will have the single largest impact of anything you can do to increase prescriptions of Purdue products with our core and super core prescribers.' Additionally, presentations related to E2E recognized: 'Increased calls have a significant impact on OxyContin TRx.' Likewise, Purdue prepared return-on-investment analyses comparing the cost of detailing as compared to the OxyContin prescriptions that would not have been written but for Purdue's in-person marketing, as well as 'sensitivity' analyses showing the impact of Purdue's detailing on OxyContin prescribing.
context: Settlement showing how Purdue management collectively discussed detailing's causal effect on prescriptions in marketing metrics and ROI language.

label: High-volume prescribers labeled by commercial value tiers
original_label: High-volume prescribers labeled by commercial value tiers
quote: Purdue and the consulting company analyzed Purdue prescription data and other Purdue data sources broken down by deciles based on, primarily, their opioid prescribing. According to Purdue and the consulting company's deciling calculations, the prescribers writing '25 times as many OxyContin prescriptions as' other providers – those within the top five deciles – comprised less than seven percent of all prescribers nationwide, but wrote approximately as many opioid prescriptions as the remaining 93 percent of prescribers combined. The consulting company contended that, in contrast to the decile ranking undertaken by Purdue from 2010 to 2012, its rankings focused on 'value deciles,' which purported to be qualitatively different.
context: Settlement describing how Purdue and its consulting firm developed technical decile and 'value decile' language that normalized extreme prescriber outliers as desirable business targets.

label: Prescription decline attributed to regulatory safeguards, not abuse
original_label: Prescription decline attributed to regulatory safeguards, not abuse
quote: At the same time, Purdue also attributed declines in OxyContin prescription revenue post-reformulation to safeguards intended to reduce medically unnecessary opioid sales, including increased scrutiny of opioid prescribing by law enforcement, wholesalers, distributors, and retail pharmacies. For example, a Business Condition Report from a May 2-3, 2013 Board of Directors Meeting described sales as being '$144mm behind Q12013 budget' with '$36mm attributed to lower Rx demand' and stated that '[p]ossible causes of fewer tabs/Rx in the market' include 'Increased State Regulations'; 'Anti-opioid environment'; and 'Increased DEA/law enforcement scrutiny of physicians, pharmacies and wholesalers.'
context: Settlement showing how Purdue board presentations framed regulatory safeguards as market headwinds rather than responses to genuine abuse and diversion.

label: Patient abandonment rhetoric in titration messaging
original_label: Patient abandonment rhetoric in titration messaging
quote: At the November 2013 meeting concerning Purdue's 2014 budget, a Purdue executive discussed with the Board the company's plan to 'refine the message' of the company's titration up marketing campaign and specifically referenced the 'Individualize the Dose' campaign, a Conversion & Titration Guide, and the S.T.A.R.T. principles to 'highlight important elements of titration throughout the course of treatment.' Briefings to the Board also showed that the E2E marketing pushed by sales representatives in these calls specifically discussed titrating to higher dosages, initiating opioid naïve patients on opioid therapy, and switching patients from immediate release opioids to Reformulated OxyContin.
context: Settlement showing Board-level discussion of messaging campaigns framed as improving patient treatment through titration guidance.

label: Alternative distribution framed as patient access solution
original_label: Alternative distribution framed as patient access solution
quote: On August 16, 2013, one day after the Board briefing on E2E discussed above, Mortimer D. A. Sackler emailed a Purdue executive and others asking what ideas management had for creating a new distribution system 'to help relieve this problem of product access for legitimate chronic pain patients,' which would use 'an independent service to verify the legitimacy of [the patients'] prescriptions.'
context: Sackler family member framing alternative distribution strategy as addressing a patient access problem rather than circumventing pharmacy safeguards.

label: Sales representatives trained to overcome prescriber objections
original_label: Sales representatives trained to overcome prescriber objections
quote: In addition, representatives were trained to '[o]vercome . . . objection[s]' raised by providers and get physicians to 'commit' to prescribe more Purdue products. Specifically, representatives were trained to pivot from legitimate physician concerns about addiction to statements about 'dependence' and opioid 'tolerance.' When asked about the safety of high dosages, representatives were instructed to respond that OxyContin 'does not have a ceiling dose.'
context: Settlement describing formalized training that taught sales representatives how to deflect and reframe physician safety concerns.

label: Sales incentive compensation tied to high-volume prescriber performance
original_label: Sales incentive compensation tied to high-volume prescriber performance
quote: In turn, sales representatives were rewarded with incentive compensation tied to the volume of OxyContin prescriptions generated from the health care providers they had detailed and faced corrective action plans, such as performance improvement plans, when they did not meet their sales goals.
context: Settlement showing how Purdue tied sales compensation directly to extreme prescriber volume, creating financial incentives to maintain relationships with outlier prescribers.

label: Sales representative reporting discouraged by district manager review requirement
original_label: Sales representative reporting discouraged by district manager review requirement
quote: However, high-volume prescribers were often not reported and, even if they were, they were sometimes not added to Region Zero until they lost the ability to prescribe through legal or medical board action. In addition, certain Purdue policies resulted in high-volume prescribers not being reported to ADD, and thus not being added to Region Zero. For example, Purdue trained its sales representatives to only report clear instances of abuse and diversion, and sales representatives were instructed to discuss the reports with their district managers prior to filing.
context: Settlement describing organizational policies that created barriers to reporting suspicious prescribers to the ADD program.

label: Consulting company partnership embeds speakers selection discretion in sales
original_label: Consulting company partnership embeds speakers selection discretion in sales
quote: Purdue allowed its sales and marketing personnel, who had data on each doctor's prescribing of Purdue's drugs and whose compensation depended on increasing their assigned doctors' prescribing of Purdue's drugs, to select speakers instead of Purdue's medical education staff. Purdue also allowed its sales representatives to relay and endorse doctors' requests to be retained, and the doctors could be selected even if they had not been identified by the consulting company Purdue had retained for this purpose. Within Purdue, these were known as 'unsolicited requests.' Purdue vested final authority to select doctors in Purdue's Marketing department, which had data on each doctor's Purdue prescriptions.
context: Settlement describing how Purdue embedded speaker program selection in the sales organization's authority structure, creating conflict of interest.

label: Decile rankings and ROI analyses confined to senior management
original_label: Decile rankings and ROI analyses confined to senior management
quote: Purdue knew, at that time, that the three highest deciles of prescribers combined accounted for only 1.5% of all opioid prescribers nationwide, but wrote 80% of all OxyContin prescriptions nationwide. Purdue also knew that these prescribers were the most responsive to Purdue's detailing. Specifically, in June 2010, Purdue executives discussed instructing sales representatives to 'build their target list with a focus on the highest prescribers across all three categories (Tier 1), and then fill in target list with the next highest potential and keep in front of OER [opioid extended release] high prescribers.' They estimated that 'the top three deciles drive closer to 80% of all Rxs.' ... Likewise, Purdue prepared return-on-investment analyses comparing the cost of detailing as compared to the OxyContin prescriptions that would not have been written but for Purdue's in-person marketing, as well as 'sensitivity' analyses showing the impact of Purdue's detailing on OxyContin prescribing.
context: Settlement showing how Purdue's analytic understanding of detailing's causal effect on specific prescriber cohorts was embedded in senior executive planning but obscured in sales force communications.

label: ADD data and Region Zero lists not integrated with sales compensation reviews
original_label: ADD data and Region Zero lists not integrated with sales compensation reviews
quote: Although the analyses identified many red flag prescribers, only a fraction were reviewed as part of the ADD program and Purdue knowingly continued detailing others without any further scrutiny. ... In addition, although Purdue's policy stated that it required timely reporting, Purdue had few, if any, effective compliance measures to address an employee's failure to report, and very few sales representatives were penalized for failing to timely report.
context: Settlement describing organizational fragmentation where ADD findings did not result in systematic sales force accountability or correction.

label: OMS pharmacy data not systematically shared with detailing decisions
original_label: OMS pharmacy data not systematically shared with detailing decisions
quote: In addition to identifying suspicious pharmacies through referrals and data analyses, the OMS team also had the ability to see which pharmacies were filling prescriptions from Region Zero prescribers. Despite having this data, Purdue continued knowingly marketing to the pharmacies that filled the prescriptions of Region Zero and other red flag providers, which led those prescribers' medically unnecessary Purdue prescriptions to be filled.
context: Settlement showing how Purdue's OMS system possessed information about pharmacy patterns but this intelligence did not systematically inform sales detailing policy.

label: Board received selected summary data on Region Zero impact
original_label: Board received selected summary data on Region Zero impact
quote: At the December 2010 Board briefing, a Purdue executive discussed a chart stating that 'Region 0 Accounts For Much Of The TRx Decline At The Regional Level.' ... The materials provided to the Board in October 2011 also included a study, 'Changes in Prescribing Patterns Following Introduction of Reformulated OxyContin: A Window into Diversion.' The study examined a two-year period, August 2009 to July 2011, and found that data for Region Zero prescribers showed an 86% decline in their OxyContin prescriptions after Purdue's introduction of its reformulated version, and especially at the highest dosages, 40 and 80 mg tablets.
context: Settlement showing Board received analysis confirming abuse/diversion concentrated among prescribers Purdue had stopped detailing, yet continued marketing intensively to other high-volume prescribers.

label: Practice Fusion CDS design compartmentalized from clinical validation
original_label: Practice Fusion CDS design compartmentalized from clinical validation
quote: In creating a list of treatment plan options for addressing pain, Purdue employees pulled from a list of alternatives treatments to opioids in a New England Medical Journal article on opioid abuse in chronic pain. That article described several concerns about opioid use, including ' concerns about overdosing and abuse by patients' and ' [f]actors associated with the risk of opioid overdose or addiction.' Despite this, Purdue employees added opioids to the list within the CDS of potential therapies for chronic pain.
context: Settlement showing how Purdue's CDS design process allowed marketing staff to override clinical literature concerns by selecting favorable treatment options.

label: Board overrules conservative sales targets with higher growth demands
original_label: Board overrules conservative sales targets with higher growth demands
quote: The executives proposed that OxyContin growth should be pegged at 3%. Richard Sackler thought this target was too low and would 'lead to an OxyContin[] tablets forecast that is almost the same as our sales in 2009.' A Purdue executive informed Richard Sackler that 'in looking at the recent [oxycodone extended release] prescription growth trends and knowing the overall dynamics of the market OxyContin competes in – I just can't see a way of the prescription growth tracking to a level substantially higher than the 3% on which this budget is based' and that the higher target suggested by Richard Sackler would 'be interpreted as an imposition as opposed to an action that will stimulate the type of business building behaviors we want to encourage.' In response, Richard Sackler, who believed that Purdue's OxyContin growth target should be much higher, told a Purdue executive '… I'm disappointed and don't agree with you. This is a matter that the Board will have to take up and give you a settled direction.'
context: Sackler board member directly overriding executive judgment on growth targets and elevating dispute to full Board, signalling unwillingness to accept conservative business planning.

label: Sackler family endorses E2E strategy after board meeting
original_label: Sackler family endorses E2E strategy after board meeting
quote: Following the meeting, one of the consulting company partners that led the meeting with the Sacklers memorialized in an email: '[T]he room was filled with only family, including the elder statesman Dr. Raymond [Sackler]. . . . We went through exhibit by exhibit for about 2 hrs. . . . They were extremely supportive of the findings and our recommendations . . . and wanted to strongly endorse getting going on our recommendations.' Another consulting company partner further remarked in the email correspondence that their 'findings were crystal clear to' the Sacklers 'and [the Sacklers] gave a ringing endorsement of 'moving forward fast.'' After the 'ringing endorsement' by the Sacklers, Purdue, in collaboration with the consulting company, implemented many of the consulting company's recommendations.
context: Consulting partners' email documenting Sackler family's enthusiastic approval of E2E strategy targeting extreme high-volume prescribers.

label: Richard Sackler praises consulting company findings on prescriber targeting
original_label: Richard Sackler praises consulting company findings on prescriber targeting
quote: On August 23, 2013, certain Sackler family members met with the consulting company and examined its 'unvarnished' findings and recommendations. ... On August 15, 2013, two Purdue executives discussed the consulting company's progress on evaluating growth opportunities for OxyContin with the Board. Their presentation noted that the analysis would include an examination of 'relatively more sudden declines in tablets per prescriptions and prescriptions for 40 mg and 80 mg strengths' and 'prescriber segmentation and targeting.' Later that same day, Richard Sackler emailed Mortimer D. A. Sackler: 'The 'discoveries' of [the consulting company] are astonishing.'
context: Richard Sackler expressing enthusiasm and approval for consulting company's prescriber targeting analysis to other board members.

label: Board discusses E2E funding and ensures continued investment
original_label: Board discusses E2E funding and ensures continued investment
quote: In late 2013, the Board received a 2014 Budget presentation again reviewing E2E's implementation. Board notes show the Board discussed ensuring E2E's funding at that meeting.
context: Settlement noting that Board explicitly ensured continued funding for the E2E program in budget discussions.

label: Sacklers seek alternative distribution channels for rejected prescriptions
original_label: Sacklers seek alternative distribution channels for rejected prescriptions
quote: On August 16, 2013, one day after the Board briefing on E2E discussed above, Mortimer D. A. Sackler emailed a Purdue executive and others asking what ideas management had for creating a new distribution system 'to help relieve this problem of product access for legitimate chronic pain patients,' which would use 'an independent service to verify the legitimacy of [the patients'] prescriptions.' Two days later, Mortimer D.A. Sackler reiterated, 'I do think there may be an opportunity here for us to set up a complimentary business to handle this for Purdue as well as other controlled drug manufacturers. Do we have a team who could explore this possibility?' On August 18, 2013, Richard Sackler responded that he had the same idea and expressed it to a Purdue executive after a Board meeting.
context: Sackler family board members actively promoting development of alternative distribution strategy to fill prescriptions rejected by traditional pharmacies.

label: Sackler participation in daily management and operational decisions
original_label: Sackler participation in daily management and operational decisions
quote: The Sacklers, as members of the Purdue Board, exercised substantial oversight over management's operations of Purdue. For instance, in February of 2011, a memorandum observed: 'There seems to be a consensus that the role of the board and that of the management is blurred compared with the distinctions made by other major corporations,' and, historically, certain members of Sackler family functioned as 'executives, management, board, and shareholders all-in-one [and] worked collaboratively with other managers on a daily basis.' As late as 2017, a high-level Purdue executive commented: 'Three distinct business types (branded Rx [including Purdue]/biosimilars, consumer/OTC, generics) are being run through four separate regions (five if Rhodes is included), with the Board of Directors serving as the 'de-facto' CEO.'
context: Settlement describing how Sackler family board members blurred the boundary between board governance and operational management, effectively functioning as daily decision-makers.

label: Mortimer Sackler demands corrective action for sales decline
original_label: Mortimer Sackler demands corrective action for sales decline
quote: On July 17, 2012, Mortimer D.A. Sackler emailed fellow Purdue Board members stating that Purdue should 'start a search asap for a new CEO' and consider 'replacing the head of sales and marketing.'
context: Board member signalling dissatisfaction with management's inability to reverse post-reformulation sales decline and threatening personnel changes.

label: Richard Sackler demands Board investigation of sales performance
original_label: Richard Sackler demands Board investigation of sales performance
quote: On April 15, 2012, Richard Sackler emailed a Purdue executive, stating, 'We should . . . discuss the sudden decline in [OxyContin] sales in the past year or two. What are we doing to identify corrective actions?' The following day, a Purdue executive forwarded Richard Sackler's email to another Purdue executive, among others, stating, 'I am surprised that Dr. Richard is asking this. . . . Since the decline is related to reformulation I'm not sure how to proceed with him.'
context: Board member actively pressuring management to explain and correct the sales decline, with management perceiving the inquiry as difficult to address.

label: Sackler board members request prescriber-level market analysis
original_label: Sackler board members request prescriber-level market analysis
quote: In October 2013, Mortimer D.A. Sackler inquired directly with Purdue's leadership to request additional data concerning the downward trend in sales by dosage, requesting a chart to 'show the breakdown of the OxyContin market share by strength against competitors. I would like to understand more the recent dynamics of the market and where the patients are shifting to that we are losing.'
context: Sackler board member directly requesting detailed market and prescriber analysis from senior leadership, showing hands-on involvement in sales strategy.

label: Purdue representatives detail doctors despite multiple abuse-diversion reports
original_label: Purdue representatives detail doctors despite multiple abuse-diversion reports
quote: Purdue sales representatives' call notes also identified ongoing concerns regarding abuse by the doctor's patients. For example, a 2010 call note stated: 'Had a patient that died this week that was taking OxyContin (2 tablets of 80mg at Q12h). She was 45-48 years old and had been seen by [the doctor] for 10 years. The patient had complained previously (was reported) that the reformulation made her sick and tried to get a refund for the reformulation (the pharmacy refused). She did find generic OxyContin. Patient was found dead sitting at the kitchen table with a syringe beside her. It has been ruled as an accidental death by the police.' ... Months after the analysis, on August 1, 2011, Purdue completed an ADD review, deciding to take no action based on Doctor-2's explanation for why he stopped prescribing Reformulated OxyContin
context: Settlement showing Purdue's ADD program received documented evidence of patient deaths and continued to take no action against a high-volume prescriber.

label: Purdue reinstates Region Zero prescriber after limited review
original_label: Purdue reinstates Region Zero prescriber after limited review
quote: Four months later, on August 26, 2013, a Purdue sales representative requested to resume calling on the doctor. In response, the ADD program wondered if it was '[t]oo soon to put him back on the list.' It initially recommended a 'resume call' status due to a 'lack of progress on the resolution of the board's complaint and the doctor's continuation in practice,' but, after further discussion, kept him on Region Zero. In February 2015, the same Purdue sales representative again requested that the doctor be removed from the Region Zero list. The doctor was removed from the list on March 2015 after an 'Expedited Review' of requests to resume calling on several high-volume doctors.
context: Settlement showing Purdue management approved expedited reinstatement of Region Zero prescriber despite ongoing disciplinary actions and unresolved complaints.

label: OMS Committee votes to continue monitoring pharmacy despite red flags
original_label: OMS Committee votes to continue monitoring pharmacy despite red flags
quote: Despite Purdue's knowledge of the red flags indicating the pharmacy was engaged in abuse and diversion, the OMS Committee voted to 'continue to monitor' the pharmacy, and allowed the sales representatives to continue to call on the pharmacy for the next five years through 2015.
context: Settlement showing Purdue's OMS governance body chose continued detailing of suspicious pharmacy despite documented indicators of abuse and diversion.

label: Purdue directors continued detailing high-volume prescriber despite ROCs
original_label: Purdue directors continued detailing high-volume prescriber despite ROCs
quote: Purdue knew that Doctor-1 was prescribing medically unnecessary opioids. From 2009 through 2011, Purdue received at least three different ROCs about Doctor-1. ... The ADD program placed Doctor-1 on Region Zero and instructed sales representatives to cease calling on the doctor in August 2010. However, in October 2011, Purdue informed sales representatives that they may resume calling on Doctor-1, and the sales representatives did so until the spring of 2018. From January 2010 through May 2018, Purdue representatives detailed Doctor-1 at least 300 times, although calls after February 2018 did not promote opioid products.
context: Settlement showing Purdue management reinstated detailing of prescriber previously removed from Region Zero despite documented ROCs of abuse/diversion.

label: LJM partnerships approved three times with escalating scope
original_label: LJM partnerships approved three times with escalating scope
quote: Three times in 1999 and 2000, the Board was asked to and approved an unprecedented arrangement allowing Enron's CFO to set up private equity funds, the LJM partnerships, to do business with Enron for the purpose of improving Enron's financial statements.
context: Senate Subcommittee summarizing the sequence of three separate Board approvals of increasingly complex LJM arrangements from 1999-2000.

label: Board approved Raptor transactions three times despite mounting risk
original_label: Board approved Raptor transactions three times despite mounting risk
quote: Three times in 2000, the Board was asked to and approved complex transactions called the Raptors, despite questionable accounting and ongoing risk to the company.
context: Senate Subcommittee identifying a pattern of repeated Board approvals of increasingly risky Raptor structures throughout 2000.

label: Asset sales to unconsolidated affiliates characterized as balance sheet management
original_label: Asset sales to unconsolidated affiliates characterized as balance sheet management
quote: A presentation identifying $2 billion in past and planned Enron asset sales during 2000, primarily to LJM2 and two other unconsolidated affiliates, Whitewing and the Hawaii 125-0 Trust, is characterized as a '2000 Balance Sheet Management' effort.
context: Senate Subcommittee analysis of Finance Committee presentations showing systematic use of off-balance-sheet transactions framed as asset management.

label: Whitewing expanded from consolidated to unconsolidated status
original_label: Whitewing expanded from consolidated to unconsolidated status
quote: In September 1999, the Board approved a resolution to restructure Whitewing as an 'unconsolidated affiliate' that could be removed from Enron's books. At the same time, the Board approved establishment of a special purpose entity called the Osprey Trust to invest in Whitewing, and authorized Osprey to issue $1.4 billion in debt instruments that could be secured by a second series of Enron preferred shares.
context: Senate Subcommittee documenting the incremental restructuring of Whitewing from a consolidated affiliate to an off-balance-sheet vehicle, with escalating financial leverage.

label: Raptor transactions required successive reinforcement and restructuring
original_label: Raptor transactions required successive reinforcement and restructuring
quote: To shore up the SPEs' creditworthiness on paper, Enron concocted, with the assistance of Andersen, several complex financial arrangements with the Raptor SPEs including placing a 'collar' on the Raptor 'hedges' in October 2000, creating a 45-day cross guarantee arrangement to support all four Raptor transactions in December 2000, and restructuring the Raptors in March 2001, by placing additional Enron shares at risk to support them.
context: Senate Subcommittee describing how successive patches and restructurings were added to the Raptors over a nine-month period as the original structure deteriorated.

label: Lay's credit line usage escalated from monthly to multi-times weekly
original_label: Lay's credit line usage escalated from monthly to multi-times weekly
quote: Records show that Mr. Lay at first drew down the line of credit once per month, then every 2 weeks, and then, on some occasions, several days in a row. In the 1-year period from October 2000 to October 2001, Mr. Lay used the credit line to obtain over $77 million in cash from the company and repaid the loans exclusively with Enron stock.
context: Senate Subcommittee documenting the pattern of escalation in Lay's personal use of a company credit line, repaying with stock transfers over a single year.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Andersen briefed Board that Enron practices push limits and are at the edge
original_label: Andersen briefed Board that Enron practices push limits and are at the edge
quote: On February 7, 1999, Andersen informed the Audit Committee members that Enron was engaged in accounting practices that 'push limits' or were 'at the edge' of acceptable practice. In the discussion that followed, Andersen did not advocate any change in company practice, and no Board member objected to Enron's actions, requested a second opinion of Enron's accounting practices, or demanded a more prudent approach.
context: Senate Subcommittee documenting that Andersen explicitly communicated to the Board that Enron's practices were at the boundary of acceptable accounting, and the Board normalized this as acceptable.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Handwritten note by David Duncan confirming limit-pushing accounting
original_label: Handwritten note by David Duncan confirming limit-pushing accounting
quote: A handwritten note by Mr. Duncan in the lower right-hand corner of the document states: 'Obviously, we are on board with all of these, but many push limits and have a high 'others could have a different view' risk profile.'
context: Senate Subcommittee quoting Andersen's engagement partner David Duncan's talking points for the February 1999 Audit Committee briefing, acknowledging that Enron's practices push accounting limits.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Andersen described Raptors as certain to attract scrutiny but approved by auditor
original_label: Andersen described Raptors as certain to attract scrutiny but approved by auditor
quote: The Raptors are a series of four complex transactions that began in mid-2000 and terminated a little over a year later in 2001. They were presented to the Board by Enron management as ingenious accounting devices that might attract 'accounting scrutiny' but had been scrutinized and approved by Andersen.
context: Senate Subcommittee describing how Enron and Andersen jointly presented the Raptors to the Board as devices that would attract regulatory scrutiny but had been validated by Andersen, normalizing the risk.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Raptor presentation framed as transfer of P&L volatility not economic risk
original_label: Raptor presentation framed as transfer of P&L volatility not economic risk
quote: A handwritten note taken by the Corporate Secretary during Committee consideration of the Raptors states: 'Does not transfer economic risk but transfers P&L volatility.' The final page lists three risks associated with the Raptors. The first risk is 'Accounting scrutiny'; the second is 'Substantial decline in the price of [Enron] stock'; and the third is 'Counterparty credit.'
context: Senate Subcommittee documenting how the Raptor presentation framed the transaction as a legitimate accounting tool for managing financial statement volatility rather than a true hedge.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Board characterized LJM1 as single low-risk transaction despite design for multiple deals
original_label: Board characterized LJM1 as single low-risk transaction despite design for multiple deals
quote: When asked why the Board moved so quickly on such an unusual proposal, the Board members suggested during their interviews that they had seen LJM1 as involving a single transaction, the Rhythms stock 'hedge,' for which the company had obtained a fairness opinion from an outside accounting firm and which involved little risk to Enron. Although some Board members described LJM1 as an entity that engaged in a single transaction, LJM1 was designed to engage in multiple transactions and did so. LJM1's ability to engage in multiple transactions was made clear not only in the Board presentation, but also in the Board minutes which state: 'In addition, LJM may negotiate with the Company regarding the purchase of additional assets in the Merchant Portfolio.'
context: Senate Subcommittee contrasting how Board members retrospectively characterized LJM1 as low-risk single transaction versus documentary evidence it was designed for multiple transactions.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Enron accounting rules not kept up with company practices requiring interpretation
original_label: Enron accounting rules not kept up with company practices requiring interpretation
quote: Handwritten notes on the bottom of a 2001 presentation to the Audit Committee, added by the Enron Corporate Secretary during the course of Andersen's oral presentation, state: 'There are a number of areas where accounting rules have not kept up w/ the Company's practices and some interpretation is necessary.'
context: Senate Subcommittee quoting notes from an Audit Committee meeting showing that Enron's practices had outpaced formal accounting rules, normalizing the need for interpretation.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Board resolutions authorized special purpose entities and stock collateral
original_label: Board resolutions authorized special purpose entities and stock collateral
quote: Enron's extensive off-the-books activity was not only well known to the Board, but was made possible by Board resolutions authorizing new unconsolidated entities, Enron preferred shares, and Enron stock collateral that was featured in many of the off-the-books deals.
context: Senate Subcommittee finding that Board approved the structural apparatus necessary for off-the-books transactions to function.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Deal Approval Sheets formalized review of LJM transactions
original_label: Deal Approval Sheets formalized review of LJM transactions
quote: On paper, prior to Enron's engaging in a transaction with LJM, Enron personnel were supposed to complete a Deal Approval Sheet (DASH) that set out the major elements of the transaction and a LJM Approval Sheet with a checklist of items intended to ensure arms-length transactions and fair prices. These documents required signatures from two or more high level Enron officials, such as Mr. Causey, Mr. Buy, and Mr. Skilling.
context: Senate Subcommittee describing the formal control procedures established for LJM transactions, which on paper appeared to provide safeguards but were poorly executed.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Finance Committee established quarterly review and compensation controls for LJM
original_label: Finance Committee established quarterly review and compensation controls for LJM
quote: At that same October 2000 meeting, the Finance Committee decided to institute two more controls, to begin a quarterly review of LJM transactions by the Finance Committee and to conduct a one-time review of Mr. Fastow's LJM compensation by the Compensation Committee.
context: Senate Subcommittee documenting how governance controls over LJM were formally institutionalized in Board committee structure, though subsequently not effectively implemented.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Thousands of offshore entities embedded in Enron structure
original_label: Thousands of offshore entities embedded in Enron structure
