label: Muilenburg makes false certification statements to investors
original_label: Muilenburg makes false certification statements to investors
quote: But I can tell you with confidence that we understand our airplane, we understand how the design was accomplished, how the certification was accomplished, and remain fully confident in the product that we've put in the field. But we also know there are areas that we can improve, and that is the source of the software update here. But there was no surprise or gap or unknown here or something that somehow slipped through a certification process. Quite the opposite. We know exactly how the airplane was designed. We know exactly how it was certified. We have taken the time to understand that….
context: During an April 2019 earnings call, Muilenburg made comprehensive false assertions about the certification process while knowing of documentation gaps, the concerning chat, and unresolved questions about FAA-AEG disclosures.

label: Muilenburg reaffirms false certification claims at shareholders meeting
original_label: Muilenburg reaffirms false certification claims at shareholders meeting
quote: We have gone back and confirmed again … that we followed exactly the steps in our design and certification processes that consistently produce safe airplanes. It was designed per our standards. It was certified per our standards.
context: Five days after the earnings call, the CEO repeated the false assertions about certification compliance at a public shareholders meeting, reinforcing the misleading narrative.

label: FAA-AEG unaware of key facts about MCAS operational scope
original_label: FAA-AEG unaware of key facts about MCAS operational scope
quote: Prior to the April 2019 Statements, Boeing had, in responding to a subpoena issued by the U.S. Department of Justice ("DOJ") in a criminal investigation into the 737 MAX certification process, uncovered documents that suggested that key facts about MCAS's operational scope had not been disclosed to the FAA's Aircraft Evaluation Group ("FAA-AEG"), the section of the FAA responsible for the review and approval of pilot training requirements and flight manuals for the 737 MAX.
context: During DOJ discovery in January 2019, Boeing uncovered documents revealing that critical information about MCAS's expanded operational scope had not reached the FAA group responsible for training and manual approvals.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Documentation gaps identified in compliance review
original_label: Documentation gaps identified in compliance review
quote: The MCAS Certification Compliance Review ultimately concluded that the certification process with respect to MCAS was compliant with FAA regulations. However, the written report identified several documentation gaps and inconsistencies relating to MCAS and the certification process, including a lack of adequate supporting documentation for the assumption, used by Boeing engineers and test pilots throughout the design and testing process, that repeated unintended MCAS activations (as the crew of Lion Air Flight 610 experienced) would be no more hazardous than a single unintended MCAS activation – an assumption that was later called into doubt by the SRB.
context: Boeing's internal compliance review found that a critical safety assumption about MCAS (that repeated activations posed no greater risk than single activations) lacked adequate supporting documentation throughout the design process.

label: MCAS removal from training rationale not properly documented
original_label: MCAS removal from training rationale not properly documented
quote: The MCAS Certification Compliance Review report also noted that the supporting rationale for the decision to remove MCAS from the differences training and flight manuals was not properly documented and had been made contemporaneously with the MCAS Expansion. These findings raised questions as to whether the FAA-AEG had been made aware of, and had an opportunity to evaluate, the MCAS Expansion when it agreed to Boeing's proposal to remove MCAS from the differences training and manuals.
context: Boeing's compliance review uncovered that the decision to omit MCAS from pilot training occurred at the same time as the MCAS Expansion, with poor documentation of the rationale, raising questions about whether the FAA had adequate information.

label: Undisclosed MCAS framed as outside standard operating conditions
original_label: Undisclosed MCAS framed as outside standard operating conditions
quote: Boeing employees responsible for communicating with the FAA-AEG presented MCAS to the FAA-AEG as a feature that could only activate in a very specific, high-speed scenario that was outside the normal flight envelope and therefore unlikely to ever be encountered by a commercial pilot. They made these representations to FAA-AEG personnel beginning in or around June 2015.
context: Boeing developed and consistently deployed a shared characterization of MCAS as outside normal operations, which became the basis for omitting it from pilot training materials and flight manuals.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: MCAS expansion coincided with training determination
original_label: MCAS expansion coincided with training determination
quote: In or around March 2016, Boeing introduced the MCAS Expansion, significantly broadening MCAS's operational scope. No longer limited to a specific, rare high-speed scenario, MCAS could now activate at abnormally high AoA throughout the entire speed range of the 737 MAX, including during the initial climb and the final descent, and its command authority was significantly increased to allow it to function effectively at lower speeds.
context: The MCAS Expansion occurred in March 2016, five months before the FAA-AEG's August 2016 provisional determination to accept CBT-only training, showing the two decisions were procedurally linked.

label: Rhythms hedge precursor to Raptors
original_label: Rhythms hedge precursor to Raptors
quote: The Rhythms transaction was Enron's first business dealing with the LJM partnerships. The transaction is significant for several reasons. It was the first time that Enron transferred its own stock to an SPE and used the SPE to "hedge" an Enron merchant investment. In this respect, Rhythms was the precursor to the Raptor vehicles discussed below in Section V.
context: The Powers Report identifies how the Rhythms structure in 1999 established a template that would be repeated and expanded in subsequent, larger Raptor transactions.

label: Raptors expand Rhythms logic across merchant portfolio
original_label: Raptors expand Rhythms logic across merchant portfolio
quote: Expanding on the concepts underlying the Rhythms transaction (described in the preceding Section of this Report), Enron sought to use the "embedded" value of its own equity to counteract declines in the value of certain of its merchant investments. Enron used the extremely complex Raptor structured finance vehicles to avoid reflecting losses in the value of some merchant investments in its income statement.
context: The Report shows how the Raptor program escalated the hedging strategy introduced in Rhythms to cover multiple assets with a notional value of $1.5 billion by November 2000.

label: Chewco deficit financed with opaque equity structure
original_label: Chewco deficit financed with opaque equity structure
quote: In November and December of 1997, Enron and Kopper created a new capital structure for Chewco, which had three elements: $240 million unsecured subordinated loan to Chewco from Barclays Bank PLC, which Enron would guarantee; $132 million advance from JEDI to Chewco under a revolving credit agreement; and $11.5 million in equity (representing approximately 3% of total capital) from Chewco's general and limited partners. Kopper invested approximately $115,000 in Chewco's general partner, and approximately $10,000 in its limited partner before transferring his limited partnership interest to Dodson. But no third-party investors were identified to provide outside equity. Instead, to obtain the remaining $11.4 million, Enron and Kopper reached agreement with Barclays Bank to obtain what were described as "equity loans" to Big River (Chewco's limited partner) and Little River (Big River's sole member).
context: The Report documents how Chewco's capital structure was designed to appear to satisfy accounting rules while actually failing to do so, establishing a pattern that would be repeated in LJM structures.

label: First margin deterioration masked with cross-guarantee
original_label: First margin deterioration masked with cross-guarantee
quote: Raptor I and Raptor III developed significant credit capacity problems near the end of 2000. For Raptor I, the problem was that many of the derivative transactions with Enron resulted in losses to Talon, but the price of Enron stock had not appreciated significantly. In an effort to avoid having to record a loss for Raptors I and III on its 2000 financial statements, Enron's accountants, working with Andersen, decided to use the "excess" credit capacity in Raptors II and IV to shore up the credit capacity in Raptors I and III. A 45-day cross-guarantee agreement, dated December 22, 2000, essentially merged the credit capacity of all four Raptors. The effect was that Enron would not, for year end, record a credit reserve loss unless there was negative credit capacity on a combined basis.
context: Enron used a temporary accounting fix in 2000 to avoid recording losses, foreshadowing the larger Q1 2001 restructuring that would follow as the underlying problems worsened.

label: Q1 2001 restructuring transfers massive Enron shares
original_label: Q1 2001 restructuring transfers massive Enron shares
quote: To make up for this potential shortfall, Enron entered into an extremely complex transaction with Raptors II and IV. The essence of the transaction was that Enron agreed to deliver up to 18 million additional Enron shares, if necessary, to Raptors II and IV to make up any Enron stock shortfall from the original stock contracts. In return, Raptors II and IV increased their notes payable to Enron by a total of approximately $260 million. In addition, to add credit capacity to Raptors II and IV (which in turn supported Raptors I and III), Enron sold them 12 million shares of Enron stock, to be delivered on March 1, 2005, at $47 per share. In exchange, Raptors II and IV increased their notes payable to Enron by a total of $568 million.
context: The March 2001 restructuring escalated the commitment of Enron equity to the Raptors by over $800 million, moving beyond the December 2000 temporary fix to a more elaborate solution.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Chewco structured to fail SPE requirements
original_label: Chewco structured to fail SPE requirements
quote: Although Enron reviewed the transaction closely in late October and early November 2001, both Enron and Andersen concluded that Chewco was an SPE without sufficient outside equity, and that it should have been consolidated into Enron's financial statements. As a result, Enron announced in November that it would restate its prior period financial statements from 1997 through 2001. The retroactive consolidation of Chewco--and the investment partnership in which Chewco was a limited partner--had a huge impact.
context: The Report documents that Chewco's capital structure plainly did not meet the 3% outside equity requirement, yet this was not identified or corrected for four years.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Chewco reserve accounts funded retroactively
original_label: Chewco reserve accounts funded retroactively
quote: At a minimum, Chewco fell short of the required equity at risk by that amount and did not qualify as an adequately capitalized SPE. As a result, Chewco should have been consolidated into Enron's consolidated financial statements from the outset and, because JEDI's non-consolidation depended upon Chewco's non-consolidation status, JEDI also should have been consolidated beginning in November 1997. Many of the people involved in this transaction for Enron profess no recollection of the Barclays funding, the reserve accounts, or the $6.6 million in cash collateral. This group includes the Enron officer who signed the December 30 letter agreement and the authorization for the $6.6 million wire transfer to Barclays at closing. By contrast, others told us that those matters were known and openly discussed.
context: The Report shows that the $6.6 million in cash reserve collateral that violated the equity requirement was either unknown to or deliberately overlooked by Enron executives and Andersen.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Rhythms put priced as if fully creditworthy counterparty
original_label: Rhythms put priced as if fully creditworthy counterparty
quote: In order to secure its right to repayment, Barclays required Big River and Little River to establish cash "reserve accounts." The parties initially made an effort to maintain the "equity" appearance of the transaction--by providing that the reserve accounts would be funded only with the last 3% of any cash distributions from JEDI to Chewco, and that Barclays could not utilize those funds if it would bring Chewco's "equity" below 3%. But Barclays ultimately required that the reserve accounts be funded with $6.6 million in cash at closing, and that the reserve accounts be fully pledged to secure repayment of the $11.4 million. The parties initially made an effort to maintain the "equity" appearance of the transaction by providing that the reserve accounts would be funded only with the last 3% of any cash distributions from JEDI to Chewco, and that Barclays could not utilize those funds if it would bring Chewco's "equity" below 3%. But Barclays ultimately required that the reserve accounts be funded with $6.6 million in cash at closing.
context: The Report shows how initial accounting fiction about reserves was abandoned for practical financing requirements, yet the accounting treatment remained unchanged.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Raptor put option pricing assumes creditworthiness
original_label: Raptor put option pricing assumes creditworthiness
quote: In order to create the required $41 million of income for distribution to LJM2, Enron purchased from Talon a put option on Enron stock for a premium of $41 million. The put option gave Enron the right to require Talon to purchase approximately 7.2 million shares of Enron common stock on October 18, 2000, six months after the effective date of the transaction, at a strike price of $57.50 per share. The closing price of Enron stock was $68 per share when Enron purchased the put. As long as Enron's share price remained above $57.50, the put option would expire worthless to Enron, and Talon would be entitled to record the $41 million premium as income. Enron's purchase of the put option for $41 million was unusual for two reasons. First, from an economic perspective--rather than merely a means to pay LJM2--the put option was a bet by Enron that its own stock price would decline substantially. Second, the price of the put was calculated by a method appropriate only if the transaction were between two fully creditworthy parties. In fact, Talon was not sufficiently creditworthy.
context: The Report shows how the $41 million put was priced using creditworthy-party methodology despite Talon having only $71 million of assets to cover a potential $7 million+ share obligation.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Restriction on Enron stock simultaneously discounted and collared
original_label: Restriction on Enron stock simultaneously discounted and collared
quote: To protect Talon against a possible decline in Enron stock price--which would decrease the value of Talon's principal asset, and thereby decrease its credit capacity--on October 30, 2000, Enron entered into a "costless collar" on the approximately 7.6 million Enron shares and stock contracts in Talon. The "collar" provided that, if Enron stock fell below $81, Enron would pay Talon the amount of any loss. This protected Talon's credit capacity against possible future declines in Enron stock. This collar was inconsistent with certain fundamental elements of the original transaction. Enron had originally transferred $537 million of its own stock and stock contracts to Talon. It discounted the value of that stock by approximately 35% because it was restricted from being sold, pledged or hedged for a three-year period. These restrictions reduced the value of the stock, and were a key basis for PwC's fairness opinion. By agreeing to the collar, Enron had to lift, in part, the restriction that had justified the 35% discount on the stock ($187 million).
context: The Report documents how the collar undermined the accounting basis for the original discount, yet both the discount and the collar remained in the financial statements.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: LJM2 initial return guarantees equity at risk illusion
original_label: LJM2 initial return guarantees equity at risk illusion
quote: It was understood by those who structured Talon--although it is not reflected in the Talon documents or Board presentations--that Talon would not write any derivatives until LJM2 received an initial return of $41 million or a 30% annualized rate of return, whichever was greater, from income earned by Talon. Put another way, before hedging could begin, LJM2 had to have received back the entire amount of its investment plus a substantial return. This allowed LJM2 effectively to receive a return of its capital but, from an accounting perspective, leave $30 million of capital "at risk" to meet the 3% outside equity requirement for non-consolidation. If LJM2 did not receive its specified return in six months, it could require Enron to purchase its interest in Talon at a value based on the unrestricted price of Talon's Enron stock and stock contracts.
context: The Report shows how LJM2's guaranteed return mechanism violated the fundamental principle that equity must be at risk, yet this was accepted by accountants as meeting the 3% requirement.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Rhythms unwind values restricted shares at unrestricted price
original_label: Rhythms unwind values restricted shares at unrestricted price
quote: The Enron shares, however, were not unrestricted. They carried a four-year contractual restriction. Because of the restriction, at closing on June 30, 1999, those shares were given a valuation discount of 38%. Although some of the discount would have amortized from June 1999 through March 2000, a substantial amount should have remained. For example, assuming straight-line amortization of the restricted discount over four years, at the closing price on March 22, 2000, there would have been approximately $72 million of the discount left at the time of the unwind. If an appropriate valuation discount had been applied to the shares at that time, the value Enron gave up (the $207 million in Rhythms options plus $27 million in cash) exceeded the value Enron received ($161 million in restricted Enron shares) by more than $70 million. It is difficult to understand why Enron's accounting personnel did not use the discounted value of the restricted shares to assess the fairness of the exchange.
context: The Report shows that in the March 2000 Rhythms unwind, Enron valued restricted shares at unrestricted price, contrary to the methodology used when the restriction was first imposed and to standards applied later in the Raptors.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: LJM transactions integrated into approval workflows
original_label: LJM transactions integrated into approval workflows
quote: Over time, the Board required, and Management told the Board it was implementing, an ever-increasing set of procedures and controls over the related-party transactions. These included, most importantly, review and approval of all LJM transactions by Richard Causey, the Chief Accounting Officer; and Richard Buy, the Chief Risk Officer; and, later during the period, Jeffrey Skilling, the President and COO (and later CEO). The Board also directed its Audit and Compliance Committee to conduct annual reviews of all LJM transactions.
context: The Report documents how the Board formalized LJM transaction oversight into standard management procedures and committee functions.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: LJM employees paid by LJM while working in Enron offices
original_label: LJM employees paid by LJM while working in Enron offices
quote: In April 2000, Enron and LJM Management L.P. entered into a "Services Agreement" under which Enron agreed to have its staff perform certain tasks (for a fee), including opening and closing accounts, executing wire transfers, and "Investment Execution & Administration." The Services Agreement described these activities as "purely ministerial," and contemplated that LJM would pay market rates. That same month, Causey and Fastow signed an agreement regarding the use of Enron employees by LJM1 and LJM2. The employees would continue to be "regular, full-time" Enron employees for benefits purposes, but the LJM partnerships would pay the bonuses, and in some cases the base salary. LJM would also pay the costs.
context: The Report shows how a formal Services Agreement institutionalized the practice of Enron employees working for LJM partnerships while remaining in Enron offices.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: LJM Deal Approval Sheets formalize transaction review
original_label: LJM Deal Approval Sheets formalize transaction review
quote: The use within Enron of an "LJM Deal Approval Sheet"--in addition to the normal DASH--for every transaction with LJM, describing the transaction and its economics, and requiring approval by senior level commercial, technical, and commercial support professionals. The use of an "LJM Approval Process Checklist" that included matters such as alternative sales options and counter-parties; a determination that the transaction was conducted at arm's length, and any evidence to the contrary; disclosure obligations; and review not only by Causey and Buy but also by Skilling.
context: The Report documents formal procedures the Board was told had been adopted to control LJM transactions, though these were not consistently executed.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Raptor structure replicated across four vehicles
original_label: Raptor structure replicated across four vehicles
quote: The first Raptor (Raptor I), created effective April 18, 2000, was an SPE called Talon LLC ("Talon"). Talon was created solely to engage in hedging transactions with Enron. LJM2 invested $30 million in cash and received a membership interest. Enron and LJM2 then created two more Raptors--known as Raptor II and Raptor IV--that were not materially different from Raptor I. A fourth vehicle, Raptor III, is discussed in the next section.
context: The Report shows how the Raptor structure was institutionalized as a replicable template, with four separate vehicles created using the same mechanisms.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Daily tracking of Raptor credit capacity
original_label: Daily tracking of Raptor credit capacity
quote: To protect Talon against a possible decline in Enron stock price--which would decrease the value of Talon's principal asset, and thereby decrease its credit capacity--Enron's accounting department kept track of Talon's credit capacity on a daily basis.
context: The Report documents that monitoring the Raptors' deteriorating credit position became a routine daily function, enabling management to track and temporarily address the core problem.

label: Hedges described as non-economic accounting structures
original_label: Hedges described as non-economic accounting structures
quote: Handwritten notes apparently taken at the meeting by Enron's Corporate Secretary to assist her in preparing the minutes, state: "Does not transfer economic risk but transfers P&L volatility." The finance committee was also told that the Raptor vehicle was not a true economic hedge. Notes on the presentation materials, apparently taken at the meeting by Enron's Corporate Secretary to assist her in preparing the minutes, state: "Does not transfer economic risk but transfers P&L volatility."
context: The Report shows that Enron explicitly acknowledged to the Board that the Raptors did not transfer economic risk, yet the structure was presented as an acceptable 'hedging program'.

label: Transactions rationalized as beneficial to Enron
original_label: Transactions rationalized as beneficial to Enron
quote: The Board apparently believed that the conflict, and the substantial risks associated with it, could be mitigated through certain controls (involving oversight by both the Board and Senior Management) to ensure that transactions were done on terms fair to Enron. In taking this step, the Board thought that the LJM partnerships would offer business benefits to Enron that would outweigh the potential costs. The principal reason advanced by Management in favor of the relationship, in the case of LJM1, was that it would permit Enron to accomplish a particular transaction it could not otherwise accomplish. In the case of LJM2, Management advocated that it would provide Enron with an additional potential buyer of assets that Enron wanted to sell, and that Fastow's familiarity with the Company and the assets to be sold would permit Enron to move more quickly and incur fewer transaction costs.
context: The Report documents the rationale that Board and Management used to justify permitting Fastow's conflict of interest, framing LJM as providing speed and cost benefits.

label: Transactions approved as meeting accounting standards
original_label: Transactions approved as meeting accounting standards
quote: Although the minutes do not contain any detail regarding what Glisan told the Committee, it appears that his remarks were guided by a three-page written presentation provided to the Committee entitled "Project Raptor: Hedging Program for Enron Assets." The materials stated that Talon would be capitalized with $400 million in "excess [Enron] stock." It also stated that, "[i]nitially, [the] vehicle can provide approximately $200 million of P&L [profit and loss] protection to ENE. As ENE stock price increases, the vehicle's P&L protection capacity increases as well." The materials did not disclose that LJM2's contractually specified return was the greater of a 30% annualized return or $41 million.
context: The Report documents how presentations to the Board framed the Raptor structure as a legitimate risk management tool with protective capacity.

label: Accounting treatment characterized as creative and aggressive
original_label: Accounting treatment characterized as creative and aggressive
quote: On the accounting issues, V&E said that both Enron and Andersen acknowledge "that the accounting treatment on the Condor/Whitewing and Raptor transactions is creative and aggressive, but no one has reason to believe that it is inappropriate from a technical standpoint."
context: Vinson & Elkins' investigation in August-September 2001 used the term 'creative and aggressive' to normalize accounting practices that, in retrospect, violated generally accepted principles.

label: Asset sales framed as arm's-length market transactions
original_label: Asset sales framed as arm's-length market transactions
quote: Enron included the same representation and added that "[t]hese transactions occurred in the ordinary course of Enron's business and were negotiated on an arm's-length basis with senior officers of Enron other than Mr. Fastow."
context: The Report documents that proxy statements represented all LJM transactions as arm's-length, a characterization made without factual basis and used to rationalize their legitimacy.

label: Glisan designed Raptors as Treasurer while reporting to Fastow
original_label: Glisan designed Raptors as Treasurer while reporting to Fastow
quote: With the logic and seeming success (at that time) of the Rhythms hedge fresh in mind, Ben Glisan, who became Enron's Treasurer in May 2000, led the effort. Accountants from Andersen were closely involved in structuring the Raptors.
context: Glisan was promoted to Treasurer in May 2000 and immediately began structuring the Raptor vehicles while reporting to Fastow, replacing McMahon who had raised concerns about LJM conflicts.

label: Southampton Place offered to LJM-working employees
original_label: Southampton Place offered to LJM-working employees
quote: Unbeknownst to virtually everyone at Enron, several Enron employees had obtained, in March 2000, financial interests in the unwind transaction. These include Fastow, Kopper, Glisan, Kristina Mordaunt, Kathy Lynn, and Anne Yaeger Patel. Fastow's participation was inconsistent with his representation to the Board that he would not receive any "current or future (appreciated) value" of Enron stock in the Rhythms transaction. We have not seen evidence that any of the employees, including Fastow, obtained approval from the Chairman and CEO under the Code of Conduct to participate financially in the profits of an entity doing business with Enron.
context: The Report documents how Fastow and Kopper offered financial interests in Southampton Place to employees who were simultaneously working on LJM transactions for Enron, a mechanism for co-opting them into the deals.

label: Southampton employees received spectacular returns
original_label: Southampton employees received spectacular returns
quote: Even based on the limited information we have, the Enron employees received massive returns on their modest investments. We have seen documents indicating that, in return for its $25,000 investment, the Fastow Family Foundation received $4.5 million on May 1, 2000. Glisan and Mordaunt separately told us that, in return for their small investments, they each received approximately $1 million within a matter of one or two months, an extraordinary return. Mordaunt told us that she got no explanation from Kopper for the size of this return. He said only that Enron had wanted to terminate the Rhythms options early.
context: The Report shows that employees who participated in Raptor transactions for Enron were offered extraordinary returns from Southampton Place as compensation, though Mordaunt testified she received no explanation.

label: McMahon transferred after raising conflict concerns
original_label: McMahon transferred after raising conflict concerns
quote: Skilling took no action of which we are aware, and shortly thereafter McMahon accepted a transfer within Enron that removed him from contact with LJM. Neither Skilling nor McMahon raised the issue with Lay or the Board. Conflicts continued. Indeed, the Raptor transactions, which provided the most lucrative returns to LJM2 of any of its transactions with Enron, followed soon after McMahon's meeting with Skilling.
context: The Report documents that McMahon, who had raised serious concerns about Fastow's conflict of interest in March 2000, was transferred away from LJM matters shortly thereafter, and the Raptors proceeded under new leadership.

label: New Raptor employees in Fastow's group
original_label: New Raptor employees in Fastow's group
quote: In 2000, Glisan was involved on behalf of Enron in several significant transactions with LJM2. Most notably, he was a major participant in the Raptor transactions. He presented the Raptor I transaction to the Board, and was intimately involved in designing its structure. Enron approval documents show Glisan as the "business unit originator" and "person negotiating for Enron" in the Raptor I, II, and IV transactions. Another Enron employee responsible for later Raptors was Trushar Patel. He was in the Global Finance Group and married to Anne Yaeger Patel, an Enron employee who assisted Fastow at LJM2. Both Yaeger Patel and Glisan also shared in the Southampton Place partnership windfall, during the same period the Raptor transactions were in progress.
context: The Report shows that key architects and negotiators of the Raptor transactions were employees in Fastow's Global Finance group who also benefited from the Southampton Place investment.

label: Board not informed of credit capacity deficits
original_label: Board not informed of credit capacity deficits
quote: It appears that, at the meeting for the February 2001 review, the Committees were not provided with important information. The presentation included a discussion of the Raptor vehicles that had been created the preceding year. Apparently, however, the Committees were not told that two of the vehicles then owed Enron approximately $175 million more than they had the capacity to pay. This information was contained in a report that was provided daily to Causey and Buy, but it appears that neither of them brought it to either Committee's attention.
context: The Report shows that daily tracking reports of Raptor credit deficits were available to management but not disclosed to the Board oversight committees.

label: March 2001 restructuring not disclosed to Board
original_label: March 2001 restructuring not disclosed to Board
quote: Fourth, it does not appear that the Board was informed either that, by March of 2001, this deficit had grown to about $500 million, or that this would have led to a charge against Enron's earnings in that quarter if not addressed prior to March 31. Nor does it appear that the Board was informed about restructuring the Raptor vehicles on March 26, 2001, or the transfer of approximately $800 million of Enron stock contracts that was part of that transaction. The restructuring was directed at avoiding a charge to earnings. While these transactions may or may not have required Board action as a technical matter, it is difficult to understand why matters of such significance and sensitivity at Enron would not have been brought to the attention of the Board.
context: The Report documents that the major Q1 2001 Raptor restructuring involving $800 million in Enron stock transfers was not disclosed to the Board, despite the Board's approval authority over significant transactions.

label: Financial Reporting Group deferred to Global Finance
original_label: Financial Reporting Group deferred to Global Finance
quote: Preparation of the related-party transaction disclosures followed this general pattern, with one major exception: we were told that, because the related-party transactions were often extremely complex, the Enron Corp. accountants and lawyers responsible for financial reporting relied heavily on--and generally deferred to--the officers and employees in Enron Global Finance who were closer to the transactions and actually knew the details.
context: The Report documents that the Financial Reporting Group responsible for public disclosures deferred to Enron Global Finance (Fastow's group) on the substance of LJM transaction descriptions.

label: Information compartmentalized by role
original_label: Information compartmentalized by role
quote: The most fundamental management control flaw was the lack of separation between LJM and Enron personnel, and the failure to recognize that the inherent conflict was persistent and unmanageable. Fastow, as CFO, knew what assets Enron's business units wanted to sell, how badly and how soon they wanted to sell them, and whether they had alternative buyers. He was in a position to exert great pressure and influence, directly or indirectly, on Enron personnel who were negotiating with LJM. In many cases, the safeguard requiring that a transaction could be negotiated on behalf of Enron only by employees who did not report to Fastow was ignored. We have identified at least 13 transactions between Enron and LJM2 in which the individuals negotiating on behalf of Enron reported directly or indirectly to Fastow.
context: The Report documents that the control requiring non-reporting-to-Fastow negotiators was ignored, and Fastow's position enabled him to compartmentalize information and control deal flow.

label: LJM partnerships refused document production to investigators
original_label: LJM partnerships refused document production to investigators
quote: Although the Board directed that Enron employees cooperate with us, we had no power to compel third parties to submit to interviews, produce documents, or otherwise provide information. Certain former Enron employees who (we were told) played substantial roles in one or more of the transactions under investigation--including Fastow, Michael J. Kopper, and Ben F. Glisan, Jr.--declined to be interviewed either entirely or with respect to most issues. Moreover, we have not had access to information and materials in the possession of many of the relevant third parties. Arthur Andersen LLP ("Andersen") permitted the Committee to review some, but not all, of its workpapers relating to Enron. Representatives of LJM1 and LJM2 (collectively, "the LJM partnerships") declined to provide documents to the Committee and, in light of a confidentiality agreement between those entities and their limited partners, the Committee has not had access to materials in the possession of the limited partners.
context: The Report documents that key information sources regarding the LJM partnerships--the principals and the limited partners--were not accessible to the investigation, maintaining informational compartmentalization.

label: Andersen internal concerns not communicated to Board
original_label: Andersen internal concerns not communicated to Board
quote: An internal Andersen e-mail from February 5, 2001, to address serious concerns about Enron's accounting for and oversight of the LJM relationship. The people attending that meeting reportedly decided to suggest that Enron establish a special committee of the Board of Directors to review the fairness of LJM transactions or to provide for other procedures or controls, such as competitive bidding. There is no evidence of any discussion by either Andersen representative about the problems or concerns they apparently had discussed internally just one week earlier. quote: We had presentations from the Chief Accounting Officer, the Chief Risk Officer, Mr. Skilling present. We had presentations from the Chief Financial Officer, then Mr. Fastow. Well, I would have to refer to each meeting, but I recall that Mr. Causey told us at one meeting that all of the controls were being followed, and that they were all working effectively.
context: Winokur explains the Finance Committee received only high-level assurances about control effectiveness rather than detailed transaction information, maintaining compartmentalized knowledge.

label: McMahon meeting notes show CFO pressure on employees
original_label: McMahon meeting notes show CFO pressure on employees
quote: I find myself negotiating with Andy on Enron matters and am pressured to do what Andy wants. I do not believe this is in the best interest of the shareholders.
context: McMahon's March 2000 meeting notes with Skilling document pressure from Fastow on LJM negotiations, revealing a conflict that was known to senior management but not disclosed to the Board or widely known.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Handwritten economic analysis reframed as adequate review
original_label: Handwritten economic analysis reframed as adequate review
quote: My recollection is that it was a handwritten sheet of paper, and it basically was split onto two sides. And on one side it said something to the effect of total return to Mr. Fastow under a set of assumptions. The number that was shown for LJM was something on the order of one-fifth of that number.
context: Skilling describes receiving only an informal handwritten memo estimating Fastow's LJM returns, which he characterizes as an adequate basis for Board confidence in moderate compensation, redefining what constitutes proper disclosure.

label: Finance Committee relied on silence as assent
original_label: Finance Committee relied on silence as assent
quote: So by silence, you thought that was assent, correct?
context: DeGette probes Winokur's reliance on the absence of objections from senior management as evidence that controls were working, revealing how compartmentalization enabled false confidence.

label: Board claimed not to know what Kopper was doing
original_label: Board claimed not to know what Kopper was doing
quote: Did anyone ever tell the Board that Mr. Skilling wasn't going to sign off on the LJM deals?
context: Congressman Rush establishes that the Board received representations that Skilling would approve all LJM transactions, yet later testimony showed Skilling did not review or sign off on them, indicating a culture where Board representations went unchallenged.

label: Kopper's participation known to company but not Board
original_label: Kopper's participation known to company but not Board
quote: No, sir. I am sorry. I misunderstood you. We looked at—We told them, have the firewalls in place, but you did not actually have the information on every deal as the Audit Committee did.
context: Jaedicke admits the Audit Committee never received information showing Michael Kopper was negotiating for LJM on behalf of Enron, despite Kopper's participation being known throughout the company.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Asset-light strategy reinterpreted as avoiding liquidity problem
original_label: Asset-light strategy reinterpreted as avoiding liquidity problem
quote: Things called run on the bank. You can have a fundamentally solvent company that is profitable that has an illiquidity problem. That's my interpretation of what occurred.
context: Skilling reframes Enron's collapse as a liquidity crisis rather than a fundamental solvency problem caused by the asset-light strategy he championed, redefining the standard for what constitutes company health.

label: LJM structured as standard private equity fund
original_label: LJM structured as standard private equity fund
quote: Me, as a member of the Board of Directors and a member of management of Enron Corporation, knew that a private equity fund was being established, and that one of our executives, Andrew Fastow, would have a role, an economic interest in that entity.
context: Skilling normalizes Fastow's simultaneous roles as Enron CFO and LJM manager by framing LJM as a standard private equity structure, using industry vocabulary to make the conflict seem routine.

label: Mintz memo on approval requirements not received
original_label: Mintz memo on approval requirements not received
quote: To my recollection, I did not receive that memo. Second, I would have had no problem signing that, and I believe if you look at the specifics of the memo of Mr. Mintz's—in fact, do you have a reference for Mr. Mintz's memo in here? Do you have a copy of that memo?
context: Skilling claims not to have received the Mintz memo documenting that he was required to sign LJM approval sheets, a key document that was fragmented from him despite being part of formal procedures.

label: Arthur Andersen reviews scoped narrowly
original_label: Arthur Andersen reviews scoped narrowly
quote: We had Arthur Andersen reviewing the transactions, and we had Vinson & Elkins reviewing the transactions.
context: Skilling cites external auditors and counsel as controls, but testimony reveals they were not provided full information and their reviews were compartmentalized from Board-level knowledge.

label: Skilling promised to fix cesspool situation
original_label: Skilling promised to fix cesspool situation
quote: And you say, 'I will fix it. I will fix it.' And he brings additional matters up.
context: Greenwood summarizes McMahon's March 2000 plea that Skilling promised to fix the conflict-of-interest problem, yet instead reassigned McMahon three days later without addressing the underlying issues.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Transactions deemed acceptable after others signed
original_label: Transactions deemed acceptable after others signed
quote: In the next paragraph it says, 'All required signoffs for the 2000 transactions have recently been completed.' All signoffs have recently been completed. And then further in that same paragraph it says, 'In our discussions arranging for your signature,' which, as it said, the form provides for my signature, 'it says that we have—it was decided to provide you with all finalized approvals in aggregate rather than on a piecemeal fashion.'
context: Skilling indicates that once Causey and Buy had signed transaction approvals, the Mintz memo suggests providing him with approvals in bulk rather than individually, redefining his role from substantive reviewer to rubber-stamp.

label: Process established October 1999 for LJM approvals
original_label: Process established October 1999 for LJM approvals
quote: In October 1999, when the process was established for approval of transactions with LJM, the process is absolutely crystal clear. It involved approval by Mr. Causey and Mr. Buy.
context: Skilling describes formalized approval procedures for LJM transactions established in 1999, which then evolved and expanded over subsequent years without substantive Board oversight of individual transactions.

label: Board assured controls were working at October 2000 meeting
original_label: Board assured controls were working at October 2000 meeting
quote: At the October 2000 meeting, we were told they were—had been done so.
context: Winokur testifies that in October 2000, Mr. Causey, Mr. Buy, and Mr. Skilling represented to the Finance Committee that LJM approval sheets had been signed, enabling the Board to believe controls were functioning.

label: Board learned of Kopper involvement only through investigation
original_label: Board learned of Kopper involvement only through investigation
quote: The Board did not know that Mr. Kopper, Mr. Glisan, and others who participated in the Chewco and the Southhampton partnerships had taken actions that appeared to be adverse to Enron without getting code of conduct approval.
context: Winokur acknowledges in his testimony that the Board learned only during the Powers Committee investigation that Kopper participated in partnerships in which he had financial interests, revealing severe fragmentation of knowledge.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Hedges framed as managing technology investment volatility
original_label: Hedges framed as managing technology investment volatility
quote: We were creating a hedge for some highly volatile, high technology stock investments. In the first quarter of 2001, many of those high technology investments were dropping in value. The entire optical fiber business was collapsing at that point.
context: Skilling redefines the Raptor partnerships as legitimate hedges for volatile tech investments, normalizing the use of Enron stock to capitalize vehicles designed to avoid accounting charges.

label: Arthur Andersen partners raised concerns not surfaced to Board
original_label: Arthur Andersen partners raised concerns not surfaced to Board
quote: There were a number of memoranda that we read about in the paper, such as the discussion among the Arthur Andersen partners about the risks in Enron, and then 3 or 4 days later we have an Audit Committee and we don't hear word one about any of those concerns.
context: Jaedicke regrets that Arthur Andersen partner memoranda raising concerns about Enron risks were not communicated to the Audit Committee, demonstrating how auditor concerns were compartmentalized from Board knowledge.

label: Employees told LJM would never lose money
original_label: Employees told LJM would never lose money
quote: Employees quote our CFO as saying that he has a handshake deal with Skilling that LJM will never lose money.
context: Watkins' letter quotes Fastow's statement to employees about a guarantee against LJM losses, using informal vocabulary (handshake deal) to normalize the implicit protection offered to Fastow's partnership.

label: Special Committee found evidence of implicit loss protection
original_label: Special Committee found evidence of implicit loss protection
quote: We have identified some evidence that in three of the transactions where Enron ultimately bought back LJM's interest, Enron had agreed in advance to protect LJM partnerships against loss.
context: The Board's own Special Committee report documents three cases where Enron agreed to protect LJM from losses, indicating leadership tolerance for arrangements that violated arm's-length principles.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Deal approval sheets not required for all LJM transactions
original_label: Deal approval sheets not required for all LJM transactions
quote: The deal approval process was the standard capital approval process. Any time Enron was disbursing cash, any time Enron was disbursing cash of a certain level of magnitude there had to be a dash generated.
context: Skilling redefines the LJM approval sheet requirement by characterizing it as merely part of standard capital approval procedures, rather than a unique control for conflict-of-interest transactions.

label: Kopper's negotiator role hidden on deal sheets
original_label: Kopper's negotiator role hidden on deal sheets
quote: Did you ever know that Michael Kopper was involved in any of these—No, ma'am. That financial review or economic interest review ever done by the company or by your committee? Well, did they just show you some of the slides?
context: Jaedicke and DeGette establish that Kopper's name appeared on LJM deal sheets as negotiator for LJM, but these sheets were never shown to the Board, fragmenting knowledge of a key conflict.

label: Office of Chairman approved transactions but did not review
original_label: Office of Chairman approved transactions but did not review
quote: The presentation that Mr. Fastow presented to me was a projection for a cumulative 5-year rate of return. So this was from that—from the inception of LJM, for the next 5 years under a set of assumptions, which was a rate of return of the fund, how much he would make over 5 years.
context: Skilling describes Fastow providing only a handwritten projection of his expected returns, which Skilling accepted as sufficient basis for Board confidence, tolerating inadequate documentation.

label: Board did not know Southampton and Chewco details
original_label: Board did not know Southampton and Chewco details
quote: Sir, we did not know about the Southampton partnership until we read about it in the paper.
context: Jaedicke testifies that the Board learned about the Southampton partnership only through press reports, not through internal disclosure, despite Kopper and Glisan profiting enormously from it.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Control procedures listed but not verified as executed
original_label: Control procedures listed but not verified as executed
quote: Were you satisfied on every one of these transactions that either Mr. Skilling or Mr. Lay approved the transaction?
context: Tauzin questions whether Jaedicke actually verified that Skilling or Lay approved each LJM transaction, revealing that Board reliance on controls was a belief rather than verified fact.

label: LJM made money on every deal despite Enron losses
original_label: LJM made money on every deal despite Enron losses
quote: The Special Committee also reported that the LJM made money on every single deal it signed with Enron, even if Enron lost money. Wasn't that kind of strange?
context: Congressman Rush highlights the normalized pattern that LJM consistently profited while Enron lost, yet this was not flagged as a problem by Finance Committee members until the investigation.

label: Earnings increasingly dependent on LJM and Raptor transactions
original_label: Earnings increasingly dependent on LJM and Raptor transactions
quote: Later testimony from Mr. Olson stated that every investment Enron made was unsuccessful, that the international power and water projects, the broadband, and the energy supply contracts, all of these were unsuccessful. And as a result, in Enron's last year before bankruptcy, a billion dollars—well, 70 percent of its earnings came from Raptor.
context: Congressman Rush establishes that as Enron's core businesses failed, reliance on Raptor structures for reported earnings escalated, becoming a normalized emergency measure.

label: Glisan brought in to replace McMahon despite LJM conflicts
original_label: Glisan brought in to replace McMahon despite LJM conflicts
quote: When Mr. McMahon was found a new job, the guy brought in to replace him not only apparently felt it a lot easier to negotiate with Mr. Fastow but actually got in bed with him and invested in the partnerships, and in 6 weeks turned a $6,000 investment into a million dollars.
context: Tauzin documents that after McMahon objected to LJM conflicts, Skilling replaced him with Glisan, who then invested in Fastow's partnerships, showing leadership tolerance for conflict participation.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Balance sheet omission normalized as standard practice
original_label: Balance sheet omission normalized as standard practice
quote: He did not, to my recollection, raise an issue about our balance sheet. He was raising an issue about why we didn't publish our balance sheet on the same day that we came out with our earnings, which we have never done. There is a 3-day delay between the time that we issue our earnings release—or I think it is a 3-day delay—between the time we issue our earnings and when the balance sheet came out.
context: Skilling defends Enron's failure to publish balance sheets alongside earnings as standard practice, normalizing opacity that concealed the nature and extent of LJM structures.

label: Causey presentations claimed all controls working
original_label: Causey presentations claimed all controls working
quote: We had reports by other people with Mr. Skilling present about his responsibilities, that the controls were working properly.
context: Winokur testifies that the Finance Committee received reassurances from Causey that controls were working, with Skilling present, but never saw the actual deal sheets or evidence of approval.

label: Board paid $300,000 annually yet relied on management assurances
original_label: Board paid $300,000 annually yet relied on management assurances
quote: The Board has a responsibility, and it looks like from the Powers report you can only say they didn't tell us so far. And I guess that is what surprises me. The testimony from both of you today—and Mr. Skilling is that, you know, we were—maybe we were born at night but not last night. And that is just amazing what we are hearing, that we didn't know as Board members. We were paid $300,000 a year to be Board members, and you didn't ask questions.
context: Congressman Green critiques the Board's deference to management assurances despite being well-compensated to exercise oversight, indicating leadership tolerance for superficial governance.

label: Raptor restructuring hidden from Board knowledge
original_label: Raptor restructuring hidden from Board knowledge
quote: The Board did not know at all about the Raptor restructure, to the best of my knowledge.
context: Winokur testifies that the March 2001 Raptor restructuring that issued $800 million in stock was never disclosed to the Board, showing escalation occurring outside governance structures.

label: MCAS design changes official in March 2016, communicated to FAA July 2016
original_label: MCAS design changes official in March 2016, communicated to FAA July 2016
quote: Boeing's changes to the MCAS design were official in March 2016 and were communicated to the FAA in July 2016, as described in the NTSB System Safety and Certification Specialist's Report, section H, Certification of the MCAS Implementation and Function. Boeing applied for and, in March 2017, was granted an amended type certificate for the 737-8 MAX.
context: US NTSB comments responding to Ethiopian Airlines draft accident report, asserting the design changes to MCAS occurred in phased steps from March 2016 to March 2017.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: AOA sensor failure dismissed despite bird strike evidence
original_label: AOA sensor failure dismissed despite bird strike evidence
quote: Collins' report addressed the following potential AOA sensor failure modes: (1) manufacturing defects, (2) internal component failures, (3) heater failures, (4) non-impact structural failures of the AOA vane/attachment hardware, and (5) AOA vane impact failures. Through external environment testing (vibration, acceleration, and flight simulation) and physics-based performance modeling, Collins determined the following: The observed performance deviation of the left AOA sensor, which was recorded by the FDR 44 seconds after the beginning of takeoff roll, is consistent with the vane breaking at the hub and separating from the AOA sensor. A bird weighing at least 0.5 pound (0.23 kilogram) impacting the vane at 170 knots (the estimated airspeed of the airplane at the time of the left AOA sensor performance deviation) would be sufficient to cause the vane to break at the hub and separate from the AOA sensor.
context: US technical advisors and Boeing present engineering analysis to EAIB showing AOA sensor failure was caused by bird strike, redefining the root cause from sensor defect to external impact.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Bird strike hazard at Addis Ababa airport omitted from investigation
original_label: Bird strike hazard at Addis Ababa airport omitted from investigation
quote: The EAIB draft report omits factual information, analysis, findings, contributing factors, and safety recommendations regarding bird hazards and the effectiveness of bird mitigations at Addis Ababa airport. The EAIB draft report provides some details regarding a runway area search after the accident but inappropriately suggests that the lack of bird remains or AOA vane remnants indicates that the airplane was not impacted by a foreign object. The EAIB report fails to state that the search occurred 8 days after the accident and that the search did not include the area surrounding taxiway D, even though FDR data indicated that the airplane would have been positioned above the taxiway when the left AOA sensor data became erroneous.
context: US comments criticize EAIB for redefining the absence of physical evidence as proof of no bird strike, ignoring search methodology and timing deficiencies.

label: Crew not included in operational and human factors investigation
original_label: Crew not included in operational and human factors investigation
quote: The US team was not included in any postaccident interviews or on-site data gathering related to the flight crew operations and human performance aspects of the investigation.
context: US NTSB accreditation statement noting the US technical team was excluded from operational investigation components, fragmenting the investigation into separate domains.

label: EAIB declined Collins testing participation invitations
original_label: EAIB declined Collins testing participation invitations
quote: Collins invited the EAIB multiple times to participate in the simulation testing and live demonstration of the testing, but the EAIB did not accept these invitations. Nevertheless, Collins accompanied the US accredited representative to Addis Ababa in September 2019 and presented its analysis to the EAIB; this visit provided the EAIB with an unrestricted opportunity to interact with Collins staff and understand Collins' work in its entirety.
context: US comments note EAIB's repeated refusal to participate in Boeing-conducted testing of AOA sensor failure modes, creating knowledge fragmentation between investigative parties.

label: FDR not programmed to record alert message displays to crew
original_label: FDR not programmed to record alert message displays to crew
quote: Although the FDR was not programmed to record the presence or absence of the IAS DISAGREE and ALT DISAGREE messages, all conditions were met for the alerts to be presented to the crew. The systems logic (presented to the EAIB in September 2019) and flight simulations (conducted in December 2019) demonstrated the expected timing for the presentation of these alerts on the crew's primary flight displays.
context: US NTSB explains that technical limitations in flight data recording created information gaps about crew awareness, fragmenting understanding of crew performance.

label: CVR transcript incomplete and modified unilaterally by EAIB
original_label: CVR transcript incomplete and modified unilaterally by EAIB
quote: The CVR transcript provided in the EAIB report is not complete, omits key statements related to the flight crew's performance during the accident flight, and inappropriately adds analytical commentary to transcribed statements. Of immense importance is that the original transcript was developed by the entire investigative team, including international team members, whereas the changes to the transcript were made unilaterally by the EAIB.
context: US NTSB comments critique EAIB's unilateral editing of cockpit voice recorder transcript, fragmenting and obscuring the crew communication record.

label: Boeing communication to operators post-Lion Air accident
original_label: Boeing communication to operators post-Lion Air accident
quote: Boeing provided information to all 737 MAX operators in November 2018 (after the Lion Air accident but before the Ethiopian Airlines accident) to address uncommanded MCAS inputs. This information included operations manual bulletin (OMB)/FCOM bulletin ETH-12, FAA emergency AD 2018-23-51, a multi-operator message, dedicated meetings, and email messages.
context: US NTSB notes Boeing's dissemination of MCAS guidance to operators after Lion Air crash, showing organizational communication infrastructure for handling system anomalies.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: MCAS system design assumptions about pilot response
original_label: MCAS system design assumptions about pilot response
quote: We agree that the uncommanded nose-down inputs from the airplane's MCAS system should be part of the probable cause for this accident. However, the draft probable cause indicates that the MCAS alone caused the airplane to be unrecoverable, and we believe that the probable cause also needs to acknowledge that appropriate crew management of the event, per the procedures that existed at the time, would have allowed the crew to recover the airplane even when faced with the uncommanded nose-down inputs.
context: US NTSB reframes the probable cause to include crew performance factors alongside MCAS malfunction, redefining the accident as a failure of multiple systems including human performance.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: MCAS preserves flightcrew ability to control airplane
original_label: MCAS preserves flightcrew ability to control airplane
quote: The EAIB draft report incorrectly states (in several places) that the Summary of FAA's Review of Boeing 737MAX document indicates that the MCAS denies pilot control and trim authority. However, this document states the opposite: if MCAS is erroneously activated, the MCAS system preserves the flightcrew's ability, using basic piloting techniques, to control the airplane after the activation.
context: US NTSB disputes EAIB interpretation of FAA documentation, asserting MCAS was designed with assumption that pilots retain control capability despite uncommanded inputs.

label: Crew procedures for uncommanded MCAS refined post-Lion Air
original_label: Crew procedures for uncommanded MCAS refined post-Lion Air
quote: Boeing's response to Ethiopian Airlines' request for more information about the MCAS, dated December 3, 2018, provided specific guidance about the OMB and checklist prioritization. In particular, the response indicated, As is stated in the OMB, If uncommanded stabilizer trim movement is experienced in conjunction with the erroneous AOA flight deck effects, the instructed course of action is to use the Stabilizer Cutout switches per the existing runaway stabilizer procedure.
context: Boeing communication to Ethiopian Airlines in December 2018 shows procedures for managing MCAS were modified and communicated in escalating detail following Lion Air accident.

label: Design mitigation must account for human behavior but investigation lacks crew performance analysis
original_label: Design mitigation must account for human behavior but investigation lacks crew performance analysis
quote: Flight crew performance played a critical role in the accident sequence; however, a discussion of the accident flight crew's performance (including CRM) was not sufficiently developed in the EAIB draft report, which continues to focus heavily on system design issues. The absence of flight crew performance information limits the opportunity to address broader and equally important safety issues. As we have reiterated throughout the investigation, design mitigation must adequately account for expected human behavior to be successful, and a thorough understanding of the flight crew's performance in this accident is required not only for robust design mitigations but also for operational and training safety improvements necessary to achieve multiple layers of safety barriers to trap human errors and prevent accidents.
context: US NTSB assessment of investigation gaps noting human factors investigation was compartmentalized separately from technical factors investigation.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Flight crew expected to manage uncommanded MCAS via existing runaway stabilizer procedure
original_label: Flight crew expected to manage uncommanded MCAS via existing runaway stabilizer procedure
quote: Emergency AD 2018-23-51 and FCOM Bulletin ETH-12 instruct flight crews to conduct the runaway stabilizer checklist, which requires them to control airplane pitch manually with control column and main electric trim. If the crew had conducted the procedure in the emergency AD and the FCOM bulletin, the crew would have used manual electric trim to reduce control forces.
context: US NTSB describes how MCAS uncommanded inputs were redefined as manageable through existing emergency procedures rather than as a novel system failure.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: MCAS control authority and pilot responsibility reframed in probable cause
original_label: MCAS control authority and pilot responsibility reframed in probable cause
quote: We propose that the probable cause in the final report present the following causal factors to fully reflect the circumstances of this accident: uncommanded airplane-nose-down inputs from the MCAS due to erroneous AOA values and the flight crew's inadequate use of manual electric trim and management of thrust to maintain airplane control. In addition, we propose that the following contributing factors be included: the operator's failure to ensure that its flight crews were prepared to properly respond to uncommanded stabilizer trim movement in the manner outlined in Boeing's flight crew operating manual (FCOM) bulletin and the FAA's emergency airworthiness directive (AD) (both issued 4 months before the accident) and the airplane's impact with a foreign object, which damaged the AOA sensor and caused the erroneous AOA values.
context: US NTSB proposes reframing probable cause to distribute responsibility across MCAS malfunction, crew training, and bird strike, redefining the technical failure as one factor among several.

label: Operational factors investigation excluded from technical investigation team
original_label: Operational factors investigation excluded from technical investigation team
quote: The US team (National Transportation Safety Board [NTSB], Federal Aviation Administration [FAA], Boeing, and General Electric) participated in the on-scene and immediate local follow-on investigative activities. As permitted by Annex 13, the EAIB chose to have the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) and flight data recorder (FDR) downloaded and read out at the Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la Sécurité de l'Aviation Civile (BEA) and requested that the BEA name an accredited representative to assist throughout the investigation. The US team was not included in any postaccident interviews or on-site data gathering related to the flight crew operations and human performance aspects of the investigation.
context: US NTSB documents structural compartmentalization of investigation, with US technical team excluded from crew performance and operational interview portions.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Manual trim wheel forces increase with airspeed as normal expected condition
original_label: Manual trim wheel forces increase with airspeed as normal expected condition
quote: The draft report does not examine the flight crew's understanding of the effect of airspeed on the control forces required to move the control column and trim wheel. The draft report states that the FCOM did not include details on the higher trim forces required with airspeed. However, the FCOM states that the effort required to manually rotate the stabilizer trim wheels may be higher under certain flight conditions. Further, even though the FCOM did not include the effect of airspeed on the manual trim wheel forces, that information is specifically noted in the manufacturer's flight crew training manual. For example, that manual states, if manual stabilizer trim is necessary, ensure both stabilizer trim cutout switches are in CUTOUT prior to extending the manual trim wheel handles. Excessive air loads on the stabilizer may require effort by both pilots to correct the mistrim. In extreme cases it may be necessary to aerodynamically relieve the air loads to allow manual trimming.
context: US NTSB redefines operational difficulty with manual trim at high airspeed as standard training content, establishing crew responsibility for managing this known condition.

label: Crew did not see full picture of system failures and alerts
original_label: Crew did not see full picture of system failures and alerts
quote: Given that the conditions were met for the IAS DISAGREE and ALT DISAGREE messages to be annunciated to the crewmembers, their lack of conversation or action in response to the annunciations should be explored in the context of the flight deck environment, workload, crew experience, and training. The report's assumption that those messages did not appear, which is contrary to Boeing's description of the alerting system and the results of simulator testing during the investigation, severely limits the opportunity for recognizing and addressing potential crew training and experience improvements.
context: US NTSB notes crew may not have recognized all alert messages available to them, indicating informational fragmentation in the cockpit environment.

label: Repeated recalls for same defect type across vehicle lines and years
original_label: Repeated recalls for same defect type across vehicle lines and years
quote: More than 200,000 1974-1976 Volkswagen and Audi Fox model cars are being recalled to correct potentially defective accelerator cables, the U.S. Department of Transportation reported today. In a notification letter to the department's National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the federal motor vehicle safety agency, Volkswagen announced the recall of 105,000 1975-1976 Rabbits, 18,000 1975-1976 Sciroccos, 71,000 1974-1975 Dashers and 25,000 1974 Audi Fox models for the accelerator cable problem. The NHTSA has been investigating this problem since May 1977.
context: NHTSA news release, January 12, 1978, documenting how a single defect type (accelerator cable failure) had been normalized across multiple Volkswagen/Audi models and model years, with investigation ongoing since May 1977.

label: Multiple throttle/accelerator defects across different manufacturers over time
original_label: Multiple throttle/accelerator defects across different manufacturers over time
quote: An estimated 40,000 1975 model Volvo vehicles are being recalled for correction of two accelerator/throttle system problems which could result in the inability of the driver to control vehicle speed. Announcement of the recall was made today by the U.S. Department of Transportation. The department's National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the federal agency responsible for motor vehicle safety, identified the vehicles as model 240's with B20F engines, manufactured from August 1974 to May 1975. Volvo announced initiation of the recall after being notified of sticking throttle complaints received by NHTSA.
context: NHTSA news release, January 3, 1978, showing that throttle control problems in Volvo had been reported to NHTSA and persisted across a 9-month manufacturing window (August 1974-May 1975) before recall action.

label: Fuel tank defect in Pinto built into design across multiple model years
original_label: Fuel tank defect in Pinto built into design across multiple model years
quote: The U.S. Department of Transportation announced today that it has made an initial determination that a safety defect exists in the fuel systems of some 1.9 million Ford Pinto and 30,000 Mercury model years (except station wagons). An investigation conducted by the department's National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), on the crash performance of the Pinto's fuel tank and filler pipe has been completed. The findings of this investigation demonstrate that low to moderate speed rear-end collisions of Pintos produce massive fuel leaks due to puncture or tearing of the fuel tank and separation of the filler pipe from the tank.
context: NHTSA news release, May 8, 1978, announcing that the Pinto fuel system defect affected 1.9 million vehicles across multiple model years (1971-1976), indicating the problem was built into the design over time rather than a single manufacturing error.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: 1977 Pinto redesigned to meet newly effective fuel system standard
original_label: 1977 Pinto redesigned to meet newly effective fuel system standard
quote: The NHTSA also stated that its Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 301 concerning fuel system integrity became effective September 1976, to establish minimum performance levels in rear-end collisions. The fuel system of the 1977 and later model Pintos and Bobcats was redesigned, and a 1977 Pinto was tested and met the requirements of Standard 301.
context: NHTSA news release, June 9, 1978, on the Pinto recall, noting that pre-1977 models did not meet the new standard that became effective in September 1976, implying that the pre-1977 design was accepted as compliant under the prior, less stringent standard.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Cadillac fuel injection fires reclassified as requiring recall after dealer campaigns
original_label: Cadillac fuel injection fires reclassified as requiring recall after dealer campaigns
quote: This case was opened after the NHTSA reviewed a Dealer Product Campaign Bulletin published by the General Motors Corp. The bulletin, and an accompanying letter sent to 941 owners of 1975 Cadillacs with electronic fuel injected engines, concerned the replacement of a fuel hose because of leakage which could result in engine compartment fires. Three owner complaints were also received, as well as a report from the Dade County (Florida) Fire Department concerning 16 fires in late model Cadillacs. The investigation was expanded to include 1976 and 1977 models since they had similar fuel injection systems. In October, 1977 the manufacturer announced the recall of 133,419 vehicles to correct this problem.
context: NHTSA defect investigation report, October 1977, showing that GM initially handled known fuel leakage fires as routine dealer campaigns before the fire reports and NHTSA inquiry prompted reclassification as a safety defect requiring a formal recall.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Throttle cable failures embedded in multiple Volkswagen/Audi product line designs
original_label: Throttle cable failures embedded in multiple Volkswagen/Audi product line designs
quote: Volkswagen does not know how many of the recalled cars actually contain defective accelerator cables. Dealers will be instructed to inspect the cables on all recalled cars and replace the cables where necessary. VW expects to supply its dealers with parts and instructions by early February and will send out notification letters to owners at that time.
context: NHTSA news release, January 12, 1978, on Volkswagen accelerator cable recalls, noting that VW did not know the extent of the defect, suggesting the problem was embedded in standard production across multiple models rather than isolated to specific batches.
