label: MCAS scope expanded between design iterations
original_label: MCAS scope expanded between design iterations
quote: To achieve its promised fuel efficiency, the 737 MAX used larger engines than the 737 NG. These larger engines, and their placement under the airplane's wings, meant that the aerodynamics of the 737 MAX differed from those of the 737 NG. These different aerodynamics created a new handling characteristic for the 737 MAX that caused the 737 MAX's nose to pitch up during a certain flight maneuver called a high-speed, wind-up turn. To fix this pitch-up characteristic, Boeing created MCAS and incorporated it as a part of the 737 MAX's flight controls. In operation, MCAS would automatically cause the airplane's nose to pitch down by adjusting the 737 MAX's horizontal stabilizer (a horizontal tail located near the rear of the airplane). As originally designed, MCAS could only activate during a high-speed, wind-up turn. Subsequently, Boeing expanded MCAS's operational scope, including the speed range within which MCAS could activate, significantly altering its original design. Among other things, when the airplane registered a high angle of attack, the change expanded the speed range within which MCAS could activate from approximately Mach 0.6-0.8 to approximately Mach 0.2-0.8—that is, from only high-speed flight to nearly the entire speed range for the 737 MAX, including low-speed flight, which generally occurs at a lower altitude and in and around takeoff and landing.
context: The Statement of Facts describes how MCAS was initially designed for a narrow operational scope, then substantially expanded without corresponding disclosure to the FAA AEG, showing incremental design changes that compounded.

label: Initial briefing limits MCAS scope, later expansion concealed
original_label: Initial briefing limits MCAS scope, later expansion concealed
quote: In or around June 2015, Boeing Employee-1 and other Boeing employees briefed the FAA AEG on MCAS. During this briefing, Boeing described MCAS as a system that could only activate during a high-speed, wind-up turn. After the briefing, Boeing Employee-1 and another Boeing employee further discussed MCAS with an FAA AEG employee ("FAA AEG Employee-1") and reiterated to FAA AEG Employee-1 the limited operational scope of MCAS. Subsequently, Boeing expanded MCAS's operational scope, including the speed range within which MCAS could activate, significantly altering its original design. Among other things, when the airplane registered a high angle of attack, the change expanded the speed range within which MCAS could activate from approximately Mach 0.6-0.8 to approximately Mach 0.2-0.8—that is, from only high-speed flight to nearly the entire speed range for the 737 MAX, including low-speed flight, which generally occurs at a lower altitude and in and around takeoff and landing. Boeing disclosed this expansion to FAA personnel, but only to those personnel who were responsible for determining whether the 737 MAX met U.S. federal airworthiness standards. Boeing did not disclose the expansion to the FAA AEG personnel responsible for publishing the 737 MAX FSB Report and making the training-related determination.

Software Audits – Audit of the software development process was completed to verify safety requirements were appropriately coded into the software. The FAA completed an initial audit during the week of June 15, 2020, and the final audit on September 14, 2020.
context: FAA 737 MAX Timeline documents the formal certification procedures established after the crashes, showing how corrective testing and approval processes were institutionalized into structured routines with specific dates and multiple organizational units.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Cross-organizational governance structures for return to service
original_label: Cross-organizational governance structures for return to service
quote: Joint Operations Evaluation Board (JOEB)/Flight Standardization Board (FSB) – To support the review of proposed training for the Boeing 737 MAX and carry out the functions of the FSB, a JOEB was established. The JOEB was comprised of the FAA, and the civil aviation authorities of Brazil (ANAC), Canada (TCCA), and Europe (EASA). The JOEB conducted training sessions with global pilots (with varied experience in the 737 MAX) to validate proposed training requirements. The JOEB completed its work on September 22, 2020.
context: FAA 737 MAX Timeline shows how formal inter-governmental committees were institutionalized to embed certification decisions into collective organizational structures spanning multiple national regulators.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Formal independent review boards embedded in certification process
original_label: Formal independent review boards embedded in certification process
quote: Technical Advisory Board (TAB) – The FAA commissioned a TAB to independently review Boeing's proposed corrective actions. The TAB is made up of experts with no involvement in the initial certification of the 737 MAX, including members from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the United States Air Force, the Volpe National Transportation Systems Center, and the FAA. The TAB originally met in Spring 2019 and reviewed proposed MCAS changes at that time. Since that time, they reviewed all proposed modifications and made recommendations throughout the process. The FAA addressed all return to service recommendations prior to rescinding the grounding order. The TAB delivered its final report to the FAA on November 17, 2020.
context: FAA 737 MAX Timeline describes the institutionalization of independent expert review into formal organizational structures with specific membership requirements, meeting schedules, and embedded authority in the return-to-service decision process.

label: MCAS design changes multiply through development cycle
original_label: MCAS design changes multiply through development cycle
quote: Boeing's initial efforts focused on changing the activation and reset criteria for the MCAS control laws, which involved extensive pilot assessment in the simulator. As a result of continuous review and testing of Boeing's proposed software design changes, the FAA took a broader approach to how MCAS functions within the Speed Trim System (STS). The result is an extensive set of improvements to MCAS, with increased checks and balances at the system level.
context: FAA summary of Boeing's design change process from initial post-accident corrective action to final certification. Shows MCAS evolving from narrow software fix to comprehensive system redesign.

label: Original MCAS activation allowed repeated movements, design evolved toward single activation
original_label: Original MCAS activation allowed repeated movements, design evolved toward single activation
quote: The originally certified design of the MCAS control law enabled the system to activate repeatedly during manual flight (Autopilot OFF) and when the flaps are fully retracted. Once enabled, and if the airplane's AOA exceeded a threshold, MCAS provided the potential for multiple activations of the MCAS automatic airplane nose-down stabilizer trim commands if the pilot used the main electric trim switch during the high-AOA event. The new design changes this behavior.
context: FAA technical description of original versus revised MCAS design. Shows baseline design permitted escalating trim commands that later revision restricted to single activation.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Single AOA sensor reliance classified as acceptable during initial certification
original_label: Single AOA sensor reliance classified as acceptable during initial certification
quote: The MCAS flight-control law becomes active when the airplane exceeds an AOA threshold that varies depending on Mach (airspeed). If activated by a high AOA, MCAS moves the horizontal stabilizer at a rate of 0.27 degrees per second, which is the same trim rate as Speed Trim with flaps down. The magnitude of the MCAS command is a function of Mach and angle of attack.
context: FAA technical manual describing MCAS as originally designed and certified. Shows single-sensor design was baseline assumption without noted concern.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: High-AOA event effects on crew reclassified as manageable after accidents
original_label: High-AOA event effects on crew reclassified as manageable after accidents
quote: The FAA's test results found that all participants agreed that the alternative NNC (with CB pull) may not be in alignment with the intent of 14 CFR 25.777(a) and (c). The FAA concluded that due to its determination that an erroneous high-AOA event poses a major rather than a more severe threat to aircraft operations, the potential safety risk introduced by the circuit breaker pull in the NNC outweighs the safety benefit of silencing a nuisance stick shaker in the 737 MAX.
context: FAA engineering evaluation post-accidents. Shows agency reassessing severity classification of erroneous high-AOA events from hazardous to major.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Failure condition requiring timely pilot intervention deemed acceptable in original design
original_label: Failure condition requiring timely pilot intervention deemed acceptable in original design
quote: A comprehensive review of the integrated System Safety Analysis (SSA) of MCAS by Boeing and the FAA identified an extremely remote FCC failure condition that required timely pilot intervention to ensure continued safe flight and landing. Ensure that after any foreseeable failure of the stabilizer system, continued safe flight and landing is not dependent on the timeliness of the flightcrew performing a non-normal procedure.
context: FAA documenting Safety Issue #6 identified only after accidents. Shows design relying on pilot reaction time was initially approved despite later determination this was unacceptable.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: MCAS embedded in Flight Control Computer software as permanent system
original_label: MCAS embedded in Flight Control Computer software as permanent system
quote: Both the 737 NG and the 737 MAX include a Speed Trim System that automatically moves the horizontal stabilizer in response to changes from trimmed airspeed while in manual flight for speed stability. The 737 MAX includes an additional pitch augmentation flight control law called MCAS, which affects pitch characteristics in manual flight, with flaps up and at elevated angles of attack, to compensate for the aerodynamic pitch effects associated with the 737 MAX's larger, more forward located engines. MCAS enables the 737 MAX to comply with FAA regulatory requirements for certain handling qualities and cannot be removed unless replaced with a comparable system.
context: FAA system description in technical manual. Shows MCAS became embedded architectural requirement, not a feature that could be easily removed.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: MCAS design assumptions built into certification basis and type certificate
original_label: MCAS design assumptions built into certification basis and type certificate
quote: The MCAS was designed and certified for the 737 MAX to enhance the pitch stability of the airplane. As such, the design change is neither substantial (the change in design is not so extensive to require a complete investigation of compliance) nor significant (there was no change to the general configuration or the assumptions used for certification) from a product-level-change point of view. Rather, and most importantly, MCAS enhances the earlier design philosophy to be more robust. Therefore Boeing was required to demonstrate compliance with the existing 737 MAX Certification Basis.
context: FAA Type Certification decision document. Shows MCAS design assumptions embedded in formal certification basis, making deviations require new type certificate.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Single-AOA-sensor design embedded in software for months before accidents
original_label: Single-AOA-sensor design embedded in software for months before accidents
quote: In the new design, Boeing eliminated MCAS reliance on a single AOA sensor signal by using both AOA sensor inputs and through flight-control law changes that include safeguards against failed or erroneous AOA indications. The updated FCC software with revised flight-control laws uses inputs from both AOA sensors to activate MCAS. This is in contrast to the original MCAS design, which relied on data from only one sensor at a time, and allowed repeated MCAS activation as a result of input from a single AOA sensor.
context: FAA conclusion document. Shows single-sensor design was baseline built into operational aircraft software across entire fleet.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Maintenance procedures incorporated mis-calibration vulnerability into routine practice
original_label: Maintenance procedures incorporated mis-calibration vulnerability into routine practice
quote: The replacement AOA sensor that was installed on the accident aircraft had been mis-calibrated during an earlier repair. This mis-calibration was not detected during the repair. The investigation could not determine that the installation test of the AOA sensor was performed properly. The mis-calibration was not detected. As part of the KNKT investigation of Flight JT610, the FAA evaluated existing Boeing Airplane Maintenance Manual (AMM) procedures for AOA sensor installation. The KNKT investigation (Reference section 12.3) verified these existing procedures for AOA sensor installation will correctly identify a mis-calibrated AOA sensor.
context: FAA citing KNKT accident investigation findings. Shows maintenance procedures embedded in formal manuals did not catch mis-calibration, indicating procedural gaps became institutionalized.

label: MCAS function reframed as stability enhancement rather than control fix
original_label: MCAS function reframed as stability enhancement rather than control fix
quote: MCAS provides signals to move the horizontal stabilizer at elevated angles of attack to compensate for the aerodynamic effects of the 737 MAX's larger and more forward-located engines, resulting in the required column feel to the pilot. Duration of the MCAS command is a function of AOA and airspeed. At higher airspeeds, flight control surfaces are more effective than at lower airspeeds. Therefore, a smaller MCAS command at higher airspeed has the same effect as a larger MCAS command at low speeds. Without MCAS, the 737 MAX would not meet FAA's regulatory requirements.
context: FAA technical summary in Return to Service document. Shows MCAS described as compliance mechanism for handling qualities, obscuring its novel and safety-critical function.

label: MCAS non-activation assumption treated as design baseline
original_label: MCAS non-activation assumption treated as design baseline
quote: The revised MCAS activation criteria now include a requirement for the AOA to transition from a low AOA state (below the threshold) to a high AOA event (above the threshold) after the airplane is in the configuration and flight region where MCAS is utilized (flaps up and manual flight). This single activation of MCAS will be limited to maximum of 2.5 degrees of airplane nose-down stabilizer motion (which is referred to as a single MCAS command).
context: FAA technical specification of revised MCAS design. Uses euphemism single activation and frames limitation as design feature, not post-hoc safety constraint.

label: Pilot inattention to procedure reframed as normative behavior
original_label: Pilot inattention to procedure reframed as normative behavior
quote: During the accident flight, the DFDR recorded a control force of 103 lbs., after repetitive MCAS activation was responded to by the First Officer with inadequate trim to counter MCAS. At this point, the flightcrew was unable to maintain altitude. Therefore, KNKT recommends that Boeing include a larger tolerance in the design is required to allow operability by a larger population of flight-rated pilots. Rather than relying on crew procedures, the new design is such that the need for using the Stabilizer Runaway Non Normal Checklist will be extremely improbable. The procedure still exists, but should never be needed.
context: FAA response to KNKT accident investigation recommendation. Shows collective shift from expecting average pilots to execute runaway stabilizer procedure to engineering around it.

label: Flight Control Computer data sources segregated, limiting AOA sensor cross-check
original_label: Flight Control Computer data sources segregated, limiting AOA sensor cross-check
quote: Each FCC receives left and right AOA sensor values from the left and right Air Data Inertial Reference Unit (ADIRU), respectively. The AOA values are transmitted from the ADIRUs to the FCCs via databuses. During normal operation, accurate AOA values are transmitted over the databuses with a label that the values are considered valid by the ADIRU. A failure of that electrical circuit (e.g. open, short, etc.) will be detected by the ADIRU, and the ADIRU will not transmit data on the bus as being valid.
context: FAA technical description of MCAS AOA input architecture. Shows original architecture allowed single valid sensor to drive MCAS because electrical circuit isolation prevented cross-validation.

label: MCAS function not disclosed to airline pilots in standard training
original_label: MCAS function not disclosed to airline pilots in standard training
quote: The Flight Standardization Board first conducted a T2 test followed by a T1 test. It conducted both tests in accordance with FAA AC 120-53B. The T2 test evaluated pilot handling characteristics between the 737 NG and the 737 MAX series aircraft during maneuvers when MCAS was active. The FSB conducted the evaluations at the Boeing Flight Training Center using the 737-800 and the 737 MAX series full flight simulators (FFS). Following these evaluations, the FSB determined that no pilot handling differences exist between the 737 NG series and the 737 MAX series during normal operation of MCAS, as well as when the Speed Trim System (MCAS) is failed. However, it determined ground training is required for initial, transition and upgrade training.
context: FAA Flight Standardization Board findings in 2019. Shows MCAS initially determined not to require special pilot training because handling felt identical to prior model, limiting pilot knowledge.

label: Original certification did not require pilots know MCAS exists
original_label: Original certification did not require pilots know MCAS exists
quote: The FAA's Aircraft Evaluation Division (AED) is responsible for working with aircraft manufacturers and modifiers during the development and FAA certification of new and modified aircraft to determine: 1) the pilot type rating; 2) flightcrew member training, checking, and currency requirements; and 3) operational suitability. To help evaluate some of these functions for the 737 MAX aircraft, the AED formed a FSB. The AED formed the FSB consistent with FAA AC 120-53B, Guidance for Conducting and Use of Flight Standardization Board Evaluations, change 1. The evaluation results for the 737-8 MAX initial evaluation is contained in Revision 14 of the FSB Report, dated July 5, 2017.
context: FAA documenting pre-accident training certification process. Shows MCAS training not mandated in original 2017 certification, meaning pilots routinely flew aircraft without explicit system knowledge.

label: AOA DISAGREE alert capability existed but was disabled by default configuration
original_label: AOA DISAGREE alert capability existed but was disabled by default configuration
quote: The AOA DISAGREE alert message on the Primary Flight Display is not functional unless the AOA indicator option was chosen by the airline. This alert message is intended to be standard on all 737 MAX airplanes. Ensure 737 MAX Display System (MDS) software will alert the flightcrew with the AOA DISAGREE message if there is disagreement between the Left and Right AOA Sensors. Boeing has revised the AOA DISAGREE alert message implementation to achieve the original design intent to be standard on all 737 MAX aircraft.
context: FAA identifying Safety Issue #5 post-accident. Shows alert system designed but disabled unless airline paid for optional feature, fragmenting knowledge of sensor disagreement.

label: Component maintenance manual procedures at repair vendor fragmented from aircraft integration
original_label: Component maintenance manual procedures at repair vendor fragmented from aircraft integration
quote: The replacement AOA sensor that was installed on the accident aircraft had been mis-calibrated during an earlier repair. This mis-calibration was not detected during the repair. Therefore, KNKT recommends emphasizing the implementation of a company manual including equivalency assessment, training and written procedure, to ensure component being repaired are properly maintained.
context: FAA citing KNKT recommendation 04.O-2018-35.10 on Xtra Aerospace maintenance vendor. Shows repair procedures at component level lacked integration checks with aircraft installation requirements.

label: Certification testing fragmented between system levels obscured integrated hazards
original_label: Certification testing fragmented between system levels obscured integrated hazards
quote: There is no requirement for SMS for design and manufacturing organizations. The FAA currently requires an SMS only for part 121 operators. The FAA must mandate implementation of SMS for design and manufacturing organizations, thereby ensuring connection and interrelationship with the existing SMSs of airlines, airports, and service providers. The FAA should take the necessary steps to ensure a total system approach to safety, linking all safety requirements from type certification to pilot training, and operational performance of the product.
context: U.S. DOT Special Committee on FAA certification recommending systemic safety integration. Shows fragmented safety assessment across design, certification, and operations.

label: Original certification approved MCAS single-sensor design without documented hazard analysis
original_label: Original certification approved MCAS single-sensor design without documented hazard analysis
quote: During its evaluation of Boeing's proposed modifications, the FAA retained all compliance findings and approvals associated with the design changes related to MCAS. This thorough review has taken more than 22 months and included the full-time work of more than 40 engineers, inspectors, pilots, and technical support staff. The effort represents more than 60,000 FAA hours of review, certification testing, and evaluation of pertinent documents. This includes approximately 50 hours of FAA flight or simulator tests and FAA analysis of more than 4,000 hours of company flight and simulator testing.
context: FAA describing post-accident certification effort. Implicitly contrasts 22-month, 60,000-hour post-accident review with original certification that approved MCAS with apparently less scrutiny.

label: FAA approved MCAS design assuming pilot execution of runaway stabilizer procedure
original_label: FAA approved MCAS design assuming pilot execution of runaway stabilizer procedure
quote: The FAA conclusion from this analysis indicated that an average crew with no prior awareness could sort out the failure scenario and could correctly mitigate the failure using existing procedures. On November 6, 2018, the FAA issued a CANIC (see Appendix D) which notified Civil Aviation Authorities (CAA) around the world that the FAA intended to issue an Emergency AD to correct an unsafe condition on the 737 MAX.
context: FAA recounting pre-accident risk assessment after Lion Air flight JT610. Shows FAA initially accepted assumption that average pilots would correctly execute procedures during high-workload emergency.

label: FAA delegates compliance finding to Boeing ODA for MCAS certification
original_label: FAA delegates compliance finding to Boeing ODA for MCAS certification
quote: NOTE: Unless noted otherwise and in accordance with FAA rules (see 14 CFR 21.21) and policy (see FAA Order 8110.4c, paragraph 2-6.(j)(2)) Boeing developed all data (also known as substantiating data) and conducted all analysis and tests that are referenced in this report. The FAA oversees the process, reviews select substantiating data and may repeat any or all testing that the applicant conducts.
context: FAA footnote to certification compliance section. Documents that original MCAS certification involved Boeing conducting its own data development and analysis with FAA oversight, raising structural bias in favor of approval.

label: Original certification did not require system safety analysis for MCAS as novel function
original_label: Original certification did not require system safety analysis for MCAS as novel function
quote: Based on the JATR team's observations and findings related to the application of the Changed Product Rules to the certification of the flight control system of the 737 MAX, JATR team members recommend that the FAA work with other civil aviation authorities to revise the harmonized approach to the certification of changed products. Changed Product Rules (e.g., 14 CFR §§ 21.19 and 21.101) and associated guidance (e.g., AC 21.101-1B and FAA Orders 8110.4C and 8110.48A) should be revised to require a top-down approach, whereby every change is evaluated from an integrated whole-aircraft system perspective.
context: JATR recommending reforms post-accident. Implies original certification of MCAS under changed product rules lacked integrated system-level evaluation.

label: Delegation system allowed Boeing to self-certify MCAS design with limited FAA review
original_label: Delegation system allowed Boeing to self-certify MCAS design with limited FAA review
quote: In relation to the FAA's approval of the 737 MAX current design changes, the FAA addressed the impact of the JATR findings by implementing a higher degree of involvement in the design change evaluation and did not delegate any compliance findings to the Boeing ODA. In addition, the FAA supplemented BASOO resources with staff from other offices within the FAA. The additional resources compliment and expand the 737 MAX project team's knowledge, skills and abilities relative to Boeing's design change.
context: FAA response to JATR recommendation 6 on delegation system. Implicitly acknowledges original MCAS certification delegated compliance findings to Boeing ODA, which this post-accident certification explicitly reversed.

label: FAA failed to flag MCAS as novel system requiring enhanced certification scrutiny
original_label: FAA failed to flag MCAS as novel system requiring enhanced certification scrutiny
quote: Based on the JATR team's observations and findings related to human factors-related issues in the certification process, JATR team members recommend that the FAA integrate and emphasize human factors and human system integration throughout its certification process. Human factors-relevant policies and guidance should be expanded and clarified, and compliance with such regulatory requirements as 14 CFR §§ 25.1302 (Installed Systems and Equipment for Use by the Flightcrew), 25.1309 (Equipment, Systems, and Installations), and 25.1322 (Flightcrew Alerting) should be thoroughly verified and documented.
context: JATR post-accident recommendation. Indicates original MCAS certification did not subject human factors to thorough verification despite system being safety-critical and novel.

label: FAA culture prioritized production schedule over design scrutiny in 737 MAX certification
original_label: FAA culture prioritized production schedule over design scrutiny in 737 MAX certification
quote: Based on the JATR team's observations and findings related to the design process of the flight control system and the related system safety assessments for the 737 MAX, JATR team members recommend that the FAA promote a safety culture that drives a primary focus on the creation of safe products, which in turn comply with certification requirements. Aircraft functions should be assessed, not in an incremental and fragmented manner, but holistically at the aircraft level. System function and performance, including the effects of failures, should be demonstrated and associated assumptions should be challenged to ensure robust designs are realized.
context: JATR recommending cultural shift post-accident. Implies original certification culture fragmented assessment across modules rather than holistic aircraft-level analysis.

label: Flight test pilots trained to replicate average pilots despite superior skills
original_label: Flight test pilots trained to replicate average pilots despite superior skills
quote: Flight test pilots, who normally have exceptional skill and experience, are used to demonstrate compliance. Flight test pilots generally have more knowledge about the aircraft design characteristics than normal pilots do. Flight test pilots however, are trained to replicate the average flightcrew. The Aircraft Evaluation Group pilots, who have an operational flying background, also evaluate the aircraft during the certification phase.
context: FAA citing KNKT accident investigation recommendation 04.R-2018-35.12. Shows test pilots were trained to simulate average pilot behavior despite their superior capabilities, potentially masking design vulnerabilities.

label: International CAAs incorporated into joint certification process after accidents
original_label: International CAAs incorporated into joint certification process after accidents
quote: The 737 MAX Joint Operations Evaluation Board (JOEB) concluded evaluation activities at London's Gatwick Airport on September 22, 2020. The JOEB included civil aviation authorities and airline flightcrews from the United States, Canada, Brazil and the European Union. The civil aviation authorities and industry pilots selected for participation completed all scheduled tasks as planned. The JOEB determined that all design changes applicable to the 737 MAX are operationally suitable.
context: FAA describing post-accident training certification. Shows international regulators only integrated into training evaluation after accidents, suggesting original certification excluded their scrutiny.

label: Technical advisory board recruited from outside original certification team
original_label: Technical advisory board recruited from outside original certification team
quote: The FAA also commissioned a Technical Advisory Board (TAB) to independently review Boeing's proposed corrective actions. The TAB consisted of a number of technical experts with no involvement in the initial certification of the 737 MAX. Several of these experts were from other U.S. government agencies. The actions by the FAA and Boeing, summarized in this report, adopted the TAB's recommendations.
context: FAA describing post-accident oversight structure. Explicitly states TAB members had no involvement in original MCAS certification, indicating original certification team lacked independent review.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Pilot workload during MCAS malfunction reclassified from hazardous to major
original_label: Pilot workload during MCAS malfunction reclassified from hazardous to major
quote: The FAA reviewed the contributing factors and available data from both accidents and reviewed the existing MCAS design to identify issues and determine the actions necessary to safely operate the 737 MAX. Safety Item #4: FLIGHTCREW RECOGNITION AND RESPONSE: FDR data from both accidents show that the flightcrews were unable to effectively manage the stabilizer movement and multiple flight deck effects that resulted from the single AOA sensor failure. Ensure that after any foreseeable failure of the stabilizer system, safe flight is not dependent on the timeliness of the flightcrew performing a non-normal procedure.
context: FAA identifying Safety Issue #4 post-accident. Shows design requirement shifted from accepting pilot-dependent mitigation to requiring automatic protection.

label: MCAS command limit evolves from no limit to fixed 2.5 degree maximum
original_label: MCAS command limit evolves from no limit to fixed 2.5 degree maximum
quote: Safety Item #3: MCAS TRIM AUTHORITY: All MCAS commands were incremental commands, which moved the horizontal stabilizer a fixed amount, regardless of the current position of the stabilizer. Therefore, multiple MCAS commands resulted in a significant horizontal stabilizer mistrim condition, which the flightcrew could not counter using only elevator control. Ensure that if MCAS is erroneously activated, the MCAS system preserves the flightcrew's ability, using basic piloting techniques, to control the airplane after the activation. Boeing changed flight control laws to include a limit for MCAS commands. The MCAS will stop commanding stabilizer movement at a point that preserves enough elevator movement for sufficient pilot control of aircraft pitch attitude for current operating conditions.
context: FAA identifying Safety Issue #3 and corrective action post-accident. Shows MCAS authority grew unconstrained in original design, requiring post-hoc limitation.

label: MCAS function expanded from speed trim enhancement to mandatory pitch augmentation
original_label: MCAS function expanded from speed trim enhancement to mandatory pitch augmentation
quote: The 737 MAX was designed to handle and feel the same to the pilot as the 737 NG. Without the MCAS function, in some small areas of the flight envelope — such as approaching a stall and during higher g-force maneuvering — the new engines contribute to the control column feeling lighter in the 737 MAX than the regulations allow. These are not areas of the flight envelope in which the airplane normally operates. However, FAA regulations - specifically 14 CFR 25.143, 25.201, 25.203, 25.251, and 25.255 - still require the control column to have a higher pull-force feel in these flight regimes than would exist on the 737 MAX without the added stability from the STS and MCAS function.
context: FAA explaining MCAS design rationale. Shows MCAS grew from handling qualities aid for edge-of-envelope conditions to essential compliance system required across flight envelope.

label: MCAS design compartmentalized between Boeing and FAA certification teams
original_label: MCAS design compartmentalized between Boeing and FAA certification teams
quote: Based on the JATR team's observations and findings related to the FAA type certification process, JATR team members recommend that the FAA review and update guidance pertaining to the type certification process with particular emphasis on early FAA involvement to ensure the FAA is aware of all design assumptions, the aircraft design, and all changes to the design in cases where a changed product process is used. The FAA should consider adding feedback paths in the process to ensure that compliance, system safety, and flight deck/human factors aspects are considered for the aircraft design throughout its development and certification.
context: JATR recommending process improvements post-accident. Implies original certification lacked feedback paths ensuring FAA awareness of all design assumptions throughout MCAS development.

label: MCAS system design assumptions not systematically challenged across certification team
original_label: MCAS system design assumptions not systematically challenged across certification team
quote: System function and performance, including the effects of failures, should be demonstrated and associated assumptions should be challenged to ensure robust designs are realized. The safety analysis process should be integrated with the aircraft DA process to ensure all safety requirements and associated assumptions are correct, complete, and verified. The FAA should encourage applicants to have a system safety function that is independent from the design organization, with the authority to impartially assess aircraft safety and influence the aircraft/system design details.
context: JATR recommending post-accident reforms. Indicates original MCAS certification did not integrate safety analysis with design assurance or ensure independent safety function challenged design assumptions.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Erroneous multiple MCAS activations accepted in original design, eliminated post-accident
original_label: Erroneous multiple MCAS activations accepted in original design, eliminated post-accident
quote: Safety Item #2: MCAS RESET GENERATES REPETITIVE MCAS COMMANDS: When a continuous erroneous high AOA sensor value exists, the MCAS control law uses pilot release of the electric trim switch to reset MCAS activation. Once reset, the MCAS system will make another airplane nose-down stabilizer trim command after five seconds. This scenario repeats each time MCAS makes a command and the pilot makes an electric trim command of any duration and releases the trim switch. Ensure that if MCAS is activated, it will generate a single nose-down command. Boeing changed flight control laws to ensure that MCAS will not command repeated movements of the horizontal stabilizer.
context: FAA identifying Safety Issue #2 post-accident. Shows original design permitted escalating MCAS commands that post-accident revision limited to single activation.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: AOA sensor error handling embedded in flight control law as permanent feature
original_label: AOA sensor error handling embedded in flight control law as permanent feature
quote: An AOA sensor monitor was added to prevent MCAS from using an AOA input if it differs from the other AOA input by more than 5.5 degrees. Boeing incorporated a maximum command limit to disable the MCAS and speed trim operations if the stabilizer position exceeds a reference position. This limit ensures sufficient elevator control is available to provide maneuvering capability using control column inputs alone. An additional software change provides cross FCC monitoring to provide additional protections against MCAS malfunctions or any other erroneous FCC-generated stabilizer trim command.
context: FAA summarizing design changes in return to service report. Shows multiple protective mechanisms institutionalized into flight control law structure post-accident.

label: Elevator control sufficiency framed as preserving pilot authority over stabilizer
original_label: Elevator control sufficiency framed as preserving pilot authority over stabilizer
quote: The MCAS will stop commanding stabilizer movement at a point that preserves enough elevator movement for sufficient pilot control of aircraft pitch attitude for current operating conditions. This change limits the total amount of airplane nose-down stabilizer movement MCAS can command if there are repeated MCAS activations. This ensures that the flightcrew will always have maneuver capability through control column inputs alone, enabling the flightcrew to maintain level flight without requiring use of the electric trim switches or the stabilizer trim cutout switches.
context: FAA describing Safety Item #3 corrective action. Reframes stabilizer limitation as preserving pilot control rather than acknowledging original design stripped pilot authority.

label: Certification plan process permitted incremental MCAS changes to bypass re-evaluation
original_label: Certification plan process permitted incremental MCAS changes to bypass re-evaluation
quote: A type-design change is developed and assessed for effects to the overall airplane type design per requirements in 14 CFR 21.93 using an FAA-approved process. For major changes, the FAA must establish new findings of compliance for the changed areas. During a certification project, the FAA works with the applicant to manage the compliance activities and deliverables. The applicant describes the proposed change to the FAA, and includes functional and design details pertinent to the certification project. The applicant prepares a certification plan using requirements established by that model's certification basis at the time of type certification.
context: FAA describing type certification process. Shows certification plan framework allowed Boeing to define scope of changed areas, potentially compartmentalizing MCAS changes.

label: Original MCAS certification assumed pilot training not needed for operational suitability
original_label: Original MCAS certification assumed pilot training not needed for operational suitability
quote: However, it determined ground training is required for initial, transition and upgrade training. Furthermore, recurrent ground training and checking is necessary to ensure pilot knowledge and retention is achieved relating to MCAS system description, functionality, associated failure conditions and flightcrew alerting. This initial FSB training and checking determination was a provisional determination based on no design changes to the tested version of the FCC Software.
context: FAA recounting original 2019 Flight Standardization Board findings. Shows training requirements were provisional and shifted substantially post-accident after Boeing made design changes.

label: Airline pilots drawn into certification testing to validate design
original_label: Airline pilots drawn into certification testing to validate design
quote: The tests used four airline crews (three domestic crews and one international crew), each consisting of a captain and first officer. Flightcrews were from airlines operating the 737 MAX, based on employment with a U.S. or foreign air carrier, licensing level, varying experience level and crew position as a non-managerial or check pilot. Crew selection was intended to represent the cross-section of pilots expected to operate the 737 MAX in air carrier operation. FAA flight test, Human Factors (HF) specialists, and Aircraft Evaluation Division (AED) operations personnel were directly involved with the planning and execution of the evaluations.
context: FAA describing post-accident flightcrew operations compliance testing. Shows line pilots were co-opted into certification process only after accidents, suggesting original certification relied primarily on test pilots.

label: Progressive expansion of misleading claims over six years
original_label: Progressive expansion of misleading claims over six years
quote: Beginning on or about December 12, 1995, and continuing until on or about June 30, 2001, certain PURDUE supervisors and employees, with the intent to defraud or mislead, marketed and promoted OxyContin as less addictive, less subject to abuse and diversion, and less likely to cause tolerance and withdrawal than other pain medications
context: The Information charges the pattern of misconduct spanning nearly six years, showing wrongdoing extended and repeated over time rather than isolated.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Sales training embedded the misleading claims into standard practice
