original_label: Eli Lilly electricity contract recognized despite Indiana deregulation uncertainty
quote: In another example, Enron entered into a $1.3 billion, 15-year contract to supply electricity to the Indianapolis company Eli Lilly. Enron was able to show the present value of the contract, reportedly for more than half a billion dollars, as revenues. Enron then had to report the present value of the costs of servicing the contract as an expense. However, Indiana had not yet deregulated electricity, requiring Enron to predict when Indiana would deregulate and how much impact this would have on the costs of servicing the contract over the ten years.
context: Healy and Palepu show how Enron recognized half a billion dollars in present value revenue from a contract whose cost structure depended on a regulatory change that had not yet occurred.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: 3 percent independent equity threshold requirement violated
original_label: 3 percent independent equity threshold requirement violated
quote: Chewco and several other special purpose entities, however, did more than just skirt accounting rules. As Enron revealed in October 2001, they violated accounting standards that require at least 3 percent of assets to be owned by independent equity investors. By ignoring this requirement, Enron was able to avoid consolidating these special purpose entities.
context: Healy and Palepu describe how Enron redefined the 3 percent independent equity threshold as acceptable to ignore, violating a core accounting standard that determined whether consolidation was required.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Hundreds of special purpose entities embedded in financial structure
original_label: Hundreds of special purpose entities embedded in financial structure
quote: Enron had used hundreds of special purpose entities by 2001. Many of these were used to fund the purchase of forward contracts with gas producers to supply gas to utilities under long-term fixed contracts. However, several controversial special purpose entities were designed primarily to achieve financial reporting objectives.
context: Healy and Palepu document how special purpose entities became a standard institutional practice embedded in Enron's organizational structure by 2001, some created for the primary purpose of achieving accounting objectives.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Chewco entity created as standard solution to consolidation problem
original_label: Chewco entity created as standard solution to consolidation problem
quote: In 1997, Enron wanted to buy out a partner's stake in one of its many joint ventures. However, Enron did not want to show any debt from financing the acquisition or from the joint venture on its balance sheet. Chewco, a special purpose entity that was controlled by an Enron executive and raised debt that was guaranteed by Enron, acquired the joint venture stake for $383 million. The transaction was structured in such a way that Enron did not have to consolidate Chewco or the joint venture into its financials, enabling it effectively to acquire the partnership interest without recognizing any additional debt on its books.
context: Healy and Palepu show how Chewco became a structured institutional solution embedded in Enron's standard practice for handling joint ventures and debt financing through a special purpose entity model.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: EnronOnline scales trading operations into normalized business model
original_label: EnronOnline scales trading operations into normalized business model
quote: The creation of the on-line trading model, EnronOnline, in November 1999 enabled the company to develop further and extend its abilities to negotiate and manage these financial contracts. By the fourth quarter of 2000, EnronOnline accounted for almost half of Enron's transactions for all of its business units and had enabled transactions per commercial person to grow to 3,084 from 672 in 1999.
context: Healy and Palepu describe how EnronOnline institutionalized and scaled the trading model into a technological infrastructure that normalized and multiplied trading transactions across all business units.

label: Gas bank concept rationalized as risk management innovation
original_label: Gas bank concept rationalized as risk management innovation
quote: Jeff Skilling, who subsequently became Enron's CEO in August 2001, envisioned Enron's trading model during a 1988 McKinsey engagement at Enron. While deregulation generally led to lower prices and increased supply, it also introduced increased volatility in gas prices. Further, the standard contract in this market allowed suppliers to interrupt gas supply without legal penalties. By creating a natural gas 'bank,' Skilling foresaw that Enron could help both buyers and suppliers manage these risks effectively. The 'gas bank' would act just as a financial banking institution, except that it would intermediate between suppliers and buyers of natural gas.
context: Healy and Palepu document the collective organizational rationalization of the trading model as a legitimate solution to market problems caused by deregulation and volatility.

label: Information and market knowledge framed as sustainable competitive advantage
original_label: Information and market knowledge framed as sustainable competitive advantage
quote: Skilling believed that the major barrier to entry in gas trading was Enron's market knowledge achieved through its dominant market position. However, many other firms were well positioned to challenge Enron's dominance, including large gas producers, such as Mobil, gas marketers such as Coastal and Clearinghouse and financial firms such as Phibro, AIG, Chase and Citibank.
context: Healy and Palepu show how Enron's leadership rationalized that information and market knowledge constituted a durable competitive advantage, even though the authors note this belief was unwarranted given the presence of many capable competitors.

label: Complex business model characterized as extension of proven expertise
original_label: Complex business model characterized as extension of proven expertise
quote: Enron argued that the systems and expertise it had acquired in gas trading could be leveraged to the new markets. The trading model therefore was touted as a way for Enron to continue to grow spectacularly as it diversified from a pure energy firm into a broad-based financial services company.
context: Healy and Palepu document the collective organizational rationalization that expertise proven in gas trading could be reliably extended to wholly new markets and business types.

label: Structured finance transactions rationalized as proper financial innovation
original_label: Structured finance transactions rationalized as proper financial innovation
quote: Accounting rule-makers have been debating appropriate accounting rules for these transactions for several years. Meanwhile, mechanical conventions have been used to record these transactions, creating a divergence between economic reality and accounting numbers.
context: Healy and Palepu show how the absence of clear accounting standards for structured finance was collectively rationalized as allowing transactions to proceed under mechanical conventions, despite the acknowledged divergence from economic reality.

label: CFO and key employees drawn into profitable special purpose entity partnerships
original_label: CFO and key employees drawn into profitable special purpose entity partnerships
quote: Moreover, Enron allowed several key employees, including its chief financial officer Andrew Fastow, to become partners of the special purpose entities. In subsequent transactions between the special purpose entities and Enron, these employees profited handsomely, raising questions about whether they had fulfilled their fiduciary responsibility to Enron's stockholders.
context: Healy and Palepu document how key employees including the CFO were co-opted into the special purpose entity structure through financial incentives and partnership status, compromising their fiduciary role.

label: Minimal segment disclosure prevented understanding of business performance
original_label: Minimal segment disclosure prevented understanding of business performance
quote: It is difficult to figure out which parts of Enron's business model were working and which were not, since the company provided minimal segment disclosure. In addition, its 2000 domestic trading performance was affected by the California energy crisis, where illegal price manipulation by Enron and others is being investigated.
context: Healy and Palepu note that Enron's minimal segment disclosure fragmented investors' knowledge of which business units were actually performing, preventing full understanding of the business.

label: Investors unaware special purpose entities hedged with Enron stock, not protected
original_label: Investors unaware special purpose entities hedged with Enron stock, not protected
quote: In addition to the accounting failures, Enron provided only minimal disclosure on its relations with the special purpose entities. The company represented to investors that it had hedged downside risk in its own illiquid investments through transactions with special purpose entities. Yet investors were unaware that the special purpose entities were actually using Enron's own stock and financial guarantees to carry out these hedges, so that Enron was not actually protected from downside risk.
context: Healy and Palepu show how minimal disclosure about special purpose entity transactions fragmented investor knowledge, allowing Enron to represent itself as hedged when it was actually unprotected.

label: Audit committee agenda too broad and meetings too brief for oversight
original_label: Audit committee agenda too broad and meetings too brief for oversight
quote: For example, consider the agenda for Enron's Audit Committee meeting on February 12, 2001. The meeting lasted only 85 minutes, yet covered a number of important issues, including: a) a report by Arthur Andersen reviewing Enron's compliance with generally accepted accounting standards and internal controls; b) a report on the adequacy of reserves and related party transactions; c) a report on disclosures relating to litigation risks and contingencies; d) a report on the 2000 financial statements, which noted new disclosures on broadband operations and provided updates on the wholesale business and credit risks; e) a review of the Audit and Compliance Committee Report; f) discussion of a revision in the Audit and Compliance Committee Charter; g) a report on executive and director use of company aircraft; h) a review of the 2001 Internal Control Audit Plan, which included an overview of key business trends, an assessment of key business risks and a summary of changes in internal control efforts by businesses for 2001 compared to the period 1998 to 2000; and i) a review of company policy for management communication with analysts and the impact of Regulation Fair Disclosure.
context: Healy and Palepu document how the audit committee's meeting structure fragmented oversight across too many issues in too little time, preventing deep scrutiny of any single area.

label: Audit committee unable to question technical accounting on special entities
original_label: Audit committee unable to question technical accounting on special entities
quote: For most of the above agenda items, Enron's Audit Committee was in no position to second-guess the auditors on technical accounting questions related to the special purpose entities. Nor was it in a position to second-guess the validity of top management representations.
context: Healy and Palepu show how the fragmented knowledge of audit committee members prevented them from independently evaluating the complex accounting structures even when they had the agenda item.

label: Arthur Andersen Houston office overrode critical reviews from Chicago office
original_label: Arthur Andersen Houston office overrode critical reviews from Chicago office
quote: Internal controls at Andersen, designed to protect against conflicted incentives of local partners, failed. For example, Andersen's Houston office, which performed the Enron audit, was permitted to overrule critical reviews of Enron's accounting decisions by Andersen's Practice Partner in Chicago.
context: Healy and Palepu document how organizational compartmentalization allowed the local office performing the audit to override critical scrutiny from a different part of the firm.

label: Stock option compensation structured for short-term stock price focus
original_label: Stock option compensation structured for short-term stock price focus
quote: As in most other U.S. companies, Enron's management was heavily compensated using stock options. Heavy use of stock option awards linked to short-term stock price may explain the focus of Enron's management on creating expectations of rapid growth and its efforts to puff up reported earnings to meet Wall Street's expectations. In its 2001 proxy statement, Enron noted that within 60 days of the proxy date (February 15), the following stock option awards would become exercisable: 5,285,542 shares for Kenneth Lay, 824,038 shares for Jeff Skilling and 12,611,385 shares for all officers and directors combined.
context: Healy and Palepu show how Enron's leadership compensation structure culturally endorsed and incentivized aggressive earnings management and growth expectations focused on short-term stock performance.

label: Auditors faced pressure to defer write-down charges at management request
original_label: Auditors faced pressure to defer write-down charges at management request
quote: When the credit risks at the special purpose entities became clear, requiring Enron to take a write-down, the auditors apparently succumbed to pressure from Enron's management and permitted the company to defer recognizing the charges.
context: Healy and Palepu show how Enron's management pressure on auditors was tolerated and effective in deferring necessary write-downs, indicating cultural acceptance of management override.

label: Arthur Andersen Houston office size and fee dependence on Enron
original_label: Arthur Andersen Houston office size and fee dependence on Enron
quote: In 2000, Arthur Andersen earned $25 million in audit fees and $27 million in consulting fees. It is difficult to determine whether Andersen's audit problems at Enron arose from the financial incentives to retain the company as a consulting client, as an audit client or both. However, the size of the audit fee alone is likely to have had an important impact on local partners in their negotiations with Enron's management. Enron's audit fees accounted for roughly 27 percent of the audit fees of public clients for Arthur Andersen's Houston office.
context: Healy and Palepu document how Enron represented such a large portion of Andersen's Houston office revenue that leadership tolerance for the client's preferences was structurally embedded in the audit fee relationship.

label: Audit firms promoted cordial relationships with management over watchdog role
original_label: Audit firms promoted cordial relationships with management over watchdog role
quote: This approach reduced the cost of audits and provided a defense in the case of litigation. But it also meant that auditors were more likely to view their job narrowly, rather than as matters of broader business judgment. Furthermore, while mechanical standards make auditing easier, they do not necessarily increase corporate transparency. Audit firms decided that profit margins would be perpetually thin in a world of mechanized, standardized audits, and they responded in two ways. One way was by aggressively pursuing a high-volume strategy, and so audit partner compensation and promotion became more closely linked to a cordial relationship with top management that attracted new audit clients and retained existing clients. This made it difficult for partners to be effective watchdogs.
context: Healy and Palepu show how audit firms' business model and compensation structure culturally endorsed cordial relationships with management over the watchdog function, creating systemic tolerance for management preferences.

label: Audit firms pursued consulting business growth over audit quality
original_label: Audit firms pursued consulting business growth over audit quality
quote: The large audit firms also responded to challenges to their core business by developing new higher-margin, higher-growth consulting services. This diversification strategy deflected top management energy and partner talent from the audit side of the business to the more profitable consulting part.
context: Healy and Palepu document how leadership strategy and organizational incentives deflected effort away from auditing, indicating cultural endorsement of consulting revenue over audit rigor.

label: Capital markets ignored red flags and provided capital at low cost
original_label: Capital markets ignored red flags and provided capital at low cost
quote: In summary, Enron's gas trading idea was probably a reasonable response to the opportunities arising out of deregulation. However, extensions of this idea into other markets and international expansion were unsuccessful. Accounting games allowed the company to hide this reality for several years. Capital markets largely ignored red flags associated with Enron's spectacular reported performance and aided the company's pursuit of a flawed expansion strategy by providing capital at a remarkably low cost.
context: Healy and Palepu show how capital market actors tolerated and enabled Enron's strategy despite red flags, providing financial validation and resources for its continuation.

label: Institutional investors continued buying Enron stock despite accounting problems
original_label: Institutional investors continued buying Enron stock despite accounting problems
quote: By the end of 2000, some dissenting voices were speaking up with regard to Enron. The Economist ('The Energetic Messiah,' 2000) questioned Enron's performance, and James Chanos, a hedge fund manager, identified problems from disclosures on related party transactions involving the firm's senior officers and insider trading in late 2000. In November 2000, Chanos shorted the stock, and in February 2001, he tipped off a reporter at Fortune, Bethany McLean, who subsequently wrote the March article 'Is Enron Overpriced?' However, institutional ownership of Enron continued to exceed 60 percent as late as October 2001, before collapsing to around 10 percent in December 2001 after the company announced its accounting problems.
context: Healy and Palepu show how institutional leadership tolerated and continued to endorse Enron stock despite early warnings, maintaining 60 percent ownership through October 2001.

label: Gas trading success scaled to physical asset acquisitions in new markets
original_label: Gas trading success scaled to physical asset acquisitions in new markets
quote: By all accounts, the gas trading business was a huge success. By 1992, Enron was the largest merchant of natural gas in North America, and the gas trading business became a major contributor to Enron's net income, with earnings before interest and taxes of $122 million. The creation of the on-line trading model, EnronOnline, in November 1999 enabled the company to develop further and extend its abilities to negotiate and manage these financial contracts. By the fourth quarter of 2000, EnronOnline accounted for almost half of Enron's transactions for all of its business units and had enabled transactions per commercial person to grow to 3,084 from 672 in 1999. In the late 1990s, Skilling refined the trading model further.
context: Healy and Palepu trace how Enron's early trading success led to progressively larger scaling and extension of the model to new markets and asset types.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Special purpose entities used to avoid consolidation despite control
original_label: Special purpose entities used to avoid consolidation despite control
quote: For example, in 1997, Enron wanted to buy out a partner's stake in one of its many joint ventures. However, Enron did not want to show any debt from financing the acquisition or from the joint venture on its balance sheet. Chewco, a special purpose entity that was controlled by an Enron executive and raised debt that was guaranteed by Enron, acquired the joint venture stake for $383 million. The transaction was structured in such a way that Enron did not have to consolidate Chewco or the joint venture into its financials, enabling it effectively to acquire the partnership interest without recognizing any additional debt on its books.
context: Healy and Palepu show how Enron redefined accounting consolidation standards to treat controlled debt-financed entities as non-consolidated based on technicalities rather than economic control.

label: Rhythms hedge evolves from legitimate to improper structure
original_label: Rhythms hedge evolves from legitimate to improper structure
quote: Enron is not just a pipeline and energy trading company. It also had large investments in other businesses, some of which had appreciated substantially in value. These were volatile investments, and Enron was concerned because it had recognized the gains when these investments appreciated, and it didn't want to recognize the losses if the investments declined. Therefore, Enron purported to enter into certain hedging transactions in order to avoid recognizing losses from the investments. The problem was that the hedges weren't real. The idea of a hedge is normally to contract with a creditworthy outside party that is prepared, for a price, to take on the economic risk of an investment. If the value of the investment goes down, that other party will bear the loss, but that is not what happened here. If you cut through the complexity of these partnerships and transactions, here Enron was essentially hedging with itself.
context: Dean Powers explains during testimony how Enron progressively transformed a legitimate hedging need into self-dealing transactions that violated accounting principles.

label: Raptors escalate from initial structure to crisis management
original_label: Raptors escalate from initial structure to crisis management
quote: By March 2001, it appeared that Enron would be required to take a charge against earnings of more than $500 million to reflect the inability of the Raptors to pay. But then rather than take that loss, Enron compounded the problem by making even more of its own stock available to the Raptors—$800 million worth. It gave the false impression that the Raptors had enough money to pay Enron on the money it owed, on the money that the Raptors owed. This transaction was apparently hidden from the board, and it certainly was hidden from the public.
context: Powers describes to Congress how Enron escalated its Raptor scheme when faced with losses, creating new vehicles to hide the problems rather than remedying them.

label: Chewco restructuring as escalation response to disclosure risk
original_label: Chewco restructuring as escalation response to disclosure risk
quote: Fastow told Enron employees that Jeffrey Skilling, then Enron's president and chief operating officer, had approved his participation in Chewco as long as it would not have to be disclosed in Enron's proxy statement.
context: Powers testifies that when Fastow faced disclosure requirements, he escalated by moving his interest to Kopper, suggesting incremental avoidance tactics.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Accounting principles circumvented as standard practice
original_label: Accounting principles circumvented as standard practice
quote: Enron's accounting tactics went well beyond the aggressive, apparently violating or circumventing several of the accounting professions most basic rules.
context: Chairman Greenwood states the Powers Committee's core finding during opening remarks about how accounting standards were systematically reinterpreted.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Improperly structured deals treated as compliant
original_label: Improperly structured deals treated as compliant
quote: We found transactions that were improperly structured. But if they had been structured correctly, Enron could have kept assets, under accounting rules, especially debt, off of its balance sheet. But Enron did not follow those accounting rules.
context: Powers summarizes the Committee's findings about how Enron deviated from proper SPE structuring while presenting the results as acceptable.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Self-hedging with own stock redefined as acceptable
original_label: Self-hedging with own stock redefined as acceptable
quote: there is no question that virtually everyone, from the board of directors on down, understood that the company was seeking to offset its investment losses with its own stock. That is not the way it is supposed to work. Real earnings are supposed to be compared to real losses.
context: Powers testifies that knowledge was widespread but the practice was treated as acceptable despite violating fundamental accounting principles.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Raptor vehicles characterized as hedges despite lacking economic substance
original_label: Raptor vehicles characterized as hedges despite lacking economic substance
quote: The notes of Enron's corporate secretary, preparing for the minutes from a meeting of the Financial Committee of the board, a meeting that was regarding these Raptors, captures the reality of these transactions. Those notes say, quote, 'Does not transfer economic risk but transfers P+L volatility.'
context: Powers cites internal Enron documents showing that even Enron's own officials acknowledged the Raptors did not transfer real risk, yet continued to characterize them as legitimate hedges.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Accounting rule violations reframed as acceptable due diligence
original_label: Accounting rule violations reframed as acceptable due diligence
quote: We found a systematic and pervasive attempt by Enron's management to misrepresent the Company's financial condition. Enron management used these partnerships to enter into transactions that it could not, or would not, have done with unrelated commercial entities. Many of the most significant transactions apparently were not designed to achieve bona fide economic objectives.
context: Powers presents the Committee's conclusion that systematic fraud was normalized rather than questioned as a departure from legitimate practice.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Board waiver of conflict of interest as institutional approval
original_label: Board waiver of conflict of interest as institutional approval
quote: the board waived Enron conflict of interest rules for Mr. Fastow to allow him partial ownership and managerial duties in Chewco and LJM while still on the payroll of Enron as a senior executive. A provision of the waiver approval included a set of conditions that Mr. Fastow would be required to meet, but Mr. Skilling was supposed to oversee Mr. Fastow's activities
context: Representative DeGette notes during opening that the board formally waived ethical rules, institutionalizing the conflict of interest into approved structure.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Board approval process for partnership deals as routine
original_label: Board approval process for partnership deals as routine
quote: the board made the findings necessary to permit Mr. Fastow to participate in those partnerships.
context: Powers clarifies that formal board approval of Fastow's participation in LJM1 and LJM2 institutionalized the practice into corporate governance.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Review controls embedded in formal approval process
original_label: Review controls embedded in formal approval process
quote: Causey and Rick Buy and Skilling were supposed to look at these transactions and approve them to ensure that they were either arms length, or similar to arms length transactions and were not sweetheart deals. Those were the controls that were put in place.
context: Powers describes how Enron's board formally embedded control mechanisms into deal approval structures, making the process institutional.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Approval sheets signed routinely across multiple transactions
original_label: Approval sheets signed routinely across multiple transactions
quote: We produced documents indicating that when members in the corporation sent signatures sheets around to indicate approval of all these transactions that LJM1 and LJM2 were conducting, and everybody signed except one person. There is one signature missing—Jeffrey Skilling's.
context: Chairman Tauzin describes how approval sheets became routine institutional documents, with signatures expected across the organization for each transaction.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Accounting department with thousand accountants processing deals
original_label: Accounting department with thousand accountants processing deals
quote: Our investigators were also told that Enron had more than 900 accountants reporting to Mr. Causey, and I think that my colleague from Louisiana, Mr. John, pointed to this direction. And this 900 accountants does not include the nearly 100 accountants that Arthur Andersen supplied to audit Enron.
context: Representative Rush notes that Enron institutionalized the practice through a massive accounting department that processed the improper transactions as routine business.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: LJM partnerships as standing structures for ongoing transactions
original_label: LJM partnerships as standing structures for ongoing transactions
quote: Beginning with the formation of Chewco, Enron became a Ponzi scheme of self-dealing partnerships which were designed, in your own words, to mislead investors about the true financial state of the company and ultimatly resulted in its financial implosion.
context: Representative John describes how Chewco and subsequent LJM partnerships were institutionalized as permanent structures rather than one-off transactions.

label: Hedging terminology applied to self-dealing transactions
original_label: Hedging terminology applied to self-dealing transactions
quote: Enron purported to enter into certain hedging transactions in order to avoid recognizing losses from the investments. The problem was that the hedges weren't real.
context: Powers explains how Enron used standard hedging terminology to describe transactions that lacked the economic substance of genuine hedges, normalizing the deviance.

label: Structured finance and SPEs as legitimate financial tools
original_label: Structured finance and SPEs as legitimate financial tools
quote: There are legitimate accounting devices that companies use to keep transactions and debt, using structured financing, off their balance sheets.
context: Powers acknowledges that structured finance terminology could apply to legitimate devices, which may have made improper Enron structures seem standard.

label: Independence framed as reason to avoid scrutiny
original_label: Independence framed as reason to avoid scrutiny
quote: Their explanation is that they wanted to make the LJM partnerships as, 'independent' as possible, and looking into the financial structure of the partnerships would somehow be inconsistent with that.
context: Powers describes the collective rationalization used by the board and management to justify why they did not examine the fee structures Fastow would receive.

label: Accounting sign-off reframed as independent validation
original_label: Accounting sign-off reframed as independent validation
quote: the story was the accountants had signed off on it; he assumed it was an okay accounting device.
context: Powers recounts Lay's explanation that Andersen's approval provided sufficient rationalization for accepting the hedging approach despite its impropriety.

label: Complex transactions justified as business necessity
original_label: Complex transactions justified as business necessity
quote: As our Report demonstrates, these transactions were extremely complex.
context: Powers notes that complexity itself became a shared rationalization for practices that obscured improper accounting and self-dealing.

label: Risk transfer as business practice rationalization
original_label: Risk transfer as business practice rationalization
quote: Legitimately, Enron had some problems, it had some assets like Rhythms, which they put 10 million in and all of a sudden it was worth 500 million because of inflation and the value of the stock market and the run-up of the stocks. Like many corporations holding a risky stock like that, they probably had a need to put that risk off, to share that risk with someone else if the stock fell dramatically so it didn't hurt their own stock. That is a legitimate function that corporations use special-purpose entities and they use partnerships in some cases to do.
context: Chairman Tauzin articulates the legitimate rationale for SPEs that was used collectively to justify Enron's improper structures.

label: Employees offered investment returns to align with partnerships
original_label: Employees offered investment returns to align with partnerships
quote: The magnitude of these returns raises serious questions as to why Fastow and Kopper offered these investments to other employees.
context: Powers notes that Fastow and Kopper systematically co-opted employees by offering them investment opportunities in partnership structures at abnormal returns.

label: Employees recruited from Enron to manage partnerships
original_label: Employees recruited from Enron to manage partnerships
quote: You have Glisan who has presented to the Raptor I transaction to the board. He was called the business unit originator and the person negotiating for Enron. He is the guy on the other side of the table, and Fastow says, 'Come on in and be an investor on this side of the table, and you make a million dollars as a result in 6 weeks.'
context: Chairman Tauzin describes how Fastow co-opted key Enron employees by moving them to partnership roles where they profited from the same deals they had negotiated against.

label: Kopper replacing Fastow in Chewco when disclosure threatened
original_label: Kopper replacing Fastow in Chewco when disclosure threatened
quote: when Fastow faced disclosure requirements for his Chewco participation in Enron's proxy statement, he substituted Mr. Kopper.
context: Powers indicates that when Fastow's involvement threatened public disclosure, he co-opted Kopper to take his place while maintaining control.

label: Pressure and incentives used to silence objections
original_label: Pressure and incentives used to silence objections
quote: in some cases, other than offering them a chance to invest, partnerships in some cases actually threatened employees with firings and losses of bonuses
context: Chairman Tauzin notes that Fastow and Kopper used both incentives and threats to co-opt and silence employee objections.

label: Managers of partnerships threatening Enron employees
original_label: Managers of partnerships threatening Enron employees
quote: managers of the partnerships were actually threatening people at Enron with firing if they aggressively negotiated for Enron. They threatened others with loss of their bonuses.
context: Chairman Tauzin describes how Enron managers on behalf of partnerships socialized newer or lower-ranking employees through threats to prevent resistance.

label: Fastow directing employee to accept partnership terms
original_label: Fastow directing employee to accept partnership terms
quote: Mr. Fastow basically ordered him or told him to accept the terms as Mr. Kopper offered it
context: Representative Whitfield describes how Fastow co-opted an employee by directing acceptance of unfavorable partnership terms, socializing compliance.

label: Raptor restructuring hidden from board in March 2001
original_label: Raptor restructuring hidden from board in March 2001
quote: By March 2001, it appeared that Enron would be required to take a charge against earnings of more than $500 million to reflect the inability of the Raptors to pay. Rather than take that loss, Enron compounded the problem by making even more of its own stock available to the Raptors—$800 million worth. It gave the false impression that the Raptors had enough money to pay Enron what they owed. This transaction was apparently hidden from the Board, and was certainly hidden from the public.
context: Powers testifies that critical restructuring decisions were deliberately kept from the board despite their fiduciary responsibilities, fragmenting knowledge of the full scope.

label: Side agreements not revealed to board or auditors
original_label: Side agreements not revealed to board or auditors
quote: The Special Committee's report states that the critical piece of missing information relating to the Chewco transaction was the side agreement for the $6 million Enron collateralization of the partnership outside $11.4 million equity investment by Big River Funding, LLC, which is a partnership controlled by Michael Kopper and his domestic partner, William Dodson. At least one Enron official, Ben Glisan, knew of these facts. Andersen says it knew nothing about this aspect of the Chewco transaction.
context: Chairman Greenwood notes that side agreements fragmenting Chewco's structure were known only to select Enron officials and hidden from both the board and auditors.

label: Board members lack understanding of transaction complexity
original_label: Board members lack understanding of transaction complexity
quote: the board's knowledge of questionable transactions involving Chewco, LJM, Raptor and other special entities that are detailed in the Powers report as having substantial problems. When you look at those, those transactions are both structured completely differently in ways which are designed to mask losses and to maximize profits.
context: Representative DeGette describes how board members approved complex transactions without understanding their structure, creating fragmented knowledge.

label: Causey's limited review insulated from broader transaction knowledge
original_label: Causey's limited review insulated from broader transaction knowledge
quote: Causey stated that his review of the transaction was to make sure that the accounting treatment was accurate, and he did not participate in the strategic decisions. Buy stated that the Global Finance Group made the strategic decisions regarding the deals, and that his risk review had nothing to do with the big picture.
context: Representative Stearns notes that Enron's control structure fragmented knowledge by separating accounting review from strategic understanding.

label: Approval process lacked full picture of transaction economics
original_label: Approval process lacked full picture of transaction economics
quote: We have identified some evidence that in three of the transactions where Enron ultimately bought back LJM's interest, Enron had agreed in advance to protect the LJM partnerships against loss. These were informal side assurances.

label: Board committees received partial information on transactions
original_label: Board committees received partial information on transactions

context: Representative DeGette describes how the Audit Committee received only summary information from Causey without examining underlying transaction details.

label: Board approval despite knowledge of Fastow's conflicts
original_label: Board approval despite knowledge of Fastow's conflicts
quote: the board made the findings necessary to permit Mr. Fastow to participate in those partnerships.

label: Board waived ethics code to enable Fastow's outside dealings
original_label: Board waived ethics code to enable Fastow's outside dealings
quote: the board waived Enron conflict of interest rules for Mr. Fastow to allow him partial ownership and managerial duties in Chewco and LJM while still on the payroll of Enron as a senior executive.

label: Compressed development timeline enabling later compromise

context: Dowie (1977) documents how Lee Iacocca's aggressive timeline compressed the normal product development cycle nearly in half, setting up later choices to sacrifice safety.

label: Tooling locked in before defect identification
original_label: Tooling locked in before defect identification
quote: A quick glance at the bar chart below will show you what that speed-up meant. Normally, an auto company doesn't begin tooling until the other processes are almost over: you don't want to make the machines that stamp and press and grind metal into the shape of car parts until you know all those parts will work well together. But Iacocca's speed-up meant Pinto tooling went on at the same time as product development. So when crash tests revealed a serious defect in the gas tank, it was too late. context: Dowie describes how the compression of the development cycle created a structural lock-in: by the time engineers discovered the gas tank defect in crash tests, expensive tooling was already committed, making remediation harder to justify.

context: Dowie quotes an anonymous Ford engineer recounting how Iacocca's formal constraints (the "limits of 2,000") institutionalized the rejection of a proven safety device, making the unsafe choice appear to follow from product specifications rather than from deliberate risk acceptance.

original_label: Safety excluded from formal product objectives

original_label: Continued detailing of indicted prescriber and associated providers

original_label: Extreme monthly opioid volume accepted as normal

label: Practice Fusion monitoring of prescribing without disclosure
original_label: Practice Fusion monitoring of prescribing without disclosure

label: District manager flagged continued marketing to indicted prescriber's staff
original_label: District manager flagged continued marketing to indicted prescriber's staff
quote: On or about May 26, 2016, a PURDUE PHARMA district manager submitted a written ROC to the ADD Program, writing: "I have a growing concern over a legal action that has been underway for some time in the [New York] area. context: Despite a district manager's explicit concern about continued detailing of staff members at the indicted prescriber's practice, senior leadership approved ongoing marketing.

original_label: Profits from flagged prescribers over decade despite escalating evidence

original_label: Boeing emails show progressive deception about MCAS

context: A FAA Academy training manager reports that foundational ASI training was progressively cut in duration, degrading inspector competency.

label: Southwest allowed increasingly unsafe weight and balance practices
original_label: Southwest allowed increasingly unsafe weight and balance practices
quote: Southwest Airlines was allowed by FAA management to self-report compliance based on a self-audit of twenty-five percent of their daily flights. Southwest reported that seventy-eight percent of the flights audited were not compliant with FAA weight and balance regulations. In response, Southwest Airlines spent three months attempting to obtain a waiver to redefine accurate instead of correcting their weight and balance discrepancies. The regulatory definition requires a deviation of zero pounds between actual weight and weight entered into the PWB system. Southwest Airlines requested that the definition be changed to a maximum allowed deviation of 1500 pounds.
context: The report shows how FAA management permitted Southwest to progressively redefine compliance standards rather than enforce existing regulations.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: AEG training deficiencies reframed as confusion
original_label: AEG training deficiencies reframed as confusion
quote: Acting Administrator Elwell confirmed that the manager responsible for retaliating against the whistleblower was no longer employed by the FAA. In his July 2019 letter, Chairman Wicker asked that Committee staff be allowed to interview the employee, but the employee separated from the FAA before the interview could take place. The AAE report attached to Acting Administrator Elwell's letter, however, paints a starkly different picture of the training deficiencies found in both the Seattle and Long Beach AEG offices. As mentioned, AAE's investigation found that the ASIs in question did not meet training requirements under FAA policy. AAE also found that OJT for ASIs assigned to an AEG is not sufficient training to certify ASIs to issue type ratings. However, this is inconsistent with information obtained from the whistleblower who raised the initial concerns. According to several whistleblowers, work on the Gulfstream VII FSB never ceased. Chairman Wicker's July 31, 2019, letter requested documentation supporting this work stoppage, and this request remains outstanding as of the date of this report. FAA staff interviews revealed inconsistencies on how or if this directive was communicated. According to the Acting Administrator, Flight Standards found that despite AAE's assessment otherwise, the ASIs working on the Long Beach FSB had actually met the training requirements and that the complaint was merely due to confusion about the training requirements.
context: FAA management reinterpreted substantiated training failures as misunderstanding rather than accepting them as deficiencies requiring correction.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Zero-foot takeoff margin deemed acceptable
original_label: Zero-foot takeoff margin deemed acceptable
quote: Inspector Rees cites an incident in which a Southwest Airlines pilot reached out to him claiming that the PWB on their plane had calculated a stopping margin of zero feet in several instances. A margin of zero feet means that if the pilot delayed the decision to reject, or was too slow to execute the reject procedure by a fraction of a second, the zero foot margin would be inadequate and the plane would run off the end of the runway. These are the most concerning of numerous similar instances disclosed by Inspector Rees. Inspector Rees indicated that Southwest Airlines informed the FAA that the new system PWB was an apples to apples replacement of the previous system and had no differences in safety considerations. When Inspector Rees raised concerns to his manager, a Supervisory Principal Operations Inspector (POI), he was told that the changes were technically legal.
context: FAA management reframed dangerous reductions in safety margins as technically compliant with regulations.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Unknown major repairs deemed low risk
original_label: Unknown major repairs deemed low risk

context: Southwest Airlines redefined unknown major repairs to aircraft as posing low risk, a redefinition accepted by FAA management.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards

original_label: On-the-job training deemed sufficient for certification

AAE also found that OJT for ASIs assigned to an AEG is not sufficient training to certify ASIs to issue type ratings. AAE stated that: These findings are very serious and could have far-ranging ramifications regarding the type ratings of hundreds of certificate holders. Because it involves AEG ASI's, the proverbial tip of the pyramid for pilot qualification and certification, every type rating issued by an unqualified ASI potentially creates another potentially unqualified pilot, including other ASIs, and the most senior pilots and check pilots at FAA-certificated operators.
context: FAA Flight Standards management redefined OJT as sufficient for critical certification work that federal policy required formal training.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Atlas and Polar authorized to share training across separate certificates
original_label: Atlas and Polar authorized to share training across separate certificates
quote: During the Atlas Air inspection, Inspector Clemmons discovered that the Principle Operations Inspector (POI) for the local Certificate Management Office (CMO) had authorized Polar Air Cargo to transfer its pilots to Atlas Air's training program to satisfy requirements for pilot training in 2011. The CHEP team that Inspector Clemmons was working on was unable to find any regulation or FAA guidance that provided such authority to the POI. According to 14 CFR Part 121.401(a) (1) Training Program, each operator must provide enough flight instructors and approved check airmen to conduct the flight training and checks required under this part. Currently, CMO and Flight Standards management assert Atlas and Polar Air are in compliance with following the FAA's rules and regulations and maintaining all documentation required by the FAA due to this memo granted by the POI in 2011. This memo appears to be an indirect conflict with 14 CFR 121.401(a). This deviation also appears to perpetuate findings related to insufficient training and oversight of check airmen and related activities cited in a 2017 DOT OIG report.
context: A single memo from 2011 authorizing an unauthorized deviation from federal regulation became institutionalized in FAA and airline operations for nearly a decade, with management defending it as compliant.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Skyline aircraft non-compliance embedded in approval process
original_label: Skyline aircraft non-compliance embedded in approval process
quote: During the period of 2013 through 2017, Southwest Airlines procured eighty-eight airplanes, referred to by Southwest Airlines as the Skyline Aircraft. These aircraft were purchased used and previously operated by sixteen various foreign air carriers. Southwest Airlines used multiple contractors to conduct the required records review and airworthiness inspection of these aircraft. Delegated Agency Representatives (DAR) designated contractors are permitted by the FAA to examine and inspect airplanes prior to the issuance of airworthiness certificates and other approvals. After contractors conducted their reviews, Southwest Airlines, through the DAR process approved by the FAA, were issued eighty-eight aircraft Airworthiness Certificates, allowing them to enter revenue service. Beginning in late 2017 Inspector Boutris began raising safety concerns related to the Skyline Aircraft as a result of safety inspections. The inspections discovered numerous repairs to critical structures of the airplanes which did not conform to airworthiness requirements.
context: Deficient DAR contractor reviews were institutionalized into the Airworthiness Certificate approval process, allowing 88 non-compliant aircraft to enter service.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: ASAP program used to block enforcement and interviews
original_label: ASAP program used to block enforcement and interviews
quote: One whistleblower conducted his/her own ad hoc testing in a non-MCAS equipped simulator. The three flight crews presented with this scenario responded with reaction times to identify the problem in seven, nine, and eleven seconds. The time to complete the corrective action and correct the situation was forty-nine seconds, fifty-three seconds, and sixty-two seconds. In one case, involving Southwest Airlines, FAA whistleblowers reported that during takeoff, a first officer reported a malfunction in the flight elevator, a core component of a plane's flight control. The pilot in command elected to continue on with their flight instead of turning back, and encountered the same malfunction en-route, and upon arrival at their destination. Instead of reporting the issue to maintenance, they again chose to fly another leg, encountering the issue again during takeoff, en-route and on arrival. Upon arrival at their second destination, they reported the issue, and the plane was grounded for at least four days for maintenance, according to FAA whistleblowers. Despite the repair having been completed while intentionally disregarding the proper procedure, a maintenance ASAP was submitted and accepted for the initial repair. Review of the documents revealed that the pilot ASAP program improperly cited the elevator feel bearing as the cause of the flight control malfunctions experienced by the pilots. The carrier initially did not allow the crew to be interviewed. After additional discussion, the carrier reportedly agreed to allow the crew to be interviewed only if the events were accepted into ASAP unconditionally before the interviews took place.
context: ASAP became institutionalized as a tool for operators to avoid enforcement action and FAA interviews even when events involved intentional violations.

original_label: Extended Envelope Training requirements reduced through repeated approvals
quote: Inspector Rees alleges that as a part of their first EET implementation in 2017, Southwest Airlines provided insufficient training to its expert pilots. He estimates that approximately 50 percent of Southwest flight crews should have received retraining. FAA guidance was that each expert pilot spend four hours in a training simulator. Inspector Rees alleges that, with the permission of FAA management, Southwest Airlines was permitted to have three expert pilots in each four-hour training simulator, rotating in and out instead of individualized four hour blocks of instruction. Additionally, instead of choosing the cream of the crop from its 400 training pilots, Southwest Airlines was permitted to use all 400. These 400 pilots, who may have received insufficient simulator training, then went on to train all pilots at Southwest Airlines.
context: FAA management repeatedly approved deviations from EET training requirements, allowing the deficient practice to be replicated across the airline's pilot force.

original_label: MCAS classified as outside normal operating envelope

On January 17, 2017, Mark Forkner reminds an FAA employee that they had agreed to delete MCAS from the draft FSB because it is way outside the normal operating envelope.
context: Boeing and FAA officials shared a collective rationalization that MCAS could be excluded from training because it operated outside normal conditions, despite the system activating in both fatal crashes.

label: Four-second reaction time assumption normalized
original_label: Four-second reaction time assumption normalized
quote: Boeing assumes a reaction time of four seconds for a pilot to identify and begin correcting a runaway stabilizer problem. The 737 MAX Flight Control System Joint Authorities Technical Review (JATR) published in October 2019 includes a review of this assumption as one of its recommendations. Boeing considers this maneuver a memory item and assumes a pilot can recognize and act upon the situation from memory alone in four seconds. The whistleblower shared results of simulator tests in which he/she presented runaway stab trim to several randomly selected flight crews during simulator training for the Boeing 737NG. The three flight crews presented with this scenario responded with reaction times to identify the problem in seven, nine, and eleven seconds.
context: Boeing's four-second reaction time assumption became normalized in certification despite test evidence showing actual pilots required 7-11 seconds.

label: ASAP marketed as get out of jail free card
original_label: ASAP marketed as get out of jail free card
quote: Frontline inspectors and managers at the FAA report that the agency sometimes struggles to present a unified face to entities that it regulates. Several carriers and operators engaged by the Committee confirmed this perception. In fact, employees from several airlines claimed ASAP was sold to them as a get out of jail free card. Every whistleblower the Committee engaged on this topic concurred with this statement.
context: Across the aviation industry, ASAP became collectively understood and marketed as a mechanism to avoid enforcement action rather than improve safety.

label: Technical non-compliance with discretion framing
original_label: Technical non-compliance with discretion framing
quote: Multiple senior officials interviewed by the Committee indicated that ASIs have a significant amount of discretion related to compliance. They refer to these examples of discretion as technical non-compliance. FAA officials explained that these are instances where a certificate holder may not be compliant with regulations, but ASIs are encouraged to apply a risk matrix to evaluate whether a risk exists. Two managers interviewed confirmed that this process is not codified in policy or recognized by regulation, but is encouraged as part of the compliance philosophy. ASIs told Committee staff that they have no latitude on this subject. They stated that if an ASI did what these managers suggest is allowable, they could be found to be derelict in their duties.
context: FAA managers used a shared euphemism, technical non-compliance, to justify allowing operators to violate regulations when managers deemed risk acceptable, contradicting both policy and ASI understanding.

original_label: Southwest management directive to smooth things with airline

context: FAA senior management culture employed a shared vocabulary of smoothing relations with carriers as an explicit management strategy.

original_label: Coziness as legitimate regulatory partnership

context: Whistleblowers alleged that records were falsified to show OJT completion where it did not occur, reflecting a culture of accommodating unqualified employees.

label: Gulfstream VII work stoppage inconsistently communicated
original_label: Gulfstream VII work stoppage inconsistently communicated
quote: Committee staff interviewed two FAA employees with direct knowledge of the conduct of the 737 MAX Fight Standardization Board. FAA staff interviews revealed inconsistencies on how or if this directive was communicated. One manager stated that he directed the work stoppage and it was his idea. Another manager was sure it was written in an email or a memo. To date, no confirmation of any work stoppage has been provided to the Committee. The most senior FAA manager indicated he/she originated the directive, but could not recall if it was verbally, in writing, or both. The most junior manager asked about the work stoppage indicated the stoppage was his/her idea and confirmed it was verbal, but may have also sent an email. The final FAA manager, from the AEG, could not recall if the work stoppage was communicated verbally, in writing, or both.
context: FAA managers gave conflicting accounts of whether a work stoppage was ordered, how it was communicated, and whether it actually occurred, demonstrating fragmented knowledge across the organization.

label: Mark Forkner communications production withheld then released by media
original_label: Mark Forkner communications production withheld then released by media
quote: On July 31, 2019, the Committee requested Mark Forkner's communications with FAA employees. On September 5, 2019, the Committee prioritized Mark Forkner's communications with FAA employees. On October 7, 2019, the FAA sent a limited number of unimportant emails between Mark Forkner and FAA employees. On October 18, 2019: FAA transmitted instant messages from Mark Forkner to another Boeing employee that detail Forkner's concerns in 2016 about the MCAS system and his misleading statements to regulators. FAA transmitted emails from Mark Forkner to FAA employees in which Forkner asks that MCAS be removed from training and manuals and states that he is, Jedi mind tricking regulators. FAA responded to the Committee's request for all communications between Mark Forkner and FAA employees with a set of unimportant emails that did not contain disturbing ones sent earlier in the day. The content and tone of communications by Boeing employees during the certification of the 737 MAX are disturbing. It remains unknown if the Committee has received all documents related to Forkner, as requested. In addition, the documents received from FAA are redacted, obscuring critical information. The failure of DOT OGC to produce documents previously requested by the Committee only to view them in media reporting and finally from FAA legislative affairs, suggests DOT OGC intentionally withheld relevant information requested by the Committee.
context: Critical communications about MCAS misrepresentation were withheld from Congress despite formal requests, fragmented in production, and only revealed through media reporting.

label: AAE investigation audio and notes disappeared
original_label: AAE investigation audio and notes disappeared
quote: Additionally, according to Inspector Wrigley, when an Office of Special Counsel (OSC) investigator requested records of his interview performed by an AAE investigator, OSC was informed that all audio and video had been lost and that no notes had been taken. Inspector Wrigley and other FAA employees interviewed by the same AAE investigator stated the investigator took written notes in each of the respective interviews.
context: AAE investigation materials that could document investigator conduct were destroyed or claimed lost, preventing OSC from obtaining complete evidence.

original_label: Honolulu FSDO file cleanup during DOT OIG investigation

label: Southwest redacted maintenance documents in ASAP submission

No mention of the misrouted flight control cable was ever disclosed or included in any of the pilot ASAP submissions.
context: Southwest Airlines redacted documents in its ASAP submission to hide the true cause of flight control malfunctions, fragmenting the knowledge available to FAA review committees.

label: Novictor incident database fields left blank
original_label: Novictor incident database fields left blank
quote: The staff who entered these findings into the FAA database that tracks these incidents left the pilot and operator fields blank. According to Mr. Monfort, this is highly unusual and appeared to have been done to obscure attribution of the incident to the pilot and Novictor. context: FAA staff deliberately left database fields blank to prevent discovery of incident attribution, fragmenting searchable knowledge of operator safety history.

label: Skyline aircraft document review not translated from foreign languages
original_label: Skyline aircraft document review not translated from foreign languages

According to documents that I have reviewed, FASTOW initially proposed the formation of a partnership SPE to be known as Alpine Investors ("Alpine"), which would buy Enron's interest in the wind farms. The proposed investors in Alpine were all "Friends of Enron," including relatives of FASTOW's wife, CS-9, and CS-10.
context: FBI Agent Meisel describes how FASTOW systematically designed Alpine/RADR as a structured pattern using family and nominee investors.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: LJM created as institutionalized earnings management vehicle
original_label: LJM created as institutionalized earnings management vehicle
quote: By 1999, Enron was increasingly dependent on transactions with SPEs to meet its financial reporting goals. By June 1999, in order to have an off-balance-sheet SPE to which Enron could readily turn, Enron's Board of Directors (the "Board") agreed to permit FASTOW to create and serve as the managing partner of a new SPE named LJM1. The Board later approved FASTOW's participation in another even larger SPE, LJM2 (the LJM entities hereafter collectively will be referred to as "LJM" unless otherwise noted). LJM's business activity principally involved transactions with Enron and Enron affiliates.
context: FBI Agent Meisel describes how LJM was institutionalized as an approved structure specifically designed to be a ready-made vehicle for Enron transactions.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: RADR extended artificially to preserve regulatory benefits
original_label: RADR extended artificially to preserve regulatory benefits
quote: Because FASTOW knew that his participation as an equity investor in RADR would require Enron to make public disclosure, he and Kopper enlisted "Friends of Enron" to serve as the supposedly independent third party investors. Those "investors" included CS-9, CS-10, and CS-11. According to Kopper, CS-9, CS-10, and CS-11, RADR was supposed to exist for only a few months. Instead, Enron extended the life of the RADR SPE for nearly three years, enabling the wind farms unlawfully to reap the financial benefits of QF status during that time.
context: FBI Agent Meisel documents how RADR's lifespan was artificially extended well beyond its original temporary purpose to continue regulatory benefits.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: LJM used systematically for asset warehousing operations
original_label: LJM used systematically for asset warehousing operations
quote: According to Kopper and CS-1, various transactions between Enron and LJM were mere "warehousing" deals in which there was an understanding that LJM would hold Enron assets only for a short time, with Enron agreeing that LJM would make a profit on those assets. FASTOW and others caused LJM to "purchase" under-performing assets from Enron for prices that often bore no relation to the assets' true value. These assets were referred to as Enron's "nuclear waste." In undocumented side deals, Enron agreed that LJM would not lose money even if the market value of an asset declined, because Enron would attempt to arrange a sale of the asset to a third party at a profit to LJM or, if no such third party could be found, Enron itself would repurchase the asset.
context: FBI Agent Meisel describes how LJM was used as an institutionalized, systematic structure for parking unwanted assets with guaranteed profit.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Raptor structure created as balance sheet manipulation tool
original_label: Raptor structure created as balance sheet manipulation tool
quote: Enron's own documents reflect that Raptor I was designed to protect Enron's balance sheet from decreases in value of certain of these investments. Enron sought to use Raptor I to lock in the value of Enron's investments in stock, without actually selling its shares. Raptor I was created in April of 2000 through an off-balance-sheet SPE called Talon LLC ("Talon"). Talon would enter into "hedging" transactions with an Enron subsidiary that would lock in the value of Enron's stock portfolio: if the price of Enron's stock increased, Talon would reap the upside gain, and if the stock declined, Talon would pay the Enron subsidiary the amount of the loss.
context: FBI Agent Meisel describes how Raptor I was systematically designed and institutionalized as a structured tool for balance sheet manipulation.

Initially, FASTOW planned to serve as Chewco's outside equity investor and general partner. When he was advised that his direct involvement would require disclosure in Enron's financial statements, FASTOW proposed that Kopper assume that role. FASTOW explained to Kopper that his involvement would not trigger disclosure by Enron, as Kopper was not considered an executive officer of Enron for financial reporting purposes.

label: NatWest bankers recruited and promised significant returns

label: Employees authorized for LJM compensation without disclosure

quote: Nor was the Board informed that FASTOW had arranged to have Kopper, while still Enron's Managing Director of Global Finance, serve as a managing director at LJM, or that FASTOW had staffed LJM with several other Enron employees. According to interviews of Board members and a review of contemporaneous notes, FASTOW responded by saying "no." label: Financial Institution gradually pressured and accommodated
original_label: Financial Institution gradually pressured and accommodated

Such a sale would allow Enron to record $12 million of earnings, and $28 million in funds flow, in the fourth quarter of 1999, which according to CS-3 was needed to meet Enron's earnings goals.

label: Financial Institution accommodated due to revenue dependency
