LJM agreed to "buy" this interest only because Skilling, Causey, Fastow and others, in an undisclosed side deal, agreed that Enron would buy back the interest, if necessary, at a profit to LJM. Based on this purported "sale," which was in fact an asset parking or warehousing arrangement, Enron improperly recognized approximately $65 million in income in the third and fourth quarters of 1999, when it was straining to meet budget targets designed to ensure that it achieved its earnings-per-share goals.
context: SEC complaint showing how Skilling and Causey jointly designed and executed a fraudulent asset-parking scheme with a predetermined buyback agreement to manipulate earnings to meet targets.

label: Skilling and Causey delayed Cuiaba repurchase to avoid disclosure
original_label: Skilling and Causey delayed Cuiaba repurchase to avoid disclosure
quote: By 2001, the Cuiaba project was approximately $200 million over budget. Nonetheless, in the spring of 2001, Skilling, Causey, and Fastow caused Enron to agree to buy back LJM's interest in the Cuiaba project at a considerable profit to LJM, in keeping with the undisclosed oral side deal. After agreeing to execute the repurchase, Skilling, Causey, Fastow, and others decided to delay publicly consummating the deal until Fastow sold his interest in LJM so that Fastow's role in the transaction would not be disclosed.
context: SEC complaint showing how senior leaders (Skilling, Causey, Fastow) deliberately delayed a material transaction to evade disclosure obligations and prevent the public from learning about Fastow's conflicts.

label: MCAS authority expanded from normal to low Mach
original_label: MCAS authority expanded from normal to low Mach
quote: As the development of the 737 MAX progressed, the MCAS function was expanded to low Mach numbers.
context: NTSB describing how MCAS capability grew incrementally during 737 MAX development.

label: MCAS activation threshold evolved through iterations
original_label: MCAS activation threshold evolved through iterations
quote: In March 2016, Boeing determined that MCAS should be revised to improve flaps up, low Mach stall characteristics and identification. The preliminary hazard assessments of MCAS were re-evaluated after this change by pilot evaluation in the motion simulator and determined to have not changed the hazard classification.
context: NTSB footnote describing successive modifications to MCAS design with hazard classifications carried forward unchanged.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Uncommanded MCAS classified as major rather than catastrophic
original_label: Uncommanded MCAS classified as major rather than catastrophic
quote: For the normal flight envelope, Boeing identified and classified two hazards associated with "uncommanded MCAS" activation as "major." One of these hazards, applicable to the MCAS function seen in these accidents, included uncommanded MCAS operation to maximum authority.
context: NTSB analyzing Boeing's functional hazard assessment and how MCAS failures were risk-classified.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Major classification defined as remote probability with tolerable effects
original_label: Major classification defined as remote probability with tolerable effects
quote: The "major" classification used by Boeing indicated a remote probability of this hazard occurring and that it could result in reduced control capability, reduced system redundancy, or increased crew workload.
context: NTSB footnote explaining Boeing's definition of the risk severity level assigned to uncommanded MCAS.

label: Simulator tests did not include all failure modes
original_label: Simulator tests did not include all failure modes
quote: To perform these simulator tests, Boeing induced a stabilizer trim input that would simulate the stabilizer moving at a rate and duration consistent with the MCAS function. Using this method to induce the hazard resulted in the following: motion of the stabilizer trim wheel, increased column forces, and indication that the airplane was moving nose down. Boeing indicated to the NTSB that this evaluation was focused on the pilot response to uncommanded MCAS operation, regardless of underlying cause. Thus, the specific failure modes that could lead to uncommanded MCAS activation (such as an erroneous high AOA input to the MCAS) were not simulated as part of these functional hazard assessment validation tests.
context: NTSB explaining how Boeing's simulator validation did not test the underlying failure mode (erroneous AOA) that would trigger MCAS.

label: Related alerts and indications not included in safety assessment
original_label: Related alerts and indications not included in safety assessment
quote: As a result, additional flight deck effects (such as IAS DISAGREE and ALT DISAGREE alerts and stick shaker activation) resulting from the same underlying failure (for example, erroneous AOA) were not simulated and were not in the stabilizer trim safety assessment report reviewed by the NTSB.
context: NTSB describing how Boeing's safety assessment compartmentalized the evaluation of MCAS in isolation from other cockpit effects of the same failure.

label: Pilot recognition and response assumptions as standard practice
original_label: Pilot recognition and response assumptions as standard practice
quote: Boeing indicated to the NTSB that, based on FAA guidance, it used assumptions during its safety assessment of MCAS hazards in the engineering flight simulator. Four of these assumptions were the following: Uncommanded system inputs are readily recognizable and can be counteracted by overriding the failure by movement of the flight controls "in the normal sense" by the flight crew and do not require specific procedures. Action to counter the failure shall not require exceptional piloting skill or strength. The pilot will take immediate action to reduce or eliminate increased control forces by re-trimming or changing configuration or flight conditions. Trained flight crew memory procedures shall be followed to address and eliminate or mitigate the failure.
context: NTSB describing standardized assumptions that Boeing and the FAA used across all Boeing models for flight control system assessments.

label: Assumptions stated as consistent with industry practice
original_label: Assumptions stated as consistent with industry practice
quote: Boeing advised that these assumptions are used across all Boeing models when performing functional hazard assessments of flight control systems. These assumptions were consistent with requirements in 14 CFR 25.671 and 25.672 and guidance in AC 25-7C, "Flight Test Guide for Certification of Transport Category Airplanes."
context: NTSB noting that Boeing presented these pilot-response assumptions as industry-standard practice across all its aircraft.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Hazard classification justified by timely pilot response assumption
original_label: Hazard classification justified by timely pilot response assumption
quote: In a 2019 presentation to the NTSB, Boeing indicated that the MCAS hazard classification of "major" for uncommanded MCAS function in the normal flight envelope was based on the following conclusions: Unintended stabilizer trim inputs are readily recognized by movement of the stabilizer trim wheel, flightpath change, or increased column forces. Aircraft can be returned to steady level flight using available column (elevator) alone or stabilizer trim. Continuous unintended nose-down stabilizer trim inputs would be recognized as a stabilizer trim or stabilizer runaway failure and the procedure for stabilizer runaway would be followed.
context: NTSB describing Boeing's post-hoc justification for the major hazard classification, all dependent on pilot recognition and response.

label: System-level assessment ignored combined flight deck effects
original_label: System-level assessment ignored combined flight deck effects
quote: While Boeing considered the possibility of uncommanded MCAS operation as part of its functional hazard assessment, it did not evaluate all the potential alerts and indications that could accompany a failure that also resulted in uncommanded MCAS operation. Therefore, neither Boeing's system safety assessment nor its simulator tests evaluated how the combined effect of alerts and indications might impact pilots' recognition of which procedure(s) to prioritize in responding to an unintended MCAS operation caused by an erroneous AOA input.
context: NTSB analyzing how Boeing compartmentalized the evaluation of MCAS from the broader cockpit environment.

label: Industry philosophy assumes systems minimize operator error
original_label: Industry philosophy assumes systems minimize operator error
quote: Consistent with this philosophy, the NTSB notes that FAA certification guidance in AC 25.1309-1A that allows manufacturers to assume pilots will respond to failure conditions appropriately is based, in part, upon the applicant showing that the systems, controls, and associated monitoring and warnings are designed to minimize crew errors, which could create additional hazards.
context: NTSB describing the shared industry and regulatory rationale for accepting pilot-response assumptions.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Assumptions embedded in certification guidance and procedures
original_label: Assumptions embedded in certification guidance and procedures
quote: The FAA's procedures for aircraft type certification require an aircraft manufacturer ("applicant") to demonstrate that its design complies with all applicable FAA regulations and requirements. For transport-category airplanes, as part of this process, applicants must demonstrate through analysis, test, or both that their design meets the applicable requirements under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 25.
context: NTSB describing the formal regulatory framework within which Boeing's assumptions about pilot behavior were embedded and accepted.

label: FAA guidance allows pilot response assumptions without clear validation requirements
original_label: FAA guidance allows pilot response assumptions without clear validation requirements
quote: Further, because FAA guidance allows such assumptions to be made in transport-category airplane certification analyses without providing applicants with clear direction concerning the consideration of multiple flight deck alerts and indications in evaluating pilot recognition and response, the NTSB is concerned that similar assumptions and procedures for their validation may have also been used in the development of flight control system safety assessments for other airplanes.
context: NTSB identifying how the regulatory framework lacked clear requirements for validating assumptions across the industry.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Pilot-response assumptions used across all Boeing models
original_label: Pilot-response assumptions used across all Boeing models
quote: Boeing advised that these assumptions are used across all Boeing models when performing functional hazard assessments of flight control systems.
context: NTSB documenting that the MCAS assumptions were not unique to the 737 MAX but part of Boeing's standard practice.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Short-term forces assumed immediately addressed by pilot re-trimming
original_label: Short-term forces assumed immediately addressed by pilot re-trimming
quote: AC 25-7C stated that short-term forces are the initial stabilized control forces that result from maintaining the intended flightpath after configuration changes and normal transitions from one flight condition to another, "or from regaining control following a failure. It is assumed that the pilot will take immediate action to reduce or eliminate such forces by re-trimming or changing configuration or flight conditions, and consequently short-term forces are not considered to exist for any significant duration [emphasis added]."
context: NTSB quoting FAA guidance that redefines control forces from a failure as temporary and immediately manageable.

label: Erroneous AOA failure not evaluated in isolation
original_label: Erroneous AOA failure not evaluated in isolation
quote: Thus, the specific failure modes that could lead to uncommanded MCAS activation (such as an erroneous high AOA input to the MCAS) were not simulated as part of these functional hazard assessment validation tests.
context: NTSB explaining how Boeing evaluated MCAS response in the simulator but not the underlying failure cause.

label: Post-reformulation sales decline drives escalating strategy
original_label: Post-reformulation sales decline drives escalating strategy
quote: Purdue's profits declined precipitously in 2010 after the introduction of its Reformulated OxyContin, which was intended to be more difficult (though not impossible) to crush or manipulate for purposes of abuse and misuse. Purdue attributed the majority of the decline to two trends: (i) individuals abusing opioids moving from OxyContin to opioids that were easier to abuse through insufflation or injection and (ii) increased scrutiny of prescribers, pharmacists, and other actors in the opioid distribution chain. Purdue sought to recapture lost sales and increase Purdue's share of the opioid market. As a result, from 2010 through approximately February 2018, Purdue developed and implemented several strategies to ensure that the revenues generated from its opioid prescriptions, including those that Purdue knew or should have known were not medically necessary, would continue to flow to Purdue.
context: Settlement Agreement Addendum describing Purdue's strategic response to declining OxyContin sales after reformulation, establishing the context for escalating marketing and kickback schemes.

label: Shift from general detailing to targeted high-volume prescriber focus
original_label: Shift from general detailing to targeted high-volume prescriber focus
quote: From 2010 to 2013, Purdue instructed its sales force to primarily focus on the top three deciles of prescribers. The purpose of focusing the sales force on these highest deciles of prescribers was to cause an even higher volume of prescriptions to be written by them. Purdue knew, at that time, that the three highest deciles of prescribers combined accounted for only 1.5% of all opioid prescribers nationwide, but wrote 80% of all OxyContin prescriptions nationwide.
context: Settlement Agreement describing Purdue's escalation from general promotional efforts to concentrated targeting of extreme high-volume prescribers between 2010-2013.

label: E2E intensifies focus on highest-volume prescribers post-2013
original_label: E2E intensifies focus on highest-volume prescribers post-2013
quote: By 2013, Purdue intensified its detailing of the very highest-volume prescribers, i.e., those writing 25 times as many OxyContin scripts as their similarly situated peers, because it knew that its detailing was highly effective in causing these prescribers to write more prescriptions for Purdue's opioids. This strategy was referred to as the Evolve to Excellence or E2E program.
context: Settlement Agreement Addendum describing Purdue's further intensification of targeting extreme high-volume prescribers through the E2E program beginning in 2013.

label: Evolution from Region Zero do-not-call to resumed detailing
original_label: Evolution from Region Zero do-not-call to resumed detailing
quote: The ADD Program provided that Purdue could take such further steps as appropriate, including providing notice of such potential abuse or diversion to appropriate medical, regulatory or law enforcement authorities. Beginning in or about May 2007 and continuing until in or about March 2017, in the District of New Jersey and elsewhere, Purdue knowingly and intentionally conspired and agreed with others to defraud the DEA by impeding its lawful governmental functions and rights by: failing to maintain effective controls against diversion in that, with respect to more than one hundred HCPs, including ten of the HCPs the United States has identified for Purdue in the course of plea negotiations, Purdue, inter alia, failed to: (1) report and provide complete and accurate information to DEA about HCPs after the HCPs were flagged by internal anti-diversion programs, in situations in which the Company possessed sufficient information that should have led to a report; and (2) cease detailing HCPs after receiving information suggesting that those HCPs were prescribing opioid products without a legitimate medical purpose and outside the usual course of professional practice, in situations in which Purdue possessed sufficient information that a decision should have been made to cease detailing.
context: Plea Agreement charging document describing Purdue's pattern of flagging prescribers but then continuing to detail them in violation of its own anti-diversion program.

label: Detailing of pharmacies shifts from safeguard to enabler
original_label: Detailing of pharmacies shifts from safeguard to enabler
quote: From 2010 through 2012, Purdue trained its sales force to call on pharmacies that dispensed a high volume of opioid scripts and were near a large pain practice. In 2013, the same consulting company that developed E2E identified pharmacist scrutiny as a hurdle to sales and told the Board: Access to OxyContin for some patients has become quite challenging in specific local markets. This is due to a combination of factors including: regulations, DEA initiatives, [Physicians for Responsible Opioid Prescribing], wholesaler initiatives and local pharmacist perceptions.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how pharmacy detailing evolved from general practice to a tool specifically designed to overcome pharmacy safeguards against medically unnecessary prescriptions.

label: Alternative distribution through specialty pharmacies emerges from E2E constraints
original_label: Alternative distribution through specialty pharmacies emerges from E2E constraints
quote: As noted above, in July 2013, as part of the E2E program, the consulting company relayed to Purdue and the Board that OxyContin revenues were down because, among other things, entire pharmacies [are] being shut off by distributors, pharmacies themselves imposing tablet limits, decreases in channel inventory leading to greater stockouts, and pharmacies choosing to not stock OxyContin. The consulting company proposed creating an alternative model for how patients receive OxyContin. This model would bypass retail, likely through a third party vendor who would provide adjudication and direct distribution to patients. On August 16, 2013, one day after the Board briefing on E2E discussed above, Mortimer D. A. Sackler emailed a Purdue executive and others asking what ideas management had for creating a new distribution system to help relieve this problem of product access for legitimate chronic pain patients, which would use an independent service to verify the legitimacy of [the patients'] prescriptions.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how Purdue's board responded to pharmacy safeguards by developing specialty pharmacy kickback arrangements to bypass traditional retail oversight.

label: Titration messaging refined to promote higher dosages across time
original_label: Titration messaging refined to promote higher dosages across time
quote: For example, a 2011 script stated: We discussed the discontinuation rate of extended-release opioids by day 35. One of the potential reasons for discontinuation is the lack of efficacy perhaps as a result of lack of titration. E2E created a refreshed 2014 version of the script that stated: According to an analysis … 57% of patients initiated on some commonly prescribed extended-release opioids are no longer on those products by day 35, Assuming a patient discontinues therapy by day 35 due to their perceived lack of pain relief, what is the impact on your patient, you and your staff? (pause for effect), and then Doctor, working with you and your staff, I can provide support to you when initiating and titrating dosages on my products.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how Purdue refined and escalated its titration messaging between 2011 and 2014 to more aggressively encourage high-dose prescribing.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Reformulated OxyContin reframed as not eliminating abuse potential
original_label: Reformulated OxyContin reframed as not eliminating abuse potential
quote: Reformulated OxyContin was more difficult to crush or dissolve, but FDA cautioned that Reformulated OxyContin is not completely tamper-resistant and those intent on abusing this new formulation will likely find a means to do so. In addition, the product can still be misused or abused and result in overdose by simply administering or ingesting larger than recommended oral doses.
context: Settlement Agreement describing FDA's formal warning that Reformulated OxyContin did not eliminate abuse potential, which Purdue sales representatives knew but reframed in marketing.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Addiction reframed as dependence and tolerance
original_label: Addiction reframed as dependence and tolerance
quote: In addition, representatives were trained to [o]vercome . . . objection[s] raised by providers and get physicians to commit to prescribe more Purdue products. Specifically, representatives were trained to pivot from legitimate physician concerns about addiction to statements about dependence and opioid tolerance. When asked about the safety of high dosages, representatives were instructed to respond that OxyContin does not have a ceiling dose.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how Purdue trained sales representatives to reframe physicians' concerns about addiction by using different terminology and emphasizing lack of ceiling dose.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Region Zero prescribers redefined based on business value
original_label: Region Zero prescribers redefined based on business value
quote: When the sales force petitioned for a prescriber to be removed from Region Zero so that detailing of him or her could resume, and when ADD reviewed such petitions, both the sales force and ADD were aware of the volume of sales generated by that prescriber. Purdue's Sales and Marketing Department tracked prescribing of opioids by all health care providers, including providers included in ADD and Region Zero, placing them into deciles as described above. ADD contained a field that reflected whether a health care provider was a high-volume prescriber.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how Purdue integrated sales volume data into the Region Zero removal process, allowing business considerations to override safety concerns.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Declining high-dosage prescriptions attributed to regulation not abuse
original_label: Declining high-dosage prescriptions attributed to regulation not abuse
quote: The Board received information concerning OxyContin strength Rx history as well as statistical projections that attributed the decline in sales of the high dosage tablets to DEA pressures and good faith dispensing policies at large chain pharmacies, fewer patients switching into the ERO market from other products, and there are fewer patients titrating to the higher strengths from the lower ones.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how Purdue's Board was presented with information redefining declining high-dose prescriptions as a regulatory problem rather than a safety signal of abuse.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Abuse and Diversion Detection program institutionalizes yet enables continued detailing
original_label: Abuse and Diversion Detection program institutionalizes yet enables continued detailing
quote: In an effort to identify HCPs potentially engaged in abuse and diversion, Purdue implemented Standard Operating Procedure 1.7.1—later rebranded as the Abuse and Diversion Detection Program (ADD Program)—in 2002. Through the ADD Program, Purdue required every member of its field organization, including sales representatives, to report to Purdue upon learning of circumstances or making observations that may suggest potential abuse or diversion of opioids. Purdue called these Reports of Concern or ADD Reports. Circumstances requiring the submission of an ADD Report included, but were not limited to: an HCP engaging in an atypical pattern of prescribing techniques; information from a highly credible source or multiple sources (e.g., pharmacists, law enforcement, or others) that an HCP, or patients of the HCP, were engaging in diversion; unlicensed individuals signing or dispensing prescriptions; a large number of patients traveling considerable distance for visits to the practice; long lines of patients waiting for prescriptions from an HCP; an HCP's waiting room being filled to capacity; exceedingly brief or non-existent contact between a patient and an HCP; and credible allegations that an HCP is under active investigation related to diversion or substance abuse by any law enforcement or regulatory authority.
context: Plea Agreement describing Purdue's ADD program, which was institutionalized as a formal structure with detailed reporting procedures beginning in 2002.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Sales compensation tied to high-volume prescriber targeting
original_label: Sales compensation tied to high-volume prescriber targeting
quote: While the targeting strategies and terminology differed over time, from 2010 through 2013, sales representatives were instructed to develop call plans around these high volume prescribers and detail them with the most frequency. In turn, sales representatives were rewarded with incentive compensation tied to the volume of OxyContin prescriptions generated from the health care providers they had detailed and faced corrective action plans, such as performance improvement plans, when they did not meet their sales goals.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how Purdue institutionalized high-volume prescriber targeting through formal compensation structures and performance management systems.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: E2E program embedded in formal organizational structure with Board oversight
original_label: E2E program embedded in formal organizational structure with Board oversight
quote: E2E was overseen by the consulting company and some of Purdue's top executives through the creation of the E2E Executive Oversight Team (EOT) and Project Management Office (PMO). Based on a study showing that providers in deciles 7-10 were most responsive to sales calls and were the most prolific writers, the E2E call plans instructed sales representatives to call on the very highest deciles of high-volume prescribers with the most frequency. Specifically, Purdue instructed its sales representatives to call on the highest volume OxyContin prescribers (i.e., those in so-called deciles 7 through 10) at least 24 times a year and heavily favor promoting OxyContin over other Purdue opioids in their messaging.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how E2E was institutionalized through formal organizational structures with board-level oversight and specific call frequency requirements.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Sales messaging materials embed titration promotion across product line
original_label: Sales messaging materials embed titration promotion across product line
quote: Purdue's sales and marketing departments prepared scripts, visual aids, brochures, and messaging for representatives to use with the providers they called on. A large part of this marketing was intended to cause the highest volume prescribers in the nation to commit to writing more OxyContin prescriptions. At the same time, Purdue also refined its marketing message through the S.T.A.R.T. (Supplement, Titrate, Adjust, Reassess, Tailor) initiative by focusing sales conversations with prescribers on titrating patients to dosages. The goal of the program was to discourage patient discontinuation of OxyContin due to perceived lack of pain relief by encouraging providers to increase the OxyContin dosage, or titrate up.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how Purdue institutionalized titration promotion through formal sales messaging materials and named programs like S.T.A.R.T.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Prescription data analytics embedded in decile-based targeting system
original_label: Prescription data analytics embedded in decile-based targeting system
quote: Purdue ranked the prescribers based on their aggregate opioid prescriptions in deciles from numbers 1 through 10, with 10 being the highest. From 2010 to 2013, Purdue instructed its sales force to primarily focus on the top three deciles of prescribers. Purdue executives closely analyzed Purdue's internal data, including data purchased from vendors, in order to target high-volume prescribers and monitor their prescriptions.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how Purdue institutionalized high-volume prescriber targeting through formal decile-based data systems integrated into sales operations.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Pharmacy detailing embedded in sales training and tactics
original_label: Pharmacy detailing embedded in sales training and tactics
quote: To ensure that prescriptions from extreme high-volume prescribers would be filled, Purdue engaged in certain strategies, including instructing its sales representatives to detail pharmacies and paying kickbacks to specialty pharmacies to fill red flag prescriptions, which is discussed further below. Purdue also sought to encourage the pharmacists to reach out to a Prescriber to recommend that a patient be switched from immediate release oxycodone to OxyContin. In other words, Purdue's pharmacy calls both functioned to assuage pharmacists' concerns about filling prescriptions for OxyContin and at times served as a proxy or indirect call on the very Region Zero prescribers Purdue allegedly precluded the sales force from directly contacting.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how pharmacy detailing was institutionalized as a formal sales tactic to circumvent prescriber safeguards.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Order Monitoring System detects but continues marketing to suspicious pharmacies
original_label: Order Monitoring System detects but continues marketing to suspicious pharmacies
quote: At the same time, Purdue had the means and ability to detect suspicious pharmacies through its Order Monitoring System (OMS). Like Purdue's ADD team (and comprised of many of the same personnel), the OMS Committee was empowered to flag suspicious pharmacies, instruct distributors to pause or cancel orders to those pharmacies, and instruct sales representatives not to call on the pharmacies. In addition to identifying suspicious pharmacies through referrals and data analyses, the OMS team also had the ability to see which pharmacies were filling prescriptions from Region Zero prescribers. Despite having this data, Purdue continued knowingly marketing to the pharmacies that filled the prescriptions of Region Zero and other red flag providers, which led those prescribers' medically unnecessary Purdue prescriptions to be filled.
context: Settlement Agreement describing Purdue's Order Monitoring System infrastructure and how it was used to identify yet continue marketing to suspicious pharmacies.

label: Prescriber-level redefinition of abuse and diversion as non-urgent
original_label: Prescriber-level redefinition of abuse and diversion as non-urgent
quote: Purdue trained its sales representatives to only report clear instances of abuse and diversion, and sales representatives were instructed to discuss the reports with their district managers prior to filing. In addition, although Purdue's policy stated that it required timely reporting, Purdue had few, if any, effective compliance measures to address an employee's failure to report, and very few sales representatives were penalized for failing to timely report.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how Purdue's training embedded a rationalization that only very clear cases of abuse warranted reporting, reducing the practical trigger for action.

label: Medically unnecessary prescriptions reframed as patient choice and access
original_label: Medically unnecessary prescriptions reframed as patient choice and access
quote: As an additional means to circumvent safeguards intended to prevent the filling of suspicious prescriptions, from October 2015 through 2018, Purdue and certain of the Sacklers sought to find a pharmacy mechanism to fill OxyContin prescriptions that other traditional pharmacies had rejected. On August 16, 2013, one day after the Board briefing on E2E discussed above, Mortimer D. A. Sackler emailed a Purdue executive and others asking what ideas management had for creating a new distribution system to help relieve this problem of product access for legitimate chronic pain patients, which would use an independent service to verify the legitimacy of [the patients'] prescriptions.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how Purdue leadership rationalized circumventing pharmacy safeguards as a matter of patient access rather than enabling abuse.

label: DEA safeguards and pharmacist concerns reframed as market obstacles
original_label: DEA safeguards and pharmacist concerns reframed as market obstacles
quote: In 2013, the consulting company informed Purdue and its Board, that [t]he retail channel, both pharmacies and distributors, is under intense scrutiny and direct risk. More specifically, the consulting company explained [t]here are reports of wholesalers stopping shipments entirely to an increasing number of pharmacies, [m]any wholesalers are also imposing hard quantity limits on orders based on prior purchase levels, and [p]harmacy chains are implementing guidelines for which patients can fill opioid prescriptions. Later, Purdue's 2014 budget presentation to the Board listed these safeguards – intended to prevent medically unnecessary prescriptions of opioids, including OxyContin – among the challenges to achieving revenue goals.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how Purdue's consulting company and leadership collectively reframed government and pharmacy safeguards against abuse as business challenges rather than legitimate protections.

label: High-dose prescribing justified as medical titration standard
original_label: High-dose prescribing justified as medical titration standard
quote: The Board received information concerning OxyContin strength Rx history as well as statistical projections that attributed the decline in sales of the high dosage tablets to DEA pressures and good faith dispensing policies at large chain pharmacies, fewer patients switching into the ERO market from other products, and there are fewer patients titrating to the higher strengths from the lower ones (emphasis in original). At the November 2013 meeting concerning Purdue's 2014 budget, a Purdue executive discussed with the Board the company's plan to refine the message of the company's titration up marketing campaign and specifically referenced the Individualize the Dose campaign, a Conversion & Titration Guide, and the S.T.A.R.T. principles to highlight important elements of titration throughout the course of treatment.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how Purdue leadership collectively rationalized high-dose promotion through medical concepts like individualized dosing and titration principles.

label: Sales representatives trained to promote high-volume prescriber targets
original_label: Sales representatives trained to promote high-volume prescriber targets
quote: Purdue executives also emphasized the focus of E2E at national sales meetings: The single core objective of E2E…is to make sure that we're making calls on the highest potential customers with the right frequency to maximize prescribing potential. An email between two Purdue executives dated October 23, 2013, entitled S&P Final Version attached Board presentations, a 2014 Budget Presentation to the Board on OxyContin Tablets, which reflected that the extreme high-volume prescribers that E2E targeted were most sensitive to Purdue's marketing.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how Purdue socialized all sales representatives through national meetings and training to embrace E2E's high-volume prescriber targeting.

label: Representatives trained to overcome physician objections with reframed safety claims
original_label: Representatives trained to overcome physician objections with reframed safety claims
quote: In addition, representatives were trained to [o]vercome . . . objection[s] raised by providers and get physicians to commit to prescribe more Purdue products. Specifically, representatives were trained to pivot from legitimate physician concerns about addiction to statements about dependence and opioid tolerance. When asked about the safety of high dosages, representatives were instructed to respond that OxyContin does not have a ceiling dose.
context: Settlement Agreement describing standardized training that socialized sales representatives into particular reframings of safety concerns.

label: Region Zero reinstatement process co-opts management through sales metrics
original_label: Region Zero reinstatement process co-opts management through sales metrics
quote: For example, in 2012, Purdue employees petitioned for over 180 mid to high-decile Region Zero providers to be reinstated. Purdue also failed to maintain updated and complete Region Zero lists. Purdue knowingly continued detailing prescribers suspected of abuse and diversion, including at times after a ROC was filed with ADD.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how the Region Zero reinstatement process socialized managers into circumventing anti-diversion safeguards by treating high-revenue prescribers as deserving of reinstatement.

label: Sackler family co-opted consulting company findings into E2E endorsement
original_label: Sackler family co-opted consulting company findings into E2E endorsement
quote: Following the meeting, one of the consulting company partners that led the meeting with the Sacklers memorialized in an email: [T]he room was filled with only family, including the elder statesman Dr. Raymond [Sackler]. . . . We went through exhibit by exhibit for about 2 hrs. . . . They were extremely supportive of the findings and our recommendations . . . and wanted to strongly endorse getting going on our recommendations. Another consulting company partner further remarked in the email correspondence that their findings were crystal clear to the Sacklers and [the Sacklers] gave a ringing endorsement of moving forward fast.
context: Settlement Agreement describing how consulting company partners were co-opted into enthusiastically endorsing E2E through a meeting with Sackler family members who gave ringing endorsement of accelerated implementation.

label: Sales force discretion removed but decile-based targeting rationale concealed
original_label: Sales force discretion removed but decile-based targeting rationale concealed
quote: Better targeting meant focusing sales calls on extreme high-volume opioid prescribers and removing sales representative discretion with respect to call plans. context: Boeing Employee-1's email showing the organizational culture held individuals personally accountable for Level B achievement, creating pressure to protect that status regardless of technical changes.

label: Post-discovery continued concealment of MCAS from FAA AEG
original_label: Post-discovery continued concealment of MCAS from FAA AEG
quote: Despite knowing that the FAA AEG had issued its provisional 'Level B' determination without any awareness that MCAS's operational scope had been expanded to include high angle of attack conditions in nearly the entire speed range of ordinary commercial flight, Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 did not correct the FAA AEG's understanding of MCAS's operational scope or otherwise ensure that the FAA AEG's 'Level B' determination was based on an accurate understanding of MCAS's operation. Instead, Boeing—through Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2—intentionally withheld and concealed from the FAA AEG their knowledge of MCAS's expanded operational scope.
context: Statement of Facts showing the transition from initial non-disclosure to deliberate concealment after discovery, demonstrating escalation of the wrongful conduct.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: MCAS provisional approval conditioned on no significant system changes
original_label: MCAS provisional approval conditioned on no significant system changes
quote: Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 also understood, as Boeing Employee-1 acknowledged in his email on or about August 16, 2016, that the FAA AEG's 'Level B' differences determination for the 737 MAX was only a 'provisional approval [. . .] assuming no significant systems changes to the airplane.' For example, in an email to Boeing employees including Boeing Employee-2 discussing a potential change to another part of the 737 MAX's flight controls on or about November 10, 2016, Boeing Employee-1 emphasized that '[o]ne of the Program Directives we were given was to not create any differences [. . .]. This is what we sold to the regulators who have already granted us the Level B differences determination. To go back to them now, and tell them there is in fact a difference [. . .] would be a huge threat to that differences training determination.'
context: Statement of Facts showing Boeing understood the provisional nature of Level B approval and the requirement to disclose significant system changes, yet redefined the expanded MCAS scope as not meeting the threshold for re-disclosure.

label: Boeing Employee-2 becoming Chief Technical Pilot after Employee-1
original_label: Boeing Employee-2 becoming Chief Technical Pilot after Employee-1
quote: From in or around early 2012 until in or around early 2014, Boeing Employee-1 was a Technical Pilot for Boeing's 737 MAX Flight Technical Team. In or around early 2014, Boeing Employee-1 became Boeing's 737 MAX Chief Technical Pilot. In that role, Boeing Employee-1 led the 737 MAX Flight Technical Team. In or around July 2018, Boeing Employee-1 left Boeing to work for a major U.S.-based airline. From in or around mid-2014 until in or around July 2018, Boeing Employee-2 was a Technical Pilot for Boeing's 737 MAX Flight Technical Team. In or around July 2018, after Boeing Employee-1 left Boeing, Boeing Employee-2 became Boeing's 737 MAX Chief Technical Pilot.
context: Statement of Facts showing Employee-2's progression from technical pilot to Chief Technical Pilot, succeeding Employee-1 in a role central to the deceptive practices, suggesting continuity of institutional knowledge about MCAS concealment.

label: Employee-1 and Employee-2 jointly discuss MCAS discovery
original_label: Employee-1 and Employee-2 jointly discuss MCAS discovery
quote: On or about that same day, Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 discussed MCAS in an internal Boeing electronic chat communication, writing in part: Boeing Employee-1: Oh shocker alerT! [sic] / MCAS is now active down to [Mach] .2 / It's running rampant in the sim on me / at least that's what [a Boeing simulator engineer] thinks is happening Boeing Employee-2: Oh great, that means we have to update the speed trim description in vol 2 Boeing Employee-1: so I basically lied to the regulators Boeing Employee-2: it wasn't a lie, no one told us that was the case
context: Statement of Facts showing the immediate co-optation of Employee-2 into the MCAS concealment through a shared moment of discovery and rationalization, establishing common understanding between the two senior technical pilots.

label: Rationalization that no one told them of expanded MCAS scope
original_label: Rationalization that no one told them of expanded MCAS scope
quote: Boeing Employee-1: so I basically lied to the regulators Boeing Employee-2: it wasn't a lie, no one told us that was the case
context: Boeing Employee-2's response to Employee-1's acknowledgment of deception, offering a shared rationalization that reframes deliberate concealment as passive ignorance, establishing a collective narrative.

label: MCAS concealment maintained through multiple FSB Report draft cycles
original_label: MCAS concealment maintained through multiple FSB Report draft cycles
quote: On or about November 17, 2016, the FAA AEG emailed three Boeing employees, including Boeing Employee-1, Boeing Employee-2, and another Boeing employee, a draft of the forthcoming 737 MAX FSB Report. That same day, Boeing Employee-1 asked Boeing Employee-2 and the other Boeing employee to review the draft 737 MAX FSB Report 'for any glaring issues.' On or about November 22, 2016, the other Boeing employee emailed the draft 737 MAX FSB Report back to the FAA AEG with proposed edits. Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 were included on this email. Boeing Employee-1 included a proposed edit to delete a reference to MCAS, and wrote, 'We agreed not to reference MCAS since it's outside normal operating envelope.'
context: Statement of Facts showing the concealment became embedded in a formal review workflow spanning weeks, with deliberate edits to delete MCAS references across multiple document iterations.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Reframing expanded MCAS as 'way outside the normal operating envelope'
original_label: Reframing expanded MCAS as 'way outside the normal operating envelope'
quote: On or about January 17, 2017, Boeing Employee-1 again reminded the FAA AEG in an email to delete any reference to MCAS from the forthcoming 737 MAX FSB Report, and wrote, 'Flight Controls: Delete MCAS, recall we decided we weren't going to cover it [. . .] since it's way outside the normal operating envelope.'
context: Boeing Employee-1's repeated email months after discovering the expanded operational scope, invoking the 'normal operating envelope' standard to justify non-disclosure of a system now active across nearly the entire flight envelope.

label: Shared understanding that FAA AEG should not know of MCAS changes
original_label: Shared understanding that FAA AEG should not know of MCAS changes
quote: Neither Boeing Employee-1 nor Boeing Employee-2 shared the fact of MCAS's expanded operational scope with the FAA AEG or otherwise corrected the FAA AEG's misimpression that MCAS's operational scope was limited to high-speed, wind-up turns. In doing so, Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 deceived the FAA AEG into believing that the basis upon which the FAA AEG had initially 'agreed' to remove any information about MCAS from the 737 MAX FSB Report—that MCAS could only activate during the limited operational scope of a high-speed, wind-up turn—remained the same.
context: Statement of Facts documenting the joint, intentional strategy of the two chief technical pilots to maintain regulatory deception by withholding information they both knew to be material.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: MCAS deletion embedded in FSB Report preparation workflow
original_label: MCAS deletion embedded in FSB Report preparation workflow
quote: By concealing MCAS's expanded operational scope from the FAA AEG, Boeing, through Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2, defrauded, impaired, obstructed, defeated, and interfered with the FAA AEG's lawful function to evaluate MCAS and to include information about MCAS in the 737 MAX FSB Report. Based on Boeing's misleading statements, half-truths, and omissions to the FAA AEG about MCAS, and in reliance on those statements and omissions, the FAA AEG agreed to delete all information about MCAS from the 737 MAX FSB Report.
context: Statement of Facts showing the deception became institutionalized in the final FSB Report itself, which lacked MCAS information as a direct result of the concealment embedded in the review process.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: MCAS absence propagated into airline manuals and training materials
original_label: MCAS absence propagated into airline manuals and training materials
quote: From in or around January 2017 through in or around July 2017 (when the 737 MAX FSB Report was published), Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 sent and caused to be sent emails to representatives of various Boeing airline customers that had agreed to purchase the 737 MAX, including major U.S.-based airlines. In these emails, Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 or members of their 737 MAX Flight Technical Team referenced and included drafts of the forthcoming 737 MAX FSB Report and airplane manuals and pilot-training materials for Boeing's 737 MAX airline customers. None of these items contained any information about MCAS, consistent with Boeing Employee-1's and Boeing Employee-2's efforts to deceive the FAA AEG into deleting information about MCAS.
context: Statement of Facts showing how the MCAS concealment was systematically embedded in and propagated through official operational documents distributed to airlines over a six-month period.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Final FSB Report published without MCAS information
original_label: Final FSB Report published without MCAS information
quote: On or about July 5, 2017, the FAA AEG published the first 737 MAX FSB Report, which included the FAA AEG's 'Level B' differences-training determination for the 737 MAX. Because of Boeing's intentional withholding of information from the FAA AEG, the final version of the 737 MAX FSB Report lacked information about MCAS, and relevant portions of this 737 MAX FSB Report were materially false, inaccurate, and incomplete. In turn, airplane manuals and pilot-training materials for U.S.-based airlines lacked information about MCAS, and relevant portions of these manuals and materials were similarly materially false, inaccurate, and incomplete as a result. After the FAA AEG published the final version of the 737 MAX FSB Report, Boeing continued to sell, and Boeing's U.S.-based airline customers were permitted to fly, the 737 MAX. Pilots flying the 737 MAX for Boeing's airline customers were not provided any information about MCAS in their airplane manuals and pilot-training materials.
context: Statement of Facts showing the institutionalization of MCAS absence across all regulatory, operational and training documents that governed 737 MAX operations from July 2017 forward.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Post-crash reframing of regulatory agreement as mutual decision
original_label: Post-crash reframing of regulatory agreement as mutual decision
quote: Boeing investigated, among other things, what information Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 provided to the FAA AEG about MCAS. In connection with this investigation, Boeing Employee-2 caused Boeing to represent in a presentation to the FAA AEG that, during the training-evaluation process, Boeing and the FAA AEG had 'discussed and agreed on [the] removal of MCAS' from the 737 MAX FSB Report and associated materials. This representation was misleading because Boeing Employee-2 had failed to disclose the 'shocker alert' chat communication and the fact that the FAA AEG was deprived of relevant information about MCAS.
context: Statement of Facts showing how after the Lion Air crash, Boeing Employee-2 reframed the concealment as a joint decision, creating a false narrative that hid the deception and the FAA's lack of full information.

label: Post-crash misleading presentation to FAA AEG
original_label: Post-crash misleading presentation to FAA AEG
quote: Also, in and around the same time, Boeing Employee-2 caused Boeing to present a false and misleading presentation to the FAA AEG about MCAS. Boeing investigated, among other things, what information Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 provided to the FAA AEG about MCAS. In connection with this investigation, Boeing Employee-2 caused Boeing to represent in a presentation to the FAA AEG that, during the training-evaluation process, Boeing and the FAA AEG had 'discussed and agreed on [the] removal of MCAS' from the 737 MAX FSB Report and associated materials.
context: Statement of Facts showing escalation of the concealment after crashes were discovered: rather than disclose the deception, Boeing Employee-2 orchestrated a misleading presentation that falsely characterized the removal decision.

label: MCAS operational scope expanded between design iterations
original_label: MCAS operational scope expanded between design iterations
quote: MCAS was originally designed to operate only under conditions involving both high speeds (Mach 0.6-0.8) and high AoA, conditions that were "outside the normal flight envelope." MCAS was therefore not expected to engage during the course of a normal commercial flight. Later in the design and certification process, however, Boeing expanded the operational scope of MCAS to address a tendency of the 737 MAX to pitch upwards at high AoA even at lower speeds. To achieve this, Boeing widened the speed range within which MCAS could operate to Mach 0.2-0.8, now encompassing speeds at which a commercial flight would regularly travel, and also expanded MCAS's command authority, or the degree to which MCAS could push down the nose of the plane, at lower speeds (the "MCAS Expansion").
context: SEC finding documenting the technical design history showing successive expansion of MCAS capabilities from high-altitude rare scenario to normal flight envelope.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: MCAS classified as outside normal operating envelope to justify minimal disclosure
original_label: MCAS classified as outside normal operating envelope to justify minimal disclosure
quote: Boeing employees responsible for communicating with the FAA-AEG presented MCAS to the FAA-AEG as a feature that could only activate in a very specific, high-speed scenario that was outside the normal flight envelope and therefore unlikely to ever be encountered by a commercial pilot.
context: SEC finding describing how Boeing characterized MCAS to regulators to justify excluding it from pilot training and flight manuals.

label: MCAS Expansion introduced after FAA provisional approval
original_label: MCAS Expansion introduced after FAA provisional approval
quote: In or around August 2016, the FAA-AEG made a provisional determination to accept Boeing's proposal of CBT-only and to omit MCAS from the differences training and flight manuals. At that time, the FAA-AEG was not aware of the MCAS Expansion. In or around March 2016, Boeing introduced the MCAS Expansion, significantly broadening MCAS's operational scope.
context: SEC finding showing Boeing expanded MCAS capabilities after securing preliminary regulatory approval based on narrower scope representation.

label: FAA-AEG unaware of MCAS Expansion while different FAA group received certification documents
original_label: FAA-AEG unaware of MCAS Expansion while different FAA group received certification documents
quote: The MCAS Expansion was reflected in certification documents provided to a different group within the FAA that was responsible for determining whether the 737 MAX met U.S. federal airworthiness certification standards; however, that group was not involved in the review and approval of pilot training requirements and flight manuals.
context: SEC footnote explaining organizational compartmentalization at FAA that resulted in pilot-training regulators lacking knowledge of MCAS scope changes that other FAA divisions possessed.

label: Employee acknowledges MCAS now active at lower Mach numbers than originally represented
original_label: Employee acknowledges MCAS now active at lower Mach numbers than originally represented
quote: On or about November 15, 2016, during a test flight of the 737 MAX in a simulator, Boeing Employee-1 experienced what Boeing Employee-1 recognized as MCAS operating at lower speed. Later that day, Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 discussed MCAS in an electronic chat (the "November 15, 2016 Chat") which contained the following exchange: Boeing Employee-1: Oh shocker alerT! / MCAS is now active down to M[ach] .2 / It's running rampant in the sim[ulator] on me… / so I basically lied to the regulators (unknowingly) Boeing Employee-2: [I]t wasn't a lie, no one told us that was the case
context: SEC finding quoting internal Boeing employee exchange documenting awareness that MCAS expansion contradicted earlier representations to FAA.

label: Rationalization that undisclosed MCAS expansion was not a lie because no one communicated it
original_label: Rationalization that undisclosed MCAS expansion was not a lie because no one communicated it
quote: Boeing Employee-2: [I]t wasn't a lie, no one told us that was the case
context: SEC finding quoting Boeing Employee-2's response to Employee-1's admission of misrepresenting MCAS to regulators, rationalizing it as not a lie.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: MCAS omitted from official FAA Flight Standardization Board Report
original_label: MCAS omitted from official FAA Flight Standardization Board Report
quote: On or about July 5, 2017, the FAA-AEG published the FSB Report, which omitted any information about MCAS. Consistent with the determinations made by the FAA-AEG as reflected in the published FSB Report, MCAS was not described in the 737 MAX flight manuals or pilot training materials, and was not part of the required differences training for pilots transitioning to the 737 MAX when the 737 MAX entered into service in mid-2017.
context: SEC finding documenting institutionalization of MCAS omission through official regulatory documentation and operational procedures.

label: CEO directs removal of MCAS software redesign discussion from public statement
original_label: CEO directs removal of MCAS software redesign discussion from public statement
quote: After reviewing the draft, Muilenburg directed that the Draft Press Release be modified to incorporate a discussion of facts drawn from the Lion Air Preliminary Report, and also suggested removing discussion of the planned MCAS software redesign from the Draft Press Release.
context: SEC finding describing CEO Dennis Muilenburg's editorial direction to exclude mention of MCAS software redesign from press release.

label: CEO emphasizes need to shift from defensive to offensive public messaging
original_label: CEO emphasizes need to shift from defensive to offensive public messaging
quote: On November 20, 2018, Muilenburg expressed disappointment in Boeing's response to the negative post-crash media coverage, stating in an email that "[w]e are spending too much time playing defense… [we] need to start playing some offense."
context: SEC finding quoting CEO email directing messaging strategy shift away from addressing safety concerns toward aggressive public relations.

label: Draft press release progressively modified to remove safety remediation discussion
original_label: Draft press release progressively modified to remove safety remediation discussion
quote: From that point forward, the Draft Press Release no longer mentioned the development of an "MCAS software update," and also stated that Boeing's customers and passengers "have [Boeing's] assurance that the 737 MAX is as safe as any airplane that has ever flown the skies."
context: SEC finding describing how Boeing's draft press release evolved to remove mention of MCAS software redesign while adding strong safety assurance language.

label: CEO approves final press release with safety assurance despite known safety issue
original_label: CEO approves final press release with safety assurance despite known safety issue
quote:
On the afternoon of November 27, 2018, Muilenburg approved the issuance of the November 2018 Press Release via email, writing, "Looks great – factual, and sticks to the report while making our key points. Good to go here …."
The November 2018 Press Release highlighted certain facts from the Lion Air Preliminary Report suggesting that pilot error and poor airplane maintenance by Lion Air had contributed to the crash. The November 2018 Press Release did not mention that the SRB had identified an ongoing "airplane safety issue" associated with MCAS or the planned software redesign – indeed, it did not mention MCAS at all. The final November 2018 Press Release also contained the statement: "As our customers and their passengers continue to fly the 737 MAX to hundreds of destinations around the world every day, they have our assurance that the 737 MAX is as safe as any airplane that has ever flown the skies."
context: SEC finding documenting CEO approval of press release containing strong safety assurances while omitting known MCAS safety issue requiring remediation.

label: Compliance review team unaware of critical November 2016 employee chat about MCAS misrepresentation
original_label: Compliance review team unaware of critical November 2016 employee chat about MCAS misrepresentation
quote: The MCAS Certification Compliance Review team was not aware of the November 15, 2016 Chat. Consequently, the November 15, 2016 Chat was not referenced in the MCAS Certification Compliance Review report and did not factor into its findings and conclusions.
context: SEC finding noting that Boeing's internal compliance review team lacked knowledge of critical communications revealing misrepresentation to regulators.

label: DOJ investigation uncovers November 2016 chat documenting MCAS misrepresentation to regulators
original_label: DOJ investigation uncovers November 2016 chat documenting MCAS misrepresentation to regulators
quote: In the wake of the Lion Air Crash, the DOJ began an investigation into the 737 MAX certification process. In January 2019, while collecting documents in connection with the DOJ's investigation, members of Boeing's Legal Department uncovered a series of communications that raised questions about the disclosures made to the FAA-AEG concerning the differences training and manuals certification, including the November 15, 2016 Chat in which Boeing Employee-1 wrote that he had "lied to regulators (unknowingly)" about MCAS.
context: SEC finding describing discovery during DOJ document collection of internal Boeing communications showing employee acknowledged lying to regulators about MCAS.

label: CEO briefed on concerning communications about MCAS misrepresentation to FAA
original_label: CEO briefed on concerning communications about MCAS misrepresentation to FAA
quote: In or around January 2019, Boeing's in-house counsel informed Muilenburg and other senior executives about the existence of the November 15, 2016 Chat. Following that communication, Muilenburg understood the November 15, 2016 Chat to be "concerning."
context: SEC finding documenting that CEO Muilenburg was informed of the problematic chat and recognized it as concerning but took no public corrective action.

label: CEO makes certification process statements despite known documentation gaps and employee admissions
original_label: CEO makes certification process statements despite known documentation gaps and employee admissions
quote: During the questioning, one analyst asked in relevant part: "how did this slip through the engineering organization? How did it slip through the FAA…" Muilenburg's answer stated in relevant part: [T]here is no technical slip or gap here… But I can tell you with confidence that we understand our airplane, we understand how the design was accomplished, how the certification was accomplished, and remain fully confident in the product that we've put in the field… But there was no surprise or gap or unknown here or something that somehow slipped through a certification process. Quite the opposite. We know exactly how the airplane was designed. We know exactly how it was certified.
context: SEC finding quoting CEO statements on April 24, 2019 earnings call denying gaps in certification while being aware of November 2016 chat and compliance review concerns.

label: CEO assures shareholders of adherence to design and certification standards despite known issues
original_label: CEO assures shareholders of adherence to design and certification standards despite known issues
quote: Five days later, on April 29, during a press conference following Boeing's annual shareholders' meeting, a reporter asked Muilenburg whether the MCAS design was deeply flawed. Muilenburg, on behalf of Boeing, responded in relevant part: "We have gone back and confirmed again … that we followed exactly the steps in our design and certification processes that consistently produce safe airplanes. It was designed per our standards. It was certified per our standards."
context: SEC finding quoting CEO April 29, 2019 statements to shareholders and media asserting strict compliance with design and certification standards.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Compliance review documents critical assumption about MCAS hazard lacking adequate support
original_label: Compliance review documents critical assumption about MCAS hazard lacking adequate support
quote: The MCAS Certification Compliance Review ultimately concluded that the certification process with respect to MCAS was compliant with FAA regulations. However, the written report identified several documentation gaps and inconsistencies relating to MCAS and the certification process, including a lack of adequate supporting documentation for the assumption, used by Boeing engineers and test pilots throughout the design and testing process, that repeated unintended MCAS activations (as the crew of Lion Air Flight 610 experienced) would be no more hazardous than a single unintended MCAS activation – an assumption that was later called into doubt by the SRB.
context: SEC finding describing Boeing's compliance review identifying critical undocumented assumption about repeated MCAS activations that later proved false.

label: FAA-AEG lacked awareness of MCAS Expansion when approving CBT-only training
original_label: FAA-AEG lacked awareness of MCAS Expansion when approving CBT-only training
quote: In or around March 2016, Boeing introduced the MCAS Expansion, significantly broadening MCAS's operational scope. No longer limited to a specific, rare high-speed scenario, MCAS could now activate at abnormally high AoA throughout the entire speed range of the 737 MAX, including during the initial climb and the final descent, and its command authority was significantly increased to allow it to function effectively at lower speeds. In or around August 2016, the FAA-AEG made a provisional determination to accept Boeing's proposal of CBT-only and to omit MCAS from the differences training and flight manuals. At that time, the FAA-AEG was not aware of the MCAS Expansion.
context: SEC finding documenting temporal sequence showing MCAS scope expanded before regulatory approval was obtained, with regulators unaware of the expansion.

label: Software redesign timeline compressed after second fatal crash
original_label: Software redesign timeline compressed after second fatal crash
quote: On or about November 15, 2018, Boeing safety engineers concluded that, in light of the SRB's findings, the MCAS software should be redesigned and re-installed on the 737 MAX fleet to remediate the high crew workload "airplane safety issue." They determined that the software redesign had to be completed within approximately 27 months, but that the 737 MAX fleet could continue to operate in the interim in light of Boeing's bulletin and the FAA emergency airworthiness directive. Around the same time, the FAA conducted its own safety analysis and reached conclusions similar to those reached by the Boeing SRB, including that the Boeing 737 MAX could continue to operate pending remediation of the MCAS-related crew workload issue; however, the FAA review concluded that a software redesign would have to be completed within approximately 8 months (later shortened to approximately 7 months).
context: SEC finding showing Boeing's initial 27-month remediation timeline was much longer than FAA's requirement of 8 months, revealing tension over safety urgency.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: FAA issues emergency airworthiness directive instructing pilots to use existing 'runaway stabilizer' procedures
original_label: FAA issues emergency airworthiness directive instructing pilots to use existing 'runaway stabilizer' procedures
quote: On November 7, 2018, the FAA issued a public emergency airworthiness directive to airlines operating the 737 MAX, informing them of the potential for repeated nose-down movements of the aircraft which, "if not addressed, could cause the flight crew to have difficulty controlling the airplane … and [could result in] possible impact with terrain." The airworthiness directive identified the issue as an "unsafe condition" on the 737 MAX, and, as an "interim action" pending further analysis, referred crews to the runaway stabilizer procedures described in Boeing's November 6 bulletin.
context: SEC finding describing institutionalization of interim safety fix through FAA emergency directive routing pilots to undocumented emergency procedures.

label: Escalating use of SPEs from LJM to LJM2 to Raptors
original_label: Escalating use of SPEs from LJM to LJM2 to Raptors
quote: By 1999, Enron was increasingly dependent on transactions with SPEs to meet its financial reporting goals. In June 1999, in order to have an off-balance-sheet SPE to which Enron could readily and repeatedly turn to achieve its desired financial reporting results, Enron's Board of Directors (the "Board") agreed to permit CFO Fastow to create and serve as the managing partner of a new SPE named LJM. The Board later approved Fastow's participation in another even larger SPE named LJM2 (the LJM entities are collectively referred to as "LJM" unless otherwise noted). LJM's business activity principally involved transactions with Enron and Enron affiliates. "Raptor" Hedges: Beginning in the spring of 2000, Enron and LJM2 engaged in a series of financial transactions with four SPEs called Raptor I, Raptor II, Raptor Ill and Raptor IV (collectively referred to as the "Raptors").
context: The indictment describes a progression of increasingly complex SPE structures used to achieve off-balance-sheet accounting, from LJM (1999) to LJM2 (later approved) to four Raptor entities (spring 2000), each building on the previous.

label: Raptor I structure expanded after side deal secured
original_label: Raptor I structure expanded after side deal secured
quote: After satisfying the conditions of the side deal by providing LJM2 with a guaranteed return on its investment, Enron began to use Raptor I to hedge the value of Enron's assets. Enron employees manipulated the book values of Enron assets, many of which were expected to decline in value, before they were hedged, knowing that the Raptor I structure ensured that Eron would not suffer the financial reporting consequences of subsequent, and anticipated, declines in the value of those assets. CAUSEY and Fastow further used Raptor I fraudulently to promote Enron's financial position by back-dating a hedge to Enron's advantage, capturing the all-time high stock value of one of the Enron assets at a time when they knew that value already had declined.
context: The indictment shows how once the initial side deal with LJM2 was satisfied, the Raptor I structure was then used for increasingly aggressive asset manipulation, including back-dating hedges.

label: Scheme persists and grows from 1999 through 2001
original_label: Scheme persists and grows from 1999 through 2001
quote: From at least 1999 through late 2001, defendant RICHARD A. CAUSEY, together with other Enron executives and senior managers, engaged in a wide-ranging scheme, through a variety of devices, to deceive the investing public about the true performance and profitability of Enron's businesses by manipulating Enron's publicly reported financial results and making false and misleading public representations about Enron's financial results and the performance of its various business units.
context: The indictment establishes the temporal scope of the conspiracy, showing sustained fraudulent activity over more than two years involving multiple executives.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Raptor I reframed as valid hedge despite accounting rule violations
original_label: Raptor I reframed as valid hedge despite accounting rule violations
quote: The Raptor I structure, however, was invalid under applicable accounting rules because Talon was not independent from Enron, and LJM2's investment in Talon was not at risk. Defendant RICHARD A. CAUSEY and Fastow had an oral side deal that LJM2 would receive its initial investment in Talon plus a profit of $11 million from Enron, all prior to Talon engaging in any of the hedging transactions for which it was created. As a quid pro quo for this payment to LJM2, Fastow agreed with CAUSEY that Enron employees could use Raptor I to manipulate Enron's balance sheet, including by allowing Enron employees, without negotiation or due diligence on behalf of LJM2, to select the values at which the Enron assets were hedged with Talon.
context: The indictment describes how CAUSEY and Fastow treated an inherently invalid structure (Talon lacked independence and LJM2's investment was not at risk) as acceptable through an oral side deal that circumvented the accounting rules requiring independence and risk.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Budget targets reframed as derived from earnings goals rather than business forecasts
original_label: Budget targets reframed as derived from earnings goals rather than business forecasts
quote: In order to achieve their objectives, Enron's executives and senior managers, including defendant RICHARD A. CAUSEY, imposed annual and quarterly earnings targets ("budget targets") on each of the company's business units. These budget targets were derived from earnings-per-share goals rather than on forecasts derived from the projected earnings likely to be generated by the company's various commercial operations. When the budget targets were not met through results from business operations, they were achieved through the use of various earnings "levers," many of which involved fraudulent devices, including but not limited to those described below.
context: The indictment shows how Enron redefined normal budgeting practice by inverting the relationship between targets and operations: instead of forecasts driving targets, earnings goals drove targets, making fraud the mechanism to bridge the gap.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Fraudulent devices justified through misleading descriptions dovetailed with accounting requirements
original_label: Fraudulent devices justified through misleading descriptions dovetailed with accounting requirements
quote: Enron's executives and senior managers frequently explained the use of these devices to Enron's outside auditors, and at times to the investing public, through misleading descriptions and justifications that were designed to dovetail with accounting and financial reporting requirements but which masked the true intent of Enron''s executives and senior managers to present a false and misleading portrait of Enron's current and likely future financial condition.
context: The indictment describes how executives reframed fraudulent accounting devices as compliant with accounting rules through selective and misleading explanations given to auditors and the public.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Trading profits reclassified from speculation to intermediation
original_label: Trading profits reclassified from speculation to intermediation
quote: During 2000 and 2001, the profitability of Enron's wholesale energy trading business, primarily based in its ENA business unit, dramatically increased for reasons including rapidly rising energy prices in the western United States, especially in California. This sudden and large increase in trading profits, which exceeded $1 billion, threatened to undermine Enron's description and presentation of itself as the dominant "intermediator" in the energy markets, rather than as a speculative (and therefore risky) trading company whose stock would trade at a much lower price-to-earnings ratio. In order to mask these earnings and preserve them for later use, defendant RICHARD A. CAUSEY and others fraudulently created and used reserve accounts within ENA both to conceal the extent of ENA's trading profits and, as set forth above, to avoid reporting large losses in other areas of its business.
context: The indictment shows how Enron reframed its actual speculative trading business as intermediation, and manipulated financial reporting to preserve this redefined identity even as trading profits threatened to expose the truth.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Budget targets imposed as regular system on all business units
original_label: Budget targets imposed as regular system on all business units
quote: In order to achieve their objectives, Enron's executives and senior managers, including defendant RICHARD A. CAUSEY, imposed annual and quarterly earnings targets ("budget targets") on each of the company's business units. These budget targets were derived from earnings-per-share goals rather than on forecasts derived from the projected earnings likely to be generated by the company's various commercial operations.
context: The indictment describes how inverted budgeting (targets derived from EPS goals rather than business forecasts) was institutionalized as a regular system applied to every business unit.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
