LJM Cayman had two limited partners, an entity owned by Credit Suisse First Boston ("CSFB") and an entity owned by National Westminster Bank ("NatWest"). Each invested $7.5 million.
context: The Information describes how LJM Cayman was structured through multiple tiers of entities and partnerships, making it difficult for external parties to trace ownership and control back to Enron insiders.

label: Elaborate scheme with systematic masking
original_label: Elaborate scheme with systematic masking
quote: Lay, Skilling, and their numerous co-conspirators perpetrated an elaborate scheme to mislead analysts and investors about Enron's true financial picture. Their efforts to mislead the markets were protracted, deliberate and dishonest. At a time when the company was floundering, these defendants perpetrated a lie – that Enron was a robust and growing company in the strongest financial condition it had ever been in. As they knew, the truth was something very different. Enron faced significant financial difficulties that had been systematically masked by a series of deceptive accounting tricks.
context: Deputy Attorney General Paul McNulty describes the charges against Lay and Skilling in a DOJ statement following their conviction in May 2006, indicating that the wrongdoing involved a series of deceptive accounting techniques that masked financial problems over time.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology

original_label: Multiple co-conspirators in elaborate scheme
quote: Lay, Skilling, and their numerous co-conspirators perpetrated an elaborate scheme to mislead analysts and investors about Enron's true financial picture.
context: McNulty's statement indicates that the fraudulent scheme involved multiple participants across the organization, suggesting the wrongdoing was embedded in organizational structures rather than confined to individual actors.

label: MCAS changes unfamiliar to pilots across iterations
original_label: MCAS changes unfamiliar to pilots across iterations
quote: Both planes were Boeing 737 MAX airliners. The crashes were caused by pilots' unfamiliarity with Boeing's changes to the 737 MAX's Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS).
context: Fifth Circuit opinion describing the technical cause of the two crashes, establishing that Boeing had made changes to MCAS that were not adequately communicated or trained, suggesting incremental system modifications.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Boeing employees intentionally misled FAA on MCAS changes
original_label: Boeing employees intentionally misled FAA on MCAS changes
quote: In January 2021, the Department charged Boeing with conspiracy to defraud the United States under 18 U.S.C. § 371, alleging that two Boeing employees had intentionally misled the FAA regarding changes to the MCAS system.
context: Fifth Circuit opinion summarizing the DOJ criminal charge against Boeing, showing that the deviation from standard practice was deliberate misrepresentation to regulators about technical changes.

label: Department's initial miscommunication about investigation status
original_label: Department's initial miscommunication about investigation status
quote: In February 2020, a representative of the Flight 302 crash victims' families contacted the Department, which told them that Boeing was not currently under criminal investigation. The Department later apologized for failing to meet and confer with the families, claiming it was caused by 'a regrettable and inadvertent internal miscommunication.'
context: Fifth Circuit opinion describing the Department's failure to inform crash victims of the investigation, attributed to internal communication silos within the DOJ.

label: District court accepted legal error as justification for CVRA violation
original_label: District court accepted legal error as justification for CVRA violation
quote: It found that, although the Department had violated the CVRA by denying the families' right to confer prior to reaching an agreement with Boeing, see 18 U.S.C. § 3771(a), it had done so not out of bad faith but due to 'legal error.'
context: Fifth Circuit opinion describing the district court's 2023 decision, showing how a violation of statutory victim rights was excused as an innocent mistake rather than sanctioned.

label: Families excluded from negotiation of DPA terms
original_label: Families excluded from negotiation of DPA terms
quote: In January 2021, the Department charged Boeing with conspiracy to defraud the United States under 18 U.S.C. § 371, alleging that two Boeing employees had intentionally misled the FAA regarding changes to the MCAS system. The same day, the Department filed a Deferred Prosecution Agreement (DPA) it had negotiated with Boeing, in which Boeing admitted responsibility for the acts charged. The district court approved the DPA a few weeks later.
context: Fifth Circuit opinion describing how the DOJ negotiated and finalized a deferred prosecution agreement with Boeing without notifying or consulting the crash victim families.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Department's mistaken belief crash victims were not crime victims
original_label: Department's mistaken belief crash victims were not crime victims
quote: That error, the court explained, was the Department's mistaken belief that the crash victims were not 'crime victims' under the CVRA. Ibid.; see 18 U.S.C. § 3771(e)(2)(A) (defining 'crime victim' as 'a person directly and proximately harmed as a result of the commission of a Federal offense or an offense in the District of Columbia').
context: Fifth Circuit opinion explaining the district court's 2023 finding, showing how the Department redefined the legal standard to exclude persons directly harmed by the crash.

label: Department told families it was considering NPA without committing to victim consultation
original_label: Department told families it was considering NPA without committing to victim consultation
quote: In May 2025, the Department held a video call with the victims' families about its renewed case against Boeing. The Department told the families it was considering resolving the case through a motion to dismiss and a non-prosecution agreement (NPA). It explained that an NPA meant it would agree not to prosecute Boeing, which would 'require the Department to move to dismiss the charge pending against Boeing.' In exchange, Boeing would agree to 'various undertakings, such as paying a penalty, improving compliance, etc.' The Department would agree not to revive the case unless it determined that Boeing had breached the NPA.
context: Fifth Circuit opinion describing the May 2025 call where DOJ notified families of its intended NPA, framing it as informational rather than consultative.

label: Families excluded from knowing timing of NPA and dismissal motion
original_label: Families excluded from knowing timing of NPA and dismissal motion
quote: The families had mixed opinions about the proposed NPA. In response to some concerns, the prosecution assured the families that their attorneys could 'talk to [them] about the legal authority a judge has to deny the government's motion to dismiss.' It also told the families that any NPA with Boeing would include a provision stating that if Boeing breached the NPA, 'the Department could refire the charge and prosecute the case, notwithstanding the passage of time.' Finally, the prosecution stated it would 'support the victims' families right to be heard in front of Judge O'Connor' while he was considering whether to grant the motion to dismiss.
context: Fifth Circuit opinion describing how the Department provided assurances to families about judicial review and refiling rights while keeping them uncertain about the actual sequence of NPA signing and dismissal filing.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: NPA treated as allowing refiling despite apparent statute of limitations bar
original_label: NPA treated as allowing refiling despite apparent statute of limitations bar
quote: The prosecution was also not misleading when it promised it could renew charges 'notwithstanding the passage of time.' Contrary to the families' argument, the NPA allows future charges against Boeing if Boeing violates the NPA. The NPA expressly permits prosecution for conduct that is 'not time-barred by the applicable statute of limitations on the date of the signing of this Agreement.' The NPA was signed in May 2025. As of that date, the pending section 371 charge was not time-barred because the prosecution tolled limitations by filing an information in 2021.
context: Fifth Circuit opinion defending the DOJ's representation to families about its ability to prosecute Boeing after an NPA, redefining when the statute of limitations runs.

label: District court granted dismissal despite victim objections
original_label: District court granted dismissal despite victim objections
quote: The district court granted the motion to dismiss, holding the Department had not 'acted with bad faith' and had 'given more than mere conclusory reasons for its dismissal.' United States v. Boeing Co., No. 4:21-CR-5, 2025 WL 3095958, at *5 (N.D. Tex. Nov. 6, 2025).
context: Fifth Circuit opinion describing the district court's November 2025 approval of the DOJ's dismissal motion, requiring only that the Department show lack of bad faith rather than affirmative justification.

label: Court of appeals lacks jurisdiction to review substance of dismissal decision
original_label: Court of appeals lacks jurisdiction to review substance of dismissal decision
quote: The CVRA provides that victims' rights 'shall be asserted in the district court,' and '[i]f the district court denies the relief sought, the movant may petition the court of appeals for a writ of mandamus.' 18 U.S.C. § 3771(d)(3). Because the CVRA mentions mandamus petitions only in the context of protecting the rights of crime victims, it confers no jurisdiction to review the underlying merits of a Rule 48 dismissal.
context: Fifth Circuit opinion establishing that appellate review of CVRA violations does not extend to review of the prosecution's underlying decision to dismiss, fragmenting accountability.

label: Appellate court declined to read fairness requirement into dismissal review
original_label: Appellate court declined to read fairness requirement into dismissal review
quote: The families respond that by applying the 'wrong legal standard,' a district court fails to treat crime victims' families 'with fairness' as the CVRA requires, making the underlying dismissal reviewable. See 18 U.S.C. § 3771(a)(8). We disagree. We decline to read into the CVRA an unlimited right for victims to appeal the dismissal of criminal prosecutions. Such a sweeping right would be inconsistent with the basic proposition that nonparties lack a 'judicially cognizable interest' in the prosecution of another.
context: Fifth Circuit opinion rejecting families' argument that fairness requirements extend to reviewing the merits of a Rule 48 dismissal, narrowing the scope of victim protections.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Conferral defined as merely comparing views, not meaningful consultation
original_label: Conferral defined as merely comparing views, not meaningful consultation
quote: They were afforded this right when the prosecution met with them via video call in May 2025. During that call, the prosecution 'compare[d] [its] views' with those of the families, thereby conferring with them as the CVRA requires. 18 U.S.C. § 3771(a)(5); see, e.g., In re Dean, 527 F.3d 391, 394–95 (5th Cir. 2008) (per curiam) (CVRA affords victims the right to 'communicate meaningfully with the government, personally or through counsel'). They were afforded this right when the prosecution met with them via video call in May 2025. During that call, the prosecution 'compare[d] [its] views' with those of the families, thereby conferring with them as the CVRA requires.
context: Fifth Circuit opinion redefining the CVRA's conferral requirement as satisfied by a single one-way informational call where the government presents its position to families.

label: Boeing's DPA breach alleged only after it was no longer binding
original_label: Boeing's DPA breach alleged only after it was no longer binding
quote: In May 2024, the Department notified the district court that Boeing had breached the DPA by 'failing to design, implement, and enforce a compliance and ethics program to prevent and detect violations of the U.S. fraud laws throughout its operations.'
context: Fifth Circuit opinion describing how the DOJ discovered and reported Boeing's breach of its compliance obligations under the DPA, fragmenting when this information became known to stakeholders.

label: First NPA superseded DPA after breach discovery, repeated with different terms
original_label: First NPA superseded DPA after breach discovery, repeated with different terms
quote: About two weeks later, the prosecution and Boeing signed an NPA in line with the one it had discussed with the families. The finalized NPA and its attachments contained numerous references to the earlier DPA. One of the NPA's provisions required Boeing to agree that if it breached the NPA, it could be prosecuted for conduct 'not time-barred by the applicable statute of limitations on the date of the signing of this [NPA].'
context: Fifth Circuit opinion describing how the DOJ replaced the 2021 DPA with a 2025 NPA after Boeing's breach, maintaining continuity through cross-references but redefining the statute of limitations provisions.

label: MCAS operational scope expanded from certification maneuver to takeoff and landing
original_label: MCAS operational scope expanded from certification maneuver to takeoff and landing
quote: As originally designed, MCAS operated only during a maneuver called a high-speed, wind-up turn, in which the airplane turns sharply in a corkscrew-like pattern at speeds of Mach 0.6 to 0.8. A high-speed, wind-up turn is a "certification" maneuver that a pilot would never perform on a typical commercial passenger flight. But sometime after June 2015, MCAS's operational scope was expanded, allowing MCAS to activate at speeds as low as Mach 0.2. The low-speed expansion meant that MCAS could activate during takeoff and landing.
context: Court's factual background describing how MCAS capability grew incrementally from a narrow certification-only function to activation during routine flight operations.

label: Boeing employees hid MCAS low-speed expansion from FAA certification group
original_label: Boeing employees hid MCAS low-speed expansion from FAA certification group
quote: The Government alleges that two Boeing employees hid MCAS's low-speed expansion from the AEG. Both employees held the position of chief technical pilot for the 737 MAX program at different times. Part of the chief technical pilot's duties were to work with the AEG on the differences training level determination. According to the Government, the chief technical pilots intentionally hid MCAS's low-speed expansion from the AEG so that they could secure the less rigorous—and less expensive—Level B training.
context: Court describing the deliberate concealment strategy: Boeing employees with direct responsibility to inform the FAA withheld material information.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Training certification decision embedded in AEG's formal FSB Report process
original_label: Training certification decision embedded in AEG's formal FSB Report process
quote: The Aircraft Evaluation Group ("AEG") is the sub-group that determines the minimum level of training required for U.S.-based airline pilots to fly a new version of an aircraft. The AEG does that by evaluating the differences between the new and old aircraft versions, then publishing a "differences training" determination for the new version. Training levels range from Level A, the least intensive, to Level E, the most intensive. The AEG publishes its determination in a Flight Standardization Board Report ("FSB Report"). Airlines must train their pilots in accordance with the FSB Report, and more intensive training tends to be more expensive for the airlines.
context: Court describing the formal institutional structure through which Boeing's deception was embedded—the FSB Report as a standardized, mandatory document affecting all operators.

label: Boeing's business goal to limit training to Level B to minimize customer costs
original_label: Boeing's business goal to limit training to Level B to minimize customer costs
quote: One of Boeing's goals in designing the 737 MAX was to ensure the designated differences training would be no greater than Level B. Levels of training greater than Level B may require expensive, time-consuming flight-simulator training, while Level B training can be completed anywhere in a matter of hours using a computer or tablet. According to one of Boeing's chief technical pilots, differences training above Level B could have cost Boeing and its customers "tens of millions of dollars."
context: Court describing Boeing's organizational objective that motivated the deception—framed as a cost-minimization goal endorsed at the engineering leadership level.

label: FAA AEG relied primarily on Boeing's chief technical pilots for MCAS information
original_label: FAA AEG relied primarily on Boeing's chief technical pilots for MCAS information
quote: The AEG principally relied on Boeing's chief technical pilots for information relevant to its 737 Max FSB Report, including for information necessary to determine the appropriate level of differences training the AEG would certify. Boeing's employees knew the agency relied on their input in making this certification decision but withheld from AEG the fact that MCAS could activate at low speeds, including during takeoffs and landings—a fact highly relevant for purposes of pilot training.
context: Court finding that the FAA's specialized dependence on Boeing's designated technical representatives created a structural vulnerability that Boeing's employees deliberately exploited.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: MCAS omission from FSB Report propagated through global training materials
original_label: MCAS omission from FSB Report propagated through global training materials
quote: The AEG also removed all references to MCAS from its FSB Report based upon Boeing's misrepresentations about the system's low-speed capabilities. On multiple occasions, Boeing employees concealed their knowledge of MCAS's low-speed expansion from AEG and suggested the agency remove all reference to MCAS in its FSB Report based on the misrepresentation that the system would not activate during routine flight operating procedures. AEG's Level B training certification and material omissions from the FSB Report, in turn, led to global adoption of equivalent training standards and distribution of training materials that made no mention of MCAS. Because the FSB Report omitted material information related to MCAS, U.S.-based airplane manuals and pilot-training materials, relying on the report, did not include related information about the system.
context: Court describing how the falsified FSB Report became embedded in formal documentation systems that cascaded globally, so the deception became institutionalized across the industry.

label: Industry-wide reliance on FAA as gold standard created expectation of cascade
original_label: Industry-wide reliance on FAA as gold standard created expectation of cascade
quote: Because the FSB Report omitted material information related to MCAS, U.S.-based airplane manuals and pilot-training materials, relying on the report, did not include related information about the system. By extension, foreign entities did the same. As a matter of common aviation industry practice, it is well-known that foreign airlines and foreign civil aviation authorities rely on the FAA's guidance regarding airplane certification, training requirements, and other relevant information. "The FAA is perceived to be the world's eminent aviation authority, the gold standard . . . and [] foreign carriers follow their lead."
context: Court citing expert testimony about shared industry understanding that FAA decisions would be automatically adopted globally, showing Boeing relied on this collective belief.

label: Boeing's admission of awareness that FAA guidance creates global compliance
original_label: Boeing's admission of awareness that FAA guidance creates global compliance
quote: Not only was this outcome generally foreseeable, Boeing admitted as much: "FAA is pretty powerful and most countries defer to what the FAA does[.]"
context: Court citing an internal Boeing email showing senior personnel explicitly acknowledged that false FAA guidance would propagate globally.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Boeing employees misrepresented MCAS as not activating during routine flight
original_label: Boeing employees misrepresented MCAS as not activating during routine flight
quote: On multiple occasions, Boeing employees concealed their knowledge of MCAS's low-speed expansion from AEG and suggested the agency remove all reference to MCAS in its FSB Report based on the misrepresentation that the system would not activate during routine flight operating procedures.
context: Court describing Boeing's deliberate mischaracterization of a system's operational envelope to falsely categorize it as outside the scope requiring pilot training.

label: Boeing continued misleading FAA even after first crash investigation began
original_label: Boeing continued misleading FAA even after first crash investigation began
quote: Importantly, during the FAA's investigation in the months following the first crash, Boeing's employees continued to mislead the government about their knowledge of MCAS.
context: Court noting that Boeing's deceptive practice persisted and escalated—not ending after the Lion Air crash but continuing through the investigation phase, leading to the second crash.

label: Sales force expansion approved to grow prescriptions
original_label: Sales force expansion approved to grow prescriptions
quote: In February, the Sacklers used their power on the Board of Directors to order Purdue to "begin expanding the sales force by an additional 100 sales representatives beginning effective as of April 1, 2008." The Sacklers knew and intended that, because of their orders, more sales reps would promote opioids to prescribers in Massachusetts. In preparation for the Sacklers' vote, staff told them that adding 100 sales reps would allow Purdue to make 12,000 more sales visits to prescribers every month.
context: Complaint narrative describing Board decision in 2008 to expand sales force by 100 reps after 2007 convictions, with explicit knowledge this would increase visits to prescribers.

label: Successive sales force expansions over decade
original_label: Successive sales force expansions over decade
quote: From the 2007 convictions until today, the Sacklers ordered Purdue to hire hundreds of sales reps to carry out their deceptive sales campaign. [Chart showing growth from ~300 reps in 2007 to ~600 reps by 2011]
context: Complaint summary of pattern showing repeated Board-authorized expansions of sales force each year from 2007-2018.

label: Higher doses become escalating sales target
original_label: Higher doses become escalating sales target
quote: Staff told the Sacklers that a key objective for 2010 would be to "Meet or exceed total prescriber call targets of 545,000" visits to prescribers to promote Purdue opioids. For the next four years or more, a key objective for the sales employees was to meet a quota of sales visits, and the Sacklers tracked their performance. The target rose from 545,000 prescriber visits in 2010, to 712,000 visits in 2011, 752,417 visits in 2012, and 744,777 visits in 2013.
context: Board reports to Sacklers showing escalating sales visit quotas maintained and expanded over successive years.

label: Dose climbing becomes sales strategy across products
original_label: Dose climbing becomes sales strategy across products
quote: Purdue tracked whether its sales reps were getting patients on higher doses and warned staff when doses were not increasing enough: "Titration up to higher strengths, especially the 40mg and 80mg strengths, is declining." Purdue required its sales reps to "practice verbalizing the titration message" to get patients' doses up. Purdue knew its promotion drove patients to higher doses. Purdue's internal analysis "found that there is greater loss in the 60mg and 80mg strengths (compared to other strengths) when we don't make primary sales calls."
context: Complaint describing Purdue's systematic tracking and reinforcement of dose escalation as core sales metric across sales organization.

label: Savings cards introduced then expanded to keep patients longer
original_label: Savings cards introduced then expanded to keep patients longer
quote: In June, staff reported to Richard, Jonathan, Kathe, and Mortimer Sackler that 67,951 patients had used Purdue's opioid savings cards, and that the cards provided a discount on a patient's first five prescriptions. After five prescriptions, many patients would face significant withdrawal symptoms if they tried to stop taking opioids. Staff told Richard, Jonathan, Kathe, and Mortimer Sackler that 27% of patients (more than 18,000 people) had used the cards for all five prescriptions.
context: Board reports showing Sacklers tracking use of savings cards as tool to extend duration of therapy over time.

label: Savings cards expanded with higher dollar value and longer period
original_label: Savings cards expanded with higher dollar value and longer period
quote: Staff told the Sacklers that they had increased the dollar value of opioid savings cards and set the program period to be 15 months long, in response to research showing the cards kept patients on opioids longer. Boer, Lewent, Pickett, and Costa also learned that Purdue was increasing the dollar value and set the program period to be 15 months long, in response to research showing the cards kept patients on opioids longer.
context: Board materials from 2013 showing iterative expansion of savings card incentive structure over prior years.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Pseudoaddiction reframed as indication for higher doses
original_label: Pseudoaddiction reframed as indication for higher doses
quote: Purdue presented to doctors a concept called "pseudoaddiction." A Purdue pamphlet titled Clinical Issues in Opioid Prescribing urged doctors to look for pseudoaddiction: "A term which has been used to describe patient behaviors that may occur when pain is undertreated. Patients with unrelieved pain may become focused on obtaining medications, may 'clock watch,' and may otherwise seem inappropriately 'drug-seeking.' Even such behaviors as illicit drug use and deception can occur in the patient's efforts to obtain relief. Pseudoaddiction can be distinguished from true addiction in that the behaviors resolve when the pain is effectively treated." Purdue again urged doctors to prescribe higher doses, stating that opioids "are frequently underdosed - or even withheld due to a widespread lack of information."
context: Complaint quoting Purdue educational materials that redefine addiction symptoms as inadequate dosing, justifying dose increases.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Physical dependence redefined as normal and acceptable
original_label: Physical dependence redefined as normal and acceptable
quote: To "extend average treatment duration," Purdue deceptively claimed that patients' becoming dependent on its drugs was not dangerous or deadly, but "normal." Purdue taught doctors that: "Healthcare professionals should recognize that tolerance and physical dependence are normal consequences of sustained use of opioid analgesics and are not the same as addiction." Purdue deceptively claimed that physical dependence on its opioids was "a normal physiologic response," "an expected occurrence," and no more dangerous than "many classes of medications" that are not addictive, including drugs used to treat high blood pressure.
context: Complaint describing Purdue's systematic redefinition of dependence as normal outcome rather than warning sign.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Blame patients for addiction rather than product
original_label: Blame patients for addiction rather than product
quote: In a pamphlet for doctors, Providing Relief, Preventing Abuse: A Reference Guide To Controlled Substance Prescribing Practices, Purdue wrote that addiction "is not caused by drugs." Instead, Purdue assured doctors that addiction happens when the wrong patients get drugs and abuse them: "it is triggered in a susceptible individual by exposure to drugs, most commonly through abuse." Purdue promoted its opioids to Massachusetts patients with marketing that was designed to obscure the risk of addiction. Over and over, Purdue told Massachusetts doctors and pharmacists that they could give opioids to "trusted" patients without risk of addiction, even though that was false.
context: Complaint quoting Purdue marketing materials that reframe addiction as patient characteristic rather than drug property.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Region Zero doctors tracked but not reported as suspicious
original_label: Region Zero doctors tracked but not reported as suspicious
quote: The Board — including Boer, Lewent, and Pickett — asked about the revenue from these doctors in order to make sure Purdue was maximizing its profits, and continued Purdue's policy of not disclosing Region Zero to patients, insurers, or the authorities. At that same Board meeting in Bermuda, Boer, Lewent, and Pickett voted with the Sacklers to hire 125 more sales reps by January 2011. Boer, Lewent, and Pickett knew and intended that the expanded sales force was promoting opioids in Massachusetts.
context: Complaint describing Board practice of tracking suspicious prescriber revenue while defining non-reporting as acceptable.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Sales visit quotas embedded in organizational targets
original_label: Sales visit quotas embedded in organizational targets
quote: The Sacklers required each rep to visit an average of 7.5 prescribers per day. In April 2010, staff reported that they were falling short. During Q1 2010, reps had averaged only 7.0 visits per day. Staff promised to try harder. The Sacklers continued to set a target for daily sales visits for every sales rep, and they tracked the results, quarter by quarter, for at least the next four years. The results were always close to 7 visits per day.
context: Complaint describing institutionalization of sales visit metrics as routine quarterly Board performance metric.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Sales performance plans mandate higher doses focus
original_label: Sales performance plans mandate higher doses focus
quote: Purdue put two other Massachusetts reps on probation and threatened to fire them because the doctors they visited did not put enough patients on opioids. Purdue told them that the only way they could keep their jobs was by generating more opioid sales. Purdue issued a performance enhancement plan to another Massachusetts sales rep that said: "Anticipated Challenges: Dr. trying to cut down on opioid prescribing due to abuse." "Action Steps: Sell for patients they are willing to Rx opioids …(elderly)." Purdue also ordered the rep to do a better job using gifts ("coffee, lunch") to buy time with Massachusetts prescribers.
context: Complaint describing embedded performance management system linking sales rep compensation and employment to higher prescriptions.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Opioid savings card program embedded in marketing budget
original_label: Opioid savings card program embedded in marketing budget
quote: Discounts could have cut Purdue's revenue if patients took opioids for a short time. But Purdue's internal 10-year plan highlighted its discovery that opioid savings cards kept patients on opioids longer: "more patients remain on OxyContin after 90 days." Purdue determined that opioid savings cards worked like the teaser rate on a long-term and very high-stakes mortgage. According to Purdue's internal analysis, the savings cards had the highest "return on investment" in the entire "OxyContin Marketing Mix." The return on investment for Purdue was 4.28, so that every $1,000,000 Purdue gave away in savings came back to Purdue as $4,280,000 in revenue because patients stayed on dangerous opioids longer.
context: Complaint describing savings cards as institutionalized profit-maximizing tactic with quantified ROI embedded in marketing plans.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: McKinsey analysis of high prescriber targeting embedded in budget
original_label: McKinsey analysis of high prescriber targeting embedded in budget
quote: In July and August, Boer, Lewent, Pickett, Costa, and Snyderman met, together with the Sacklers, to discuss the analyses that they had hired McKinsey to do, titled Identifying Granular Growth Opportunities for OxyContin. McKinsey recommended that they immediately order a series of actions to increase sales. McKinsey urged them to direct sales reps to visit the highest opioid prescribers, because prescribers in the most prolific group wrote 25 times more OxyContin scripts than the less prolific prescribers. McKinsey reported that sales rep visits to these prolific prescribers cause them to prescribe even more opioids.
context: Complaint describing external consultant analysis institutionalizing targeting of high prescribers as Board-approved strategy.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Individualize The Dose campaign embedded in annual sales strategy
original_label: Individualize The Dose campaign embedded in annual sales strategy
quote: Purdue created a campaign for OxyContin around the slogan, Individualize The Dose, because Purdue determined that it would Increase The Dose. Purdue's CEO prepared a presentation to the Board of Directors explaining that Purdue would use Individualize The Dose to sell more of its highest doses. When Purdue decided to refresh the campaign with a new slogan, it hired consultants to study what would increase doses the most.
context: Complaint describing core marketing campaign designed to drive dose escalation, institutionalized in annual Board presentations.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Sales rep bonuses tied to prescription volume metrics
original_label: Sales rep bonuses tied to prescription volume metrics
quote: The Sacklers voted to establish the company's scorecard for 2015: once again, the biggest factor determining employees' payout would be the total amount of Purdue opioid sales.
context: Complaint describing institutionalized compensation structure linking executive and sales rep bonuses to volume of opioid sales.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Massachusetts General Hospital partnership institutionalized to influence prescribers
original_label: Massachusetts General Hospital partnership institutionalized to influence prescribers
quote: The agreement establishing the program gave Purdue the right to influence education of doctors in Massachusetts by proposing "areas where education in the field of pain is needed" and "curriculum which might meet such needs." Purdue was also entitled to appoint a voting member of the Educational Program Committee and an advisor to the program's Oversight Board.
context: Complaint describing institutional arrangements giving Purdue formal power to shape medical education curriculum in Massachusetts.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Tufts University MSPREP program funded to influence curriculum
original_label: Tufts University MSPREP program funded to influence curriculum
quote: In 1980, three Sackler brothers, through a very large payment, established the Sackler School of Graduate Biomedical Sciences. Later, in 1999, the Sackler family made a more targeted gift, establishing Tufts Masters of Science in Pain Research, Education, and Policy ("MSPREP Program"). Kathe Sackler co-presided over the decision to fund the MSPREP Program. The Sacklers got a lot for their money. The MSPREP Program bought Purdue name recognition, goodwill in the local and medical communities, and access to doctors at Massachusetts hospitals. Purdue got to control research on the treatment of pain coming out of a prominent and respected institution of learning.
context: Complaint describing institutional relationships embedding Purdue influence into academic medical curriculum over decades.

label: Addiction blamed on patient characteristics not product
original_label: Addiction blamed on patient characteristics not product
quote: That same month, Richard Sackler wrote down his solution to the overwhelming evidence of overdose and death: blame and stigmatize people who become addicted to opioids. Sackler wrote in a confidential email: "we have to hammer on the abusers in every way possible. They are the culprits and the problem. They are reckless criminals."
context: Complaint quoting Richard Sackler's directive to blame addiction on patient behavior, establishing shared rationalization.

label: Euphemism replacing honest language about dependence
original_label: Euphemism replacing honest language about dependence
quote: Purdue secretly determined that pushing patients to higher doses would keep them on opioids longer. Purdue developed tactics specifically to keep patients hooked on opioids longer, which it called by the euphemism: "Improving the Length Of Therapy" — sometimes abbreviated as "LOT" or "LoT."
context: Complaint describing institutionalized euphemism disguising tactic to extend patient dependence on products.

label: Key messages normalize abuse-deterrent claims despite ineffectiveness
original_label: Key messages normalize abuse-deterrent claims despite ineffectiveness
quote: Staff prepared materials for sales reps that included this dangerous lie: "It's not addiction, it's abuse. It's about personal responsibility." label: Sales reps trained on deceptive messaging using standard scripts
original_label: Sales reps trained on deceptive messaging using standard scripts

label: Richard Sackler shadows sales reps to model tactics
original_label: Richard Sackler shadows sales reps to model tactics

original_label: Board approves sales force expansion despite knowing misconduct

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: Addiction risk minimized as 'less than one percent'
original_label: Addiction risk minimized as 'less than one percent'
quote: Purdue trained its sales representatives to carry the message that the risk of addiction was 'less than one percent.' The company cited studies by Porter and Jick, who found iatrogenic addiction in only 4 of 11882 patients using opioids and by Perry and Heidrich, who found no addiction among 10 000 burn patients treated with opioids. Both of these studies, although shedding some light on the risk of addiction for acute pain, do not help establish the risk of iatrogenic addiction when opioids are used daily for a prolonged time in treating chronic pain.
context: Van Zee documenting how Purdue redefined addiction risk by selectively citing acute-pain studies to support claims about chronic-pain use, converting established evidence standards.

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards
label: FDA label changed from 'very rare' addiction to 'data not available'
original_label: FDA label changed from 'very rare' addiction to 'data not available'
quote: When OxyContin entered the market in 1996, the FDA approved its original label, which stated that iatrogenic addiction was 'very rare' if opioids were legitimately used in the management of pain. In July 2001, to reflect the available scientific evidence, the label was modified to state that data were not available for establishing the true incidence of addiction in chronic-pain patients. The 2001 labeling also deleted the original statement that the delayed absorption of OxyContin was believed to reduce the abuse liability of the drug.
context: Van Zee showing how the FDA itself revised the regulatory definition of addiction risk in OxyContin's labeling, implicitly acknowledging earlier misstatement but institutionalizing the revised (weaker) standard.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Prescriber profiling embedded in marketing strategy to target high-prescribers
original_label: Prescriber profiling embedded in marketing strategy to target high-prescribers
quote: One of the cornerstones of Purdue's marketing plan was the use of sophisticated marketing data to influence physicians' prescribing. Drug companies compile prescriber profiles on individual physicians—detailing the prescribing patterns of physicians nationwide—in an effort to influence doctors' prescribing habits. Through these profiles, a drug company can identify the highest and lowest prescribers of particular drugs in a single zip code, county, state, or the entire country. One of the critical foundations of Purdue's marketing plan for OxyContin was to target the physicians who were the highest prescribers for opioids across the country.
context: Van Zee describing how Purdue systematized the targeting of high-volume opioid prescribers through data infrastructure and sales strategy, embedding the practice in formal marketing operations.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Bonus system tied to OxyContin sales increases for sales representatives
original_label: Bonus system tied to OxyContin sales increases for sales representatives

In 2001, in addition to the average sales representative's annual salary of $55 000, annual bonuses averaged $71500, with a range of $15 000 to nearly $240 000. Purdue paid $40 million in sales incentive bonuses to its sales representatives that year.
context: Van Zee documenting how Purdue embedded incentive structures into compensation systems to drive increased OxyContin prescribing, formalizing the strategy through budget allocation and performance metrics.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology
label: Free starter coupon program redeems 34,000 coupons nationally
original_label: Free starter coupon program redeems 34,000 coupons nationally

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology

original_label: Branded promotional items distributed as standard practice for Schedule II opioid

original_label: Over 40 national speaker-training conferences at resort locations

context: Van Zee showing how Purdue systematized physician training and recruitment through a formal speaker bureau infrastructure scaled across multiple sites and cohorts.

category: Institutionalization in routines, structures and technology

original_label: Purdue funded over 20,000 pain-related educational programs

original_label: Promotion of 'more liberal use of opioids' for chronic pain

quote: From 1996 to 2001, Purdue conducted more than 40 national pain-management and speaker-training conferences at resorts in Florida, Arizona, and California. quote: Through these profiles, a drug company can identify the highest and lowest prescribers of particular drugs in a single zip code, county, state, or the entire country. label: $40 million in annual sales bonuses to drive OxyContin sales

original_label: Company spending six to twelve times more on OxyContin than prior opioid products

label: OxyContin became most frequently prescribed brand-name opioid despite no superiority
original_label: OxyContin became most frequently prescribed brand-name opioid despite no superiority

category: Redefinition of acceptable risk and standards

context: Van Zee showing that the FDA's own internal review found no clinical superiority for OxyContin, yet this finding did not prevent approval or later aggressive promotion.

label: High opioid prescribing regions normalized as 'pain management' areas
original_label: High opioid prescribing regions normalized as 'pain management' areas

In some areas, such as Maine, West Virginia, eastern Kentucky, southwestern Virginia, and Alabama, from 1998 through 2000, hydrocodone and (non-OxyContin) oxycodone were being prescribed 2.5 to 5.0 times more than the national average.
